question: A patient taking an antimuscarinic drug reports reduced sweating. Which statement best classifies the three muscle-cell types of the muscular system as described in this review?

choices.text: Skeletal muscle is voluntary; cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary.
Skeletal and cardiac muscle are voluntary; smooth muscle is involuntary.
All three muscle types are under voluntary somatic control.
Cardiac muscle is voluntary; skeletal and smooth muscle are involuntary.

sourceQuote: skeletal (voluntary), cardiac (involuntary), and smooth muscle (involuntary)
explanationCorrect: The review classifies skeletal muscle as voluntary and both cardiac and smooth muscle as involuntary.

explanationWrong.B: Cardiac muscle is classified as involuntary, not voluntary.
explanationWrong.C: Only skeletal muscle is described as voluntary.
explanationWrong.D: Cardiac muscle is involuntary; skeletal muscle is the voluntary type.

question: When counseling on systemic hormone replacement, which anatomic feature of endocrine glands best explains why their secretions reach distant target tissues without a ductal delivery system?

choices.text: They empty secretions into the GI lumen via specialized ducts.
They store hormones in lymph nodes until local release.
They are ductless glands that secrete specific hormones directly into the bloodstream.
They release hormones only onto adjacent epithelial surfaces.

sourceQuote: ductless glands that secrete specific hormones directly into the bloodstream
explanationCorrect: The endocrine system is defined as ductless glands that secrete specific hormones directly into the bloodstream.

explanationWrong.A: Ductal emptying into the GI lumen describes exocrine, not endocrine, secretion.
explanationWrong.B: The review does not describe lymph-node storage as the endocrine delivery mechanism.
explanationWrong.D: Endocrine hormones enter blood for systemic distribution, not only adjacent surfaces.

question: A topical corticosteroid must traverse the outer skin before reaching dermal vasculature. Which pairing correctly identifies the two principal layers of skin?

choices.text: Outer dermis (connective tissue) and inner epidermis (epithelium)
Outer epidermis (epithelial layer) and inner dermis (connective tissue)
Outer hypodermis (adipose) and inner periosteum (bone covering)
Outer fascia (muscle sheath) and inner serosa (mesothelium)

sourceQuote: outer epithelial layer, called the epidermis, and an inner connective tissue
explanationCorrect: Skin consists of an outer epithelial epidermis and an inner connective-tissue dermis.

explanationWrong.A: The epidermis is the outer epithelial layer; the dermis is the inner connective tissue.
explanationWrong.C: Hypodermis and periosteum are not the two layers named for skin in this passage.
explanationWrong.D: Fascia and serosa are not the skin layers described here.

question: A calcium-channel blocker relaxing vascular tone acts on which muscle type, based on location and histologic features in this review?

choices.text: Multinucleated voluntary skeletal muscle attached to bone
Striated involuntary cardiac muscle confined to the heart
Multinucleated involuntary muscle lining alveolar sacs
Uninucleated involuntary smooth muscle in walls of hollow organs, including blood vessels

sourceQuote: Smooth muscle is located in the walls of hollow organs
explanationCorrect: Smooth muscle cells are uninucleated and involuntary and are located in walls of hollow organs such as blood vessels, stomach, intestines, bladder, and uterus.

explanationWrong.A: Skeletal muscle is voluntary and moves the skeleton, not vascular walls.
explanationWrong.B: Cardiac muscle is striated and limited to the heart, not vessel walls.
explanationWrong.C: The review does not describe multinucleated involuntary muscle in alveolar sacs.

question: Cholinesterase inhibitors used in myasthenia gravis prolong the action of the transmitter released at the motor end plate. Which transmitter is identified at that synapse?

choices.text: Acetylcholine released from the axon terminal into the synaptic cleft
Norepinephrine released from muscle-cell vesicles into the T-tubule
GABA released from periosteal sensory endings onto myofibrils
Dopamine released from red marrow into the neuromuscular junction

sourceQuote: releases a neurotransmitter (usually acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft
explanationCorrect: At the motor end plate, the axon terminal releases a neurotransmitter, usually acetylcholine, into the synaptic cleft.

explanationWrong.B: The neuromuscular junction transmitter named here is acetylcholine, not norepinephrine from T-tubules.
explanationWrong.C: GABA is not identified as the motor-end-plate transmitter.
explanationWrong.D: Dopamine from marrow is not the neuromuscular-junction transmitter described.

question: When distinguishing axial from appendicular injury on an imaging report, which structures compose the axial skeleton?

choices.text: Upper and lower extremities plus the pectoral and pelvic girdles
Only the ribs and sternum, excluding the vertebral column
The skull and vertebral column
Only the pectoral girdle and the bones of the hand

sourceQuote: The axial skeleton consists of the skull and vertebral column
explanationCorrect: The skeleton is subdivided into axial and appendicular units; the axial skeleton consists of the skull and vertebral column.

explanationWrong.A: Those bones constitute the appendicular skeleton, not the axial skeleton.
explanationWrong.B: The axial skeleton is defined here as skull and vertebral column, not ribs and sternum alone.
explanationWrong.D: The pectoral girdle and hand belong to the appendicular skeleton.

question: A chest radiograph shows ribs that do not reach the sternum and lack costal cartilages. Which ribs match that description?

choices.text: True ribs 1–7, which link directly to the sternum via costal cartilages
Floating ribs 11–12, which have no costal cartilages and do not attach to the sternum
False ribs 8–10, whose cartilages merge with the seventh rib cartilage
All twelve pairs, because each rib attaches independently to the xiphoid

sourceQuote: Floating (11–12) ribs have no costal cartilages and do not attach to the sternum
explanationCorrect: Floating (11–12) ribs have no costal cartilages and do not attach to the sternum.

explanationWrong.A: True ribs 1–7 attach directly to the sternum via costal cartilages.
explanationWrong.C: False ribs 8–10 have cartilages that merge with the seventh rib, so they are not cartilage-free floating ribs.
explanationWrong.D: Rib types differ; only floating ribs lack sternal attachment via costal cartilage.

question: Atherosclerotic injury to the innermost vascular lining can precipitate thrombosis and stroke. Which layer is implicated, and why is it vulnerable?

choices.text: The adventitia, because it is the thickest arterial layer of elastic laminae
The media of veins only, because veins lack any endothelial lining
The vasa vasorum, because it is the sole site of platelet adhesion
The intima, where mechanical damage or calcium and fatty deposits may cause blood clots

sourceQuote: accumulation of calcium and fatty deposits in the intima may cause blood clots
explanationCorrect: Mechanical damage or accumulation of calcium and fatty deposits in the intima may cause blood clots that can lead to strokes or coronary artery disease.

explanationWrong.A: The media, not the adventitia, is the thickest layer in arteries; clotting is attributed to intimal injury.
explanationWrong.B: The review does not locate atherothrombosis exclusively in venous media or deny an endothelial lining.
explanationWrong.C: The vasa vasorum is not identified as the clotting layer in this passage.

question: A central line terminating in the superior vena cava delivers drug into which cardiac chamber first, and what is the oxygenation status of that blood?

choices.text: Right atrium, which receives deoxygenated blood via the superior and inferior venae cavae
Left atrium, which receives deoxygenated blood via the pulmonary trunk
Right ventricle, which receives oxygenated blood via four pulmonary veins
Left ventricle, which receives deoxygenated blood via the tricuspid valve

sourceQuote: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the head
explanationCorrect: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the head, neck, and upper extremities through the SVC and from the rest of the body through the IVC.

explanationWrong.B: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins, not deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk.
explanationWrong.C: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium; pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium.
explanationWrong.D: The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium, not via the tricuspid valve.

question: After thoracic-duct ligation, lymph from most of the body would fail to re-enter venous blood at which named confluence?

choices.text: The right atrium via the inferior vena cava
The portal vein at the porta hepatis
The left brachiocephalic vein
The pulmonary trunk distal to the pulmonic valve

sourceQuote: The thoracic duct empties lymph into the left brachiocephalic vein
explanationCorrect: The thoracic duct, one of the largest lymph vessels, empties lymph into the left brachiocephalic vein.

explanationWrong.A: The thoracic duct is not described as emptying into the IVC or right atrium.
explanationWrong.B: Portal venous return is hepatic, not the thoracic-duct terminus named here.
explanationWrong.D: The pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle, not returning lymph.

question: A pharmacist reviewing a pre-op note sees planned resection of the right middle lobe. Which fissure anatomy supports the existence of that lobe on the right but not the left?

choices.text: Both lungs are divided into three lobes by a single oblique fissure only.
The right lung is divided into three lobes by the horizontal and oblique fissures; the left lung has two lobes divided by the oblique fissure.
The left lung has three lobes; the right lung has two lobes and no fissures.
Lobar division is determined by the diaphragm, not by fissures.

sourceQuote: The right lung is divided into three lobes by the horizontal and oblique fissures
explanationCorrect: The left lung has two lobes divided by the oblique fissure, whereas the right lung has three lobes divided by the horizontal and oblique fissures.

explanationWrong.A: Only the right lung has three lobes; the left is divided into two by the oblique fissure.
explanationWrong.C: The right lung, not the left, has three lobes.
explanationWrong.D: Lobar anatomy is described via fissures, not the diaphragm.

question: An oral α-amylase inhibitor is intended to act at the anatomic site where carbohydrate digestion first begins. Where does that process start, and which enzyme is named?

choices.text: In the mouth, where salivary amylase initially breaks down carbohydrates
In the gallbladder, where bile salts hydrolyze starch to glucose
In the sigmoid colon, where pancreatic lipase digests glycogen
In the portal vein, where hepatic amylase degrades circulating sucrose

sourceQuote: digestion begins in the mouth, where carbohydrates are initially broken down by amylase
explanationCorrect: Salivary glands produce amylase, and carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth.

explanationWrong.B: Bile is a fatty emulsifier from the liver/gallbladder, not the initiator of starch hydrolysis.
explanationWrong.C: The colon is not identified as the start of carbohydrate digestion, and lipase is not amylase.
explanationWrong.D: The portal vein delivers absorbed nutrients to the liver; it is not the site where digestion begins.

question: After bile is secreted by the liver, where is it stored and concentrated, and with which structure does the common hepatic duct join to form the common bile duct?

choices.text: It is stored in the pancreas and joins the thoracic duct
It is stored in the spleen and joins the portal vein
It is stored in the duodenum and joins the right hepatic artery
It is stored in the gall bladder; the common hepatic duct joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct

sourceQuote:
liver, it is stored and concentrated in the
gall bladder. Right and
explanationCorrect: Bile is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct, which joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct attaching to the descending duodenum.

explanationWrong.A: The pancreas and thoracic duct are not the storage or joining structures given.
explanationWrong.B: The spleen and portal vein are not described as storing bile or forming the CBD.
explanationWrong.C: Bile is not stored in the duodenum; the CBD attaches to the descending duodenum.

question: The portal vein supplying intestinal venous blood to the liver is formed by the juncture of which vessels?

choices.text: Right and left hepatic arteries
The superior mesenteric and splenic veins
The cystic duct and common hepatic duct
The inferior vena cava and hepatic veins

sourceQuote:
as a result of juncture of the superior
mesenteric and splenic veins.
explanationCorrect: The portal vein is formed by juncture of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins and supplies venous blood from the intestines as part of the hepatic triad; arterial supply is via the proper hepatic branch of the celiac trunk.

explanationWrong.A: Hepatic arteries are the arterial supply, not the veins that form the portal vein.
explanationWrong.C: Those ducts form the common bile duct, not the portal vein.
explanationWrong.D: IVC and hepatic veins are not described as forming the portal vein.

question: Insulin secretagogues target the pancreatic cells that perform the gland’s endocrine function. Which statement matches this review?

choices.text: Acinar cells in the tail secrete gastrin into the gastric lumen.
Chief cells of the pancreas secrete pepsinogen as the sole pancreatic hormone.
The pancreas is purely exocrine; insulin is produced only in the duodenum.
Islet pancreatic cells secrete insulin, while pancreatic ducts empty digestive enzymes into the second part of the duodenum.

sourceQuote: The islet pancreatic cells secrete insulin. The pancreas contains both
explanationCorrect: The pancreas is both endocrine and exocrine: islet cells secrete insulin, and pancreatic ducts empty enzymes into the second part of the duodenum.

explanationWrong.A: Gastrin is listed among intestinal mucosal hormones, not as the islet product named here.
explanationWrong.B: Pepsinogen is not identified as a pancreatic hormone in this passage.
explanationWrong.C: The pancreas is explicitly both endocrine and exocrine and produces insulin.

question: Enteric-coated aspirin is intended to leave the acidic stomach before dissolving. How does the duodenal chemical environment differ from that of the stomach?

choices.text: The duodenum is more acidic than gastric contents because it receives unbuffered HCl only.
The duodenum and stomach are both strongly acidic throughout digestion.
In contrast to gastric acidity, the chemical environment of the duodenum is basic.
The duodenum is chemically inert because bile and pancreatic juice are withheld until the ileum.

sourceQuote: the chemical environment of the duodenum is basic
explanationCorrect: The second part of the duodenum receives bile and pancreatic secretions, and unlike the acidic stomach, the duodenal environment is basic.

explanationWrong.A: The review contrasts duodenal basicity with gastric acidity; it does not describe a more acidic duodenum.
explanationWrong.B: The stomach is acidic; the duodenum is described as basic.
explanationWrong.D: The hepatopancreatic ampulla delivers bile and pancreatic ducts into the second part of the duodenum.

question: Appendicitis is an inflammatory disease of a cecal diverticulum. What lymphoid feature of the vermiform appendix is emphasized?

choices.text: It is a sterile muscular sphincter without immune cells.
It is filled with lymph nodules and lymphocytes.
It stores bile and secretes amylase into the ileum.
It is a retroperitoneal continuation of the left colic flexure.

sourceQuote: It is filled with lymph nodules and lymphocytes
explanationCorrect: The vermiform appendix is a worm-like diverticulum of the cecum filled with lymph nodules and lymphocytes.

explanationWrong.A: The appendix is described as lymphoid-rich, not as a sterile sphincter.
explanationWrong.C: Bile storage is a gallbladder function, not an appendiceal function.
explanationWrong.D: The appendix attaches to the cecum in the right lower quadrant, not the left colic flexure.

question: Local anesthetics slow axonal conduction. Which axon property is stated to increase action-potential speed?

choices.text: Myelination; the action potential of myelinated axons is faster than that of unmyelinated axons.
Absence of myelin, which increases capacitive current along the axon.
Replacement of sodium channels with only chloride channels.
Exclusive use of dendrites rather than axons to carry efferent output.

sourceQuote: The action potential of myelinated axons is faster than that of unmyelinated axons
explanationCorrect: Myelin is a protein-fatty insulating material, and myelinated axons conduct action potentials faster than unmyelinated axons.

explanationWrong.B: Unmyelinated axons are slower, not faster, according to this review.
explanationWrong.C: Action-potential generation is attributed to gated sodium and potassium channels, not chloride-only substitution.
explanationWrong.D: Axons, not dendrites, generally carry efferent activity away from the cell body.

question: A patient after a stroke has impaired planning and mental integration with relatively spared primary vision. Which cortical region is assigned higher cortical activity in this review?

choices.text: Occipital lobe, described here as the sole site of mental integration
Cerebellar white matter, which contains the lateral ventricles
Primary olfactory bulb, which forms gyri of the parietal lobe
Frontal lobe, which provides higher cortical activity or mental integration

sourceQuote: The frontal lobe functions to provide higher cortical activity or mental integration
explanationCorrect: The frontal lobe is described as providing higher cortical activity or mental integration.

explanationWrong.A: The occipital lobe is not assigned that integrative role in this passage.
explanationWrong.B: Lateral ventricles are CSF-filled cavities of each cerebral hemisphere, not cerebellar white matter.
explanationWrong.C: The olfactory bulb is not described as forming parietal gyri here.

question: Central analgesic pathways are often discussed at the level where pain first reaches consciousness. According to this review, where does that occur?

choices.text: Exclusively in the occipital lobe, where light also comes into consciousness
At thalamic levels
Only in the amygdala, which is confined to the frontal pole
Solely in the hypothalamus, which is the primary visual center

sourceQuote: the spinal cord. Pain comes into consciousness at thalamic levels
explanationCorrect: The dorsal thalamus is a major synaptic relay, and pain comes into consciousness at thalamic levels.

explanationWrong.A: The occipital lobe is the visual center; pain consciousness is assigned to the thalamus.
explanationWrong.C: The amygdala is an emotional center in the temporal lobe, not the site named for pain consciousness.
explanationWrong.D: The hypothalamus is not described as the primary visual center or as the site of pain consciousness.

question: Opioid-induced respiratory depression and some sudden infant death discussions implicate caudal brainstem nuclei. Which structure is linked to cardiac and respiratory control, and to SIDS when developmentally defective?

choices.text: The cerebellar cortex, which contains only visual relay nuclei
The dorsal root ganglia, which generate the respiratory rhythm
The medulla oblongata, whose nuclei control cardiac function and respiration
The frontal lobe gyri, which directly innervate alveolar smooth muscle

sourceQuote: nuclei that are related to control of cardiac function and respiration
explanationCorrect: The medulla oblongata is the most caudal brainstem component and contains nuclei related to cardiac function and respiration; defects in this complex have been implicated in SIDS.

explanationWrong.A: Cardiac and respiratory control nuclei are assigned to the medulla, not the cerebellar cortex.
explanationWrong.B: Dorsal root ganglia are spinal sensory ganglia, not the medullary respiratory controller described here.
explanationWrong.D: The frontal lobe is not identified as the cardiac-respiratory nuclear complex.

question: Epidural anesthetics act near mixed spinal nerves formed from dorsal and ventral roots. How many pairs of spinal nerves attach to the cord, and what is the motor root?

choices.text: Thirty-one pairs; ventral root fibers are motor (efferent)
Twelve pairs; only cranial nerves carry motor fibers
Twenty-four pairs; ventral roots are purely sensory
Eight pairs; dorsal and ventral roots never unite

sourceQuote: Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves are attached bilaterally to the spinal cord
explanationCorrect: Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves attach bilaterally; more distally, dorsal and ventral roots unite into mixed nerves, and ventral root fibers are motor or efferent.

explanationWrong.B: Twelve pairs refers to cranial nerves, not the spinal-nerve count given here.
explanationWrong.C: The count is 31 pairs, and ventral roots are motor, not purely sensory.
explanationWrong.D: Dorsal and ventral roots do unite to form a single mixed spinal nerve.

question: A pheochromocytoma arising from adrenal medullary cells would be expected to secrete which catecholamines, given the histologic origin described here?

choices.text: Only mineralocorticoids that regulate plasma glucose
Only parathyroid hormone that lowers serum calcium
Only estrogen and progesterone from cortical follicles
Epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine from neuron-like medullary cells

sourceQuote: secrete the hormones epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine. Ovaries The ovary
explanationCorrect: Adrenal medullary cells are neuronal in appearance and secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine; glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and androgens come from the cortex.

explanationWrong.A: Mineralocorticoids are cortical and regulate electrolytes, not medullary catecholamines.
explanationWrong.B: PTH is a parathyroid product that regulates blood calcium, not an adrenal medullary hormone.
explanationWrong.C: Estrogen and progesterone are ovarian follicular hormones, not adrenal medullary secretions.

question: Androgen-replacement therapy mimics the testicular hormone that produces male secondary sex characteristics. Which cells synthesize and release that hormone?

choices.text: Sertoli cells of the adrenal medulla
Interstitial cells of Leydig in highly vascular testicular connective tissue
Principal cells of the distal nephron
Chief cells of the parathyroid capsule

sourceQuote: produced and released by the interstitial cells of Leydig, which are located
explanationCorrect: Testosterone, responsible for male secondary sex characteristics, is produced and released by the interstitial cells of Leydig.

explanationWrong.A: Leydig cells are testicular, not adrenal medullary Sertoli cells.
explanationWrong.C: Nephron principal cells are not identified as the source of testosterone.
explanationWrong.D: Parathyroid chief cells secrete PTH, not testosterone.

question: Combined hormonal contraceptives are taken continuously to suppress the ovarian cycle. What mechanism is stated for that effect?

choices.text: They destroy mature ova stored in the uterine endometrium.
They stimulate a mid-cycle LH surge that forces daily ovulation.
Chronic presence of progesterone and estrogen hormones prevents ovulation.
They convert ovarian follicles into testosterone-secreting Leydig cells.

sourceQuote: chronic presence of progesterone and estrogen hormones that prevent ovulation
explanationCorrect: Hormonal contraception is based on the chronic presence of progesterone and estrogen hormones that prevent ovulation.

explanationWrong.A: The uterine cycle is endometrial buildup and shedding coordinated by ovarian hormones, not ovum destruction in the endometrium.
explanationWrong.B: The review describes prevention of ovulation, not daily forced ovulation.
explanationWrong.D: Leydig cells are male interstitial cells; they are not a contraceptive mechanism.

question: A patient on a loop diuretic develops muscle weakness and a low serum potassium. Which electrolyte disorder and mechanism match this review?

choices.text: Hypokalemia from diuretics that cause the kidneys to excrete excess potassium
Hyperkalemia from vitamin D deficiency reducing intestinal potassium absorption
Hyponatremia caused solely by excess parathyroid hormone
Hypercalcemia caused by diuretic-driven urinary potassium wasting

sourceQuote: the result of the use of diuretics, which cause the kidneys to excrete excess potassium
explanationCorrect: Hypokalemia is a low potassium level that may result from diuretics that increase renal potassium excretion.

explanationWrong.B: Hyperkalemia is high potassium from reduced renal excretion or potassium supplements, not vitamin D deficiency as stated here.
explanationWrong.C: Hyponatremia is low sodium; PTH disorders are linked to calcium, not this diuretic-potassium scenario.
explanationWrong.D: Diuretic potassium wasting is linked to hypokalemia, not hypercalcemia.

question: When comparing eukaryotic animal cells with plant cells for a pharmaceutics discussion of cell walls, which organelles or structures are restricted to plant cells?

choices.text: Mitochondria and rough endoplasmic reticulum
Nucleus and lysosomes
Integral membrane proteins and the glycocalyx
Chloroplasts and the cell wall

sourceQuote: Chloroplasts and the cell wall are found only in plant cells
explanationCorrect: Among listed organelles, chloroplasts and the cell wall are found only in plant cells.

explanationWrong.A: Mitochondria and ER are not described as plant-only in this passage.
explanationWrong.B: The nucleus and lysosomes are listed as cellular organelles, not as plant-exclusive structures.
explanationWrong.C: The glycocalyx and integral proteins are features of the cell membrane generally, not plant-only structures.

question: A drug that inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis acts at membranes that bear ribosomes. Which organelle is assigned protein translation in this review?

choices.text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which is involved in lipid metabolism
Rough endoplasmic reticulum, which contains ribosomes and is involved with protein translation
Lysosomes, which form the mitotic spindle
Microtubules, which store and secrete digestive enzymes

sourceQuote: rough endoplasmic reticulum and is involved with protein translation
explanationCorrect: Membranes with ribosomes constitute rough ER and are involved with protein translation; smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is often involved in lipid metabolism.

explanationWrong.A: Smooth ER is linked to lipid metabolism, not protein translation.
explanationWrong.C: Lysosomes digest proteins and carbohydrates; microtubules form the mitotic spindle.
explanationWrong.D: Microtubules form the mitotic spindle; vesicles are involved in storage and secretion.

question: Beta-blockers used for rate control act on the structure this review identifies as the heart’s natural pacemaker. Which structure is that?

choices.text: The atrioventricular bundle within the I-band
The periosteum of the sternum
The sinoatrial node
The osteoblast lining of the endosteum

sourceQuote: The sinoatrial node (natural pacemaker) is located in which of the following regions
explanationCorrect: The review identifies the sinoatrial node as the natural pacemaker of the heart.

explanationWrong.A: The I-band is a myofilament region of skeletal muscle, not the named pacemaker.
explanationWrong.B: Periosteum is the vascular connective envelope of bone, not the cardiac pacemaker.
explanationWrong.D: Osteoblasts build bone matrix; they are not the heart’s pacemaker.

question: At the neuromuscular junction, the transmitter used by skeletal muscle is released from which neuronal compartment?

choices.text: The axon terminal
The renal hilus
The portal vein lumen
The sigmoid colon mucosa

sourceQuote: released from the axon terminal of the neuromuscular junction
explanationCorrect: The review frames neuromuscular-junction transmission as neurotransmitter release from the axon terminal.

explanationWrong.B: The hilus is a renal landmark, not the NMJ release site.
explanationWrong.C: The portal vein delivers blood to the liver; it is not the NMJ terminal.
explanationWrong.D: Colonic mucosa is not the site of motor-end-plate transmitter release.

question: Pulmonary drug delivery and gas-exchange physiology both depend on which pair of gases this review describes as being exchanged in the respiratory system?

choices.text: Nitrogen and helium only
Ammonia and urea only
Methane and carbon monoxide only
Gaseous oxygen and carbon dioxide

sourceQuote: Gaseous oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged in which level of the respiratory system
explanationCorrect: The review describes gaseous oxygen and carbon dioxide as the gases exchanged in the respiratory system.

explanationWrong.A: Nitrogen and helium are not the exchanged pair named here.
explanationWrong.B: Ammonia and urea are nitrogenous metabolites, not the respiratory gases identified.
explanationWrong.C: Methane and carbon monoxide are not the gases named for respiratory exchange in this item.

question: Bisphosphonates are used in states of excessive bone resorption. Which cell type is identified as actively building bone matrix, in contrast to brain glial cells?

choices.text: Osteoclasts, which the review states are confined to the epidermis
Osteoblasts, which actively build bone matrix
Glial cells, which secrete osteoid in the marrow cavity
Chondrocytes of the cecum, which mineralize cortical bone

sourceQuote: Osteoblasts actively build bone matrix. Glial cells are located in the brain
explanationCorrect: Osteoblasts actively build bone matrix; glial cells are located in the brain and help maintain other neuronal cells.

explanationWrong.A: The answer key identifies osteoblasts, not osteoclasts, as the matrix-building cells.
explanationWrong.C: Glial cells are brain support cells, not osteoid-secreting bone cells.
explanationWrong.D: The cecum is part of the colon, not a bone-forming organ in this review.

question: This anatomy chapter’s editor’s note credits which author as the writer of the corresponding 1st-edition chapter?

choices.text: Eldridge F. Johnson
Michael C. Storm
Katherine S. Barker
Bradley A. Boucher

sourceQuote: the 1st edition chapter written by Eldridge F. Johnson
explanationCorrect: The editor’s note states that this chapter is based on the 1st edition chapter written by Eldridge F. Johnson.

explanationWrong.B: Michael C. Storm is not the 1st-edition anatomy author named on this page.
explanationWrong.C: Katherine S. Barker is not credited here as the prior anatomy chapter author.
explanationWrong.D: Bradley A. Boucher is not the 1st-edition author named in this note.

question: A missense mutation is most directly a change in which element of protein structure, as defined in this review?

choices.text: Quaternary structure only, defined as isolated cofactor binding
Secondary structure only, defined as the Michaelis constant Km
Primary structure, the linear amino acid sequence
Vmax, which is listed as a folding motif of alpha helices

sourceQuote: primary (linear amino acid sequence), secondary (alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets)
explanationCorrect: Protein structure has four elements; primary structure is the linear amino acid sequence, so a sequence change is a primary-structure alteration.

explanationWrong.A: Quaternary structure is a multisubunit protein complex, not merely cofactor binding.
explanationWrong.B: Secondary structure refers to alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets, not Km.
explanationWrong.D: Vmax is a kinetic parameter of enzymes, not a protein-folding motif.

question: Among biologics in the pipeline, which recombinant product class is identified as one of the largest areas of new therapeutics in development?

choices.text: Inhaled mineralocorticoid crystals
Monoclonal antibodies produced by recombinant technology
Short-chain fatty acid prodrugs only
Unmodified dietary cellulose fibers

sourceQuote: Monoclonal antibodies produced by recombinant technology are one of the largest areas of new therapeutics currently in development
explanationCorrect: The review states that recombinant monoclonal antibodies are one of the largest areas of new therapeutics currently in development.

explanationWrong.A: Mineralocorticoid crystals are not identified as that leading development class.
explanationWrong.C: Short-chain fatty acid prodrugs are not the recombinant class named here.
explanationWrong.D: Cellulose is a plant polymer in the biomolecule checklist, not the leading recombinant therapeutic class.

question: A nutrition-support pharmacist classifying building-block nutrients should group which four biomolecules as the major classes named in this introduction?

choices.text: Ketone bodies, urea, bilirubin, and creatinine
Only ATP, GTP, UTP, and CTP
Collagen, keratin, actin, and myosin exclusively
Amino acids, fatty acids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids

sourceQuote: The major four groups of biomolecules are amino acids, fatty acids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids
explanationCorrect: The major four groups of biomolecules are amino acids, fatty acids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids, which form proteins/enzymes, lipids, glycogen, RNA, and DNA.

explanationWrong.A: Those are metabolites, not the four major biomolecule groups named.
explanationWrong.B: Nucleotide triphosphates are not listed as the four major biomolecule groups.
explanationWrong.C: Those are proteins (macromolecules), not the four building-block groups.

question: When interpreting a single-letter protein sequence, which one-letter abbreviation is tabulated for lysine?

choices.text: K
L
I
H

sourceQuote: Isoleucine Ile I Leucine Leu L Lysine Lys K
explanationCorrect: In the table of common protein-incorporated amino acids, lysine (Lys) is abbreviated K; L is leucine, I isoleucine, and H histidine.

explanationWrong.B: L is the one-letter code listed for leucine, not lysine.
explanationWrong.C: I is listed for isoleucine.
explanationWrong.D: H is listed for histidine.

question: Maple-syrup urine disease involves the branched-chain amino acids. Which set is classified as branched-chain in this review?

choices.text: Glycine, alanine, and serine
Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan
Valine, leucine, and isoleucine
Cysteine and methionine only

sourceQuote: Branched-chain: Valine (Val), leucine (Leu), and isoleucine (Ile)
explanationCorrect: Branched-chain amino acids are valine, leucine, and isoleucine.

explanationWrong.A: Glycine and alanine are classified as small amino acids.
explanationWrong.B: Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are the aromatic group.
explanationWrong.D: Cysteine and methionine are the sulfur-containing amino acids.

question: N-acetylcysteine repletes a first-line cellular antioxidant tripeptide. From which three amino acids is that tripeptide formed?

choices.text: Arginine, ornithine, and citrulline of the urea cycle only
Glutamine, cysteine, and glycine, forming glutathione
Histidine, isoleucine, and tryptophan exclusively
Tyrosine, phenylalanine, and methionine only

sourceQuote: antioxidant formed from the amino acids glutamine, cysteine, and glycine
explanationCorrect: Glutathione is a first-line cellular antioxidant tripeptide formed from glutamine, cysteine, and glycine.

explanationWrong.A: Arginine, ornithine, and citrulline are the urea-cycle amino acids, not the glutathione tripeptide.
explanationWrong.C: Those are essential amino acids but not the glutathione constituents named.
explanationWrong.D: Tyr, Phe, and Met are not the three residues specified for glutathione.

question: Allosteric oxygen binding by hemoglobin is cited as an advantage of which level of protein organization?

choices.text: Primary sequence alone, without subunit interaction
Isolated disulfide bonds that prevent any subunit assembly
Random coil only, which abolishes cooperativity
Quaternary structure, which allows greater regulation of transport function such as hemoglobin and oxygen delivery

sourceQuote: hemoglobin and oxygen delivery) and enzyme activity (i.e., cooperativity
explanationCorrect: Quaternary structure is a multisubunit complex that allows greater regulation of transport (hemoglobin and oxygen delivery) and enzyme activity, including cooperativity.

explanationWrong.A: The review attributes cooperativity and oxygen-delivery regulation to quaternary structure, not primary sequence alone.
explanationWrong.B: Disulfide bonds are discussed as aiding folding at the tertiary level, not as blocking subunit assembly.
explanationWrong.C: Random coil is not described as the hemoglobin regulatory architecture.

question: Sickle cell disease illustrates how a coding SNP can change hemoglobin function. What residue substitution in beta globin is described?

choices.text: Valine replaces glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta globin chain
Lysine replaces glycine at the N-terminus of alpha globin only
Cysteine replaces proline throughout both globin chains
The entire beta globin gene is deleted, leaving only myoglobin

sourceQuote: a glutamic acid at the sixth position in the beta globin protein chain
explanationCorrect: Normal adult hemoglobin has glutamic acid at beta-globin position 6; a single-point mutation (A–T) places valine there, distorting the hemoglobin tetramer and red-cell shape.

explanationWrong.B: The described substitution is Glu to Val at beta-globin position 6, not a lysine-for-glycine change in alpha globin.
explanationWrong.C: A global cysteine-for-proline swap is not the sickle mutation described.
explanationWrong.D: The review describes a point mutation, not deletion of the entire beta-globin gene.

question: Kinase inhibitors used in oncology interfere with a common post-translational modification that acts as an enzymatic on–off switch. Which modification is that, and on which residues is it listed?

choices.text: Formylation of alanine, glycine, isoleucine, and valine only
GPI anchoring of the amino terminus as the sole on–off mechanism
Phosphorylation of Ser, Thr, Tyr, or Asp, commonly as an on–off switch to regulate enzyme activity
Hydroxylation of every residue except Pro and Lys in collagen

sourceQuote: Phosphorylation (commonly as an on–off switch to regulate enzyme activity)
explanationCorrect: Phosphorylation of Ser, Thr, Tyr, or Asp is commonly an on–off switch regulating enzyme activity.

explanationWrong.A: The table notes no post-translational modifications to Ala, Gly, Ile, or Val have been identified.
explanationWrong.B: GPI anchoring is listed at the carboxyl terminus for cell-surface attachment, not as the primary enzymatic on–off switch.
explanationWrong.D: Hydroxylation of Pro and Lys is cited in collagen formation, not as a universal on–off switch excluding those residues.

question: Lactase deficiency produces intolerance to which dietary sugar, based on the tabulated structure of lactose?

choices.text: An insoluble linear polymer of glucose in 1,4 linkage (cellulose)
A soluble disaccharide of 1,4-linked galactose-glucose (milk sugar)
A 1,2-linked glucose-fructose disaccharide (sucrose) only
Free dextrose used solely as an IV diluent

sourceQuote: dairy products Soluble disaccharide of 1,4-linked galactose- Glc
explanationCorrect: Lactose (milk sugar) is a soluble disaccharide of 1,4-linked galactose-glucose found in milk and dairy products.

explanationWrong.A: Cellulose is an insoluble linear glucose polymer in plant cell walls, not milk sugar.
explanationWrong.C: Sucrose is 1,2-linked Glc-Fru (cane/beet sugar), not lactose.
explanationWrong.D: D-glucose (dextrose) is a monosaccharide used as a nutrient/diluent, not the milk-sugar disaccharide.

question: In ABO typing, which genotype is described as expressing neither A-pattern nor B-pattern glycosylation genes?

choices.text: Type A, which expresses two copies of the A-pattern gene
Type B, which expresses two copies of the B-pattern gene
Type AB, which expresses one copy of A and one copy of B
Type O, which expresses neither A- nor B-pattern genes

sourceQuote: Type O people express neither A- nor B-pattern genes
explanationCorrect: Two genes control addition of the last carbohydrate; type O people express neither A- nor B-pattern genes.

explanationWrong.A: Type A people express two copies of the A-pattern gene.
explanationWrong.B: Type B people express two copies of the B-pattern gene.
explanationWrong.C: AB people express one copy of A and one copy of B.

question: Dietary counseling often contrasts saturated with unsaturated fats. How are fatty acids classified by number of double bonds in this review?

choices.text: Saturated fats have no double bonds; monounsaturated have one; polyunsaturated have two or more
Saturated fats have two or more double bonds; polyunsaturated fats have none
All triglycerides lack fatty acids and contain only cholesterol esters
Monounsaturated fats are defined solely by a chain length of five carbons or fewer

sourceQuote: saturated (no double bonds), monounsaturated (1 double bond), and polyunsaturated (2 or more double bonds)
explanationCorrect: Fatty acids are classified as saturated (no double bonds), monounsaturated (1 double bond), and polyunsaturated (2 or more double bonds).

explanationWrong.B: That reverses the definitions of saturated and polyunsaturated fats.
explanationWrong.C: Triglycerides have a glycerol backbone with three esterified fatty acids.
explanationWrong.D: Chain-length classes (short, medium, long, very long) are separate from double-bond classification; short-chain is ≤5 carbons.

question: Antimetabolites that substitute for DNA bases exploit complementary pairing. Which pairing statement is given for DNA versus RNA?

choices.text: DNA pairs adenine with cytosine; RNA replaces guanine with thymine
Both DNA and RNA use deoxyribose and pair adenine exclusively with guanine
DNA uses adenine–thymine (uracil in RNA) and cytosine–guanine base pairs
RNA stores the genetic code as a double helix of deoxyribose nucleotides only

sourceQuote: a nitrogenous base-pair (adenine–thymine [uracil in RNA], cytosine–guanine)
explanationCorrect: DNA nucleosides contain deoxyribose and nitrogenous base pairs adenine–thymine (uracil in RNA) and cytosine–guanine; RNA uses ribose.

explanationWrong.A: The named pairs are A–T (U in RNA) and C–G, not A–C or G–T substitution as stated.
explanationWrong.B: RNA uses ribose, not deoxyribose, and adenine pairs with thymine/uracil, not guanine.
explanationWrong.D: DNA, not RNA, is described as the helical double-stranded genetic-code macromolecule.

question: Mitochondrial DNA disorders reflect the small fraction of cellular DNA outside the nucleus. What distribution is stated?

choices.text: All cellular DNA is mitochondrial; the nucleus contains only RNA
Nearly all (99%) of the cell’s DNA is in the nucleus, and about 1% is in the mitochondria
Half of DNA is nuclear and half is in the Golgi complex
Introns carry specific genes, whereas exons carry no genetic information

sourceQuote: Nearly all (99%) of the cell’s DNA is found within the nucleus
explanationCorrect: Nearly all (99%) of the cell’s DNA is nuclear, and about 1% is mitochondrial; exons carry genes and introns carry no genetic information.

explanationWrong.A: The nucleus contains nearly all DNA; mitochondria hold only about 1%.
explanationWrong.C: The Golgi is not described as a DNA reservoir.
explanationWrong.D: That reverses exons and introns.

question: During translation, each amino acid is delivered by an adaptor RNA. Which statement about tRNA is given?

choices.text: There is a unique tRNA for each amino acid, selected by complementarity to the mRNA codon
A single tRNA carries all twenty amino acids without anticodons
tRNA remains in the nucleus and never binds amino acids
tRNA is identical to mRNA except that it retains all DNA introns

sourceQuote: There is a unique tRNA for each amino acid
explanationCorrect: tRNA deciphers mRNA; each amino acid has a unique tRNA whose three-base sequence is complementary to the mRNA codon.

explanationWrong.B: Each amino acid has its own tRNA; selection depends on anticodon–codon complementarity.
explanationWrong.C: tRNA binds its amino acid and carries it to the growing polypeptide as mRNA instructs.
explanationWrong.D: mRNA, not tRNA, is the fused exon sequence after intron removal.

question: Enzyme-targeted drugs often stabilize a transition state. How do enzymes accelerate conversion of substrate to product without being consumed?

choices.text: They raise the activation-energy barrier so fewer molecules react
They are stoichiometric reactants that are destroyed in each turnover
They convert equilibrium constants so the reaction becomes irreversible in all cases
Like other catalysts, they lower the activation energy, the energy barrier from substrate to product

sourceQuote: by lowering the activation energy (the energy barrier to get from substrate to product)
explanationCorrect: Enzymes are catalysts that are not consumed; they accelerate chemistry by lowering activation energy.

explanationWrong.A: Lowering, not raising, the activation-energy barrier is the catalytic mechanism stated.
explanationWrong.B: Catalysts assist reactions but are not consumed in those reactions.
explanationWrong.C: The review describes rate acceleration via a lower energy barrier, not universal conversion of all equilibria to irreversibility.

question: Modern enzymology describes substrate binding as a conformational adjustment rather than a rigid complementary mold. Which model is said to have replaced the original lock-and-key model?

choices.text: A purely random collision model with no active site
The steric or induced-fit model
A model in which enzymes raise activation energy by excluding all substrates
A model limited to metal-only catalysis without protein

sourceQuote: This model has replaced the original lock-and-key model of enzyme activity
explanationCorrect: The steric or induced-fit model—spatial configuration of the active site, with possible movement of backbone or side chains during binding—has replaced the original lock-and-key model.

explanationWrong.A: Induced fit still requires a configured active site, not the absence of one.
explanationWrong.C: Enzymes lower, rather than raise, the energy barrier to reaction.
explanationWrong.D: The protein enzyme and its active-site chemistry remain central; metals may be cofactors but are not a protein-free replacement model.

question: Niacin supplementation is used to restore redox coenzymes derived from that vitamin. Into which two coenzymes can niacin be converted?

choices.text: TPP and methylcobalamin only
Coenzyme A and biotin only
NAD and NADP, whose reduced forms NADH and NADPH report cellular redox status
Flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, which are riboflavin coenzymes

sourceQuote: Niacin can be converted into two key coenzymes, NAD and NADP
explanationCorrect: Niacin is converted into NAD and NADP; NAD/NADH and NADP/NADPH ratios mediate energy production and oxidative-reductive capacity.

explanationWrong.A: TPP is the thiamine coenzyme; methylcobalamin is a B12 form, not niacin’s products.
explanationWrong.B: CoA derives from pantothenate; biotin is its own cofactor class.
explanationWrong.D: FMN and FAD are the coenzyme forms of riboflavin, not niacin.

question: A neonate given a vitamin K antagonist in error would be at risk for the deficiency manifestation tabulated for phylloquinones. What is that manifestation?

choices.text: Impaired blood clotting
Night blindness from failed opsin complexation
Scurvy from loss of a reducing agent
Beriberi from failed oxidative decarboxylation

sourceQuote: K or phylloquinones Impaired blood clotting Green leafy vegetables
explanationCorrect: Vitamin K (phylloquinones) is tabulated with impaired blood clotting as the deficiency manifestation.

explanationWrong.B: Night blindness is listed for vitamin A (retinoids), which complexes with opsin.
explanationWrong.C: Scurvy is the deficiency of vitamin C (ascorbic acid), a reducing agent.
explanationWrong.D: Beriberi is listed for thiamine (B1) and TPP-dependent oxidative decarboxylation.

question: The Michaelis constant first developed for enzymes is said to apply analogously to which pharmacologic binding processes?

choices.text: Only irreversible covalent labeling of DNA
Only filtration of unbound drug at the glomerulus
Only partitioning of drug into expired air
Binding of drugs to cell-surface receptors or to circulating proteins

sourceQuote: binding of drugs to cell surface receptors or to circulating proteins
explanationCorrect: Km, the substrate concentration producing half-maximal enzyme velocity, has direct application in drug binding to cell-surface receptors or circulating proteins.

explanationWrong.A: The stated analog is receptor and plasma-protein binding, not DNA alkylation.
explanationWrong.B: Glomerular filtration is not the kinetic analogy named here.
explanationWrong.C: Pulmonary excretion is not the Km application described.

question: When comparing enzyme preparations, the international unit of activity is defined as which quantity under optimal pH and temperature?

choices.text: One mole of enzyme protein per liter of buffer
The amount of enzyme that produces 1 micromole of product per minute
The substrate concentration equal to Km
The turnover number when no substrate is bound

sourceQuote: produces, under optimal conditions of pH and temperature, 1 micromole of product per minute
explanationCorrect: The international unit is the amount of enzyme that produces, under optimal pH and temperature, 1 micromole of product per minute.

explanationWrong.A: The IU is a rate of product formation, not a molar concentration of enzyme.
explanationWrong.C: Km is the substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity, not the definition of the IU.
explanationWrong.D: The turnover number k is molecular activity when enzyme is saturated, not an IU defined at zero substrate.

question: Because a direct plot of velocity versus high substrate concentration is experimentally impractical, which linearization is used to estimate Km and Vmax?

choices.text: A Hill plot of log(Y) versus pH only
A Scatchard plot of bound/free versus time only
The Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of 1/v versus 1/[s]
A first-order decay plot of enzyme mass versus temperature only

sourceQuote: the Lineweaver–Burk (or double reciprocal) plot of 1/v versus 1/[s] is used to estimate Km and Vmax
explanationCorrect: Experimental limits at high substrate make the direct v versus [s] plot impractical; the Lineweaver–Burk plot of 1/v versus 1/[s] is used to estimate Km and Vmax.

explanationWrong.A: A Hill plot versus pH is not the method named for Km and Vmax estimation here.
explanationWrong.B: Scatchard analysis is not the double-reciprocal enzyme plot described.
explanationWrong.D: Thermal denaturation plots are not the linearization given in this passage.

question: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot written as y = mx + b, what does the y-axis intercept represent?

choices.text: 1/Vmax
Km without reciprocal transformation
The initial substrate concentration in each experiment
The Eadie–Hofstee slope exclusively, which equals Vmax/[s]

sourceQuote: b = 1/Vmax (i.e., the y-axis intercept) and m = Km/Vmax
explanationCorrect: The rearranged Michaelis–Menten equation is y = mx + b, where the y-axis intercept b equals 1/Vmax and the slope m equals Km/Vmax.

explanationWrong.B: Km is obtained from the slope (Km/Vmax) together with Vmax, not as the raw y-intercept.
explanationWrong.C: Initial substrate concentration is chosen experimentally; it is not the intercept definition.
explanationWrong.D: The Eadie–Hofstee plot is a separate linearization; the Lineweaver–Burk slope is Km/Vmax.

question: Aerobic oxidation of one mole of glucose is often quoted as 38 ATP. Why does this review say that yield generally is not achieved, and what maximum is considered likely?

choices.text: Glycolysis is confined to mitochondria, so the yield is always 2 ATP
ATP is not formed from carbohydrate, so the yield is zero
ATP losses from moving pyruvate, phosphate, and ADP into mitochondria lower the likely maximum to about 30–32 ATP per mole of glucose
Anabolism consumes all ATP, so net yield is 38 AMP

sourceQuote: The likely maximum is about 30–32 ATP moles per mole of glucose
explanationCorrect: Theoretically 38 ATP are produced per mole of glucose aerobically, but losses associated with moving pyruvate, phosphate, and ADP into mitochondria make about 30–32 ATP the likely maximum.

explanationWrong.A: Glycolysis occurs in all human cells; 2 ATP is not the aerobic maximum stated.
explanationWrong.B: ATP is formed from metabolism of carbohydrates, protein, and lipids.
explanationWrong.D: The review does not convert the 38 ATP figure into 38 AMP as net yield.

question: Carnitine deficiency impairs oxidation of which fatty-acid class, and at which transport step?

choices.text: Short-chain fatty acids (<C6) entering the nucleus for transcription
Long-chain fatty acids (C12 and larger) requiring carnitine for translocation into the mitochondrial matrix
All fatty acids equally, because beta-oxidation occurs only in the cytosol
Cholesterol esters that must be hydroxylated on ribosomal RNA

sourceQuote: Long-chain fatty acids (C12 and larger) require carnitine for translocation into the mitochondrial matrix
explanationCorrect: Fatty acids are oxidized in the mitochondrial matrix; long-chain fatty acids (C12 and larger) require carnitine for translocation, whereas medium- and short-chain acids are thought not to depend on that shuttle in the same way.

explanationWrong.A: Short-chain acids are distinguished from the carnitine-dependent long-chain class; oxidation is mitochondrial, not nuclear transcription.
explanationWrong.C: Beta-oxidation is mitochondrial; long-chain acids specifically need carnitine.
explanationWrong.D: Cholesterol esters and rRNA hydroxylation are not the carnitine shuttle described.

question: Nuclear targeting of a transcription-factor drug must cross how many membranes of the nuclear envelope, and what is the largest intracellular compartment named?

choices.text: One membrane; the nucleolus is larger than the nucleus
No membranes; chromatin is cytosolic only
Three membranes continuous with the plasma membrane only
Two membranes (the nuclear envelope) surrounding the nucleus, the largest intracellular compartment

sourceQuote: surrounded by two membranes called the nuclear envelope
explanationCorrect: The nucleus is the largest intracellular compartment and is surrounded by two membranes called the nuclear envelope; the nucleolus is a subcompartment within it.

explanationWrong.A: The envelope has two membranes, and the nucleolus is a subcompartment inside the nucleus, not a larger organelle.
explanationWrong.B: DNA is contained in the nucleus as chromatin, not as a membrane-free cytosolic pool in this description.
explanationWrong.C: The review specifies two membranes of the nuclear envelope, not three plasma-membrane-continuous layers.

question: Aminoglycosides bind bacterial ribosomal subunits. Which two ribosomal lobes are named for the cytoplasmic protein-synthesis machinery in this review?

choices.text: 30S and 50S lobes of the ribosome, usually attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum
40S and 60S lobes located only inside the nuclear envelope
70S and 80S lobes of the lysosome
A single 100S polymerase that replaces tRNA

sourceQuote: The ribosome consists of two large lobes, termed 30S and 50S
explanationCorrect: Protein synthesis occurs on cytoplasmic ribosomes with 30S and 50S lobes, usually attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, using mRNA and charged tRNAs.

explanationWrong.B: The passage names 30S and 50S cytoplasmic ribosomal lobes, not exclusively nuclear 40S/60S subunits.
explanationWrong.C: Lysosomes are not the ribosomal protein-synthesis machinery described.
explanationWrong.D: Translation requires mRNA and aminoacyl-tRNAs on the two-lobed ribosome, not a single polymerase replacing tRNA.

question: Industrial production of a recombinant therapeutic protein after cloning the gene into a host cell line still requires isolation. From which sources may that protein be recovered?

choices.text: Only from patient serum after in vivo gene transfer
Only from uncloned chromosomal DNA without expression
From the culture media if secreted, or by cell lysis and purification if intracellular
Only from the nucleolus, because translation is completed there

sourceQuote: from the culture media (secreted protein) or may require cell lysis
explanationCorrect: After overexpression in a microorganism or cultured cell line, the protein of interest may be isolated from culture media if secreted or may require cell lysis and purification.

explanationWrong.A: The described process is in vitro overexpression in microbes or cell lines, not recovery only from patient serum.
explanationWrong.B: Cloning into host DNA and promoting expression are required; unexpressed DNA is not the isolation source.
explanationWrong.D: Translation of the protein occurs in the cytoplasm on ribosomes, not as nucleolar isolation of the finished therapeutic.

question: Between meals, stored carbohydrate is used to support blood glucose. Under which intake condition does this review place that storage function?

choices.text: Only during intravenous lipid emulsion infusion
In the absence of intake
Only after complete depletion of all adipose triglyceride
Only when recombinant DNA is present in the cytoplasm

sourceQuote: support blood glucose levels in the absence of intake
explanationCorrect: Carbohydrate can be stored as an energy source to support blood glucose levels in the absence of intake.

explanationWrong.A: The storage function is framed for absence of intake, not lipid-emulsion infusion.
explanationWrong.C: Adipose is discussed as fat storage in a later item; this statement concerns carbohydrate stores supporting glucose without intake.
explanationWrong.D: Recombinant DNA is listed as not required for normal cytoplasmic protein synthesis, not as a condition for glycogen use.

question: Most cell-membrane phospholipids are classified chemically with which glyceride category in this item?

choices.text: Triglycerides without a side chain, as the exclusive membrane lipid
Monoglycerides that lack any phosphate
Free cholesterol with no glycerol backbone
They are the main component of human cell membranes, considered among glycerides that include phosphate-bearing forms

sourceQuote: Phospholipids are the main component of human cell membranes
explanationCorrect: The review states that phospholipids are the main component of human cell membranes and then asks in which glyceride category most membrane phospholipids fit, listing phosphate-bearing diglycerides among the options.

explanationWrong.A: Triglycerides without a side chain are listed as an option, not as the stated identity of membrane phospholipids.
explanationWrong.B: Monoglycerides without phosphate are not identified as the main membrane phospholipid class.
explanationWrong.C: Free cholesterol is not the glyceride classification named for membrane phospholipids in this stem.

question: Ribosomal RNA is discussed in this review as participating in which overall biosynthetic process?

choices.text: Protein synthesis
Beta-oxidation of fatty acids in the nucleus
Formation of corn syrup solids from ATP
Gluconeogenesis from ribosomal peptides

sourceQuote: Which part of protein synthesis involves rRNA? A. The reading
explanationCorrect: The review asks which part of protein synthesis involves rRNA, establishing rRNA as a participant in protein synthesis (assembly of amino acids on the ribosome among the listed roles).

explanationWrong.B: Beta-oxidation is a later item concerning fatty acids, not the process named for rRNA.
explanationWrong.C: Corn syrup solids are a food ingredient, not an rRNA product.
explanationWrong.D: Gluconeogenesis is not the process linked to rRNA in this item.

question: Although some vitamins can appear to be substrates, what is identified as their primary metabolic role?

choices.text: They are the sole source of essential amino acids.
They replace ribosomes during cytoplasmic translation.
They act as enzyme cofactors.
They are stored exclusively as muscle starch.

sourceQuote: the primary role of vitamins in metabolism is as an enzyme cofactor
explanationCorrect: The answer key states that although some vitamins can appear to be a substrate, their primary metabolic role is as an enzyme cofactor.

explanationWrong.A: Essential amino acids must be in the diet; vitamins are not identified as their source.
explanationWrong.B: Protein synthesis requires tRNA, mRNA, and ribosomes; vitamins are not said to replace ribosomes.
explanationWrong.D: Human carbohydrate storage is glycogen in muscle and liver, not vitamin storage as starch.

question: A patient with diabetes asks about corn syrup solids on a processed-food label. Chemically, what are they according to this review, and why might they be inappropriate?

choices.text: Completely hydrolyzed starch or free glucose units; they may not be appropriate for patients with diabetes
Unhydrolyzed cellulose that cannot raise blood glucose
A mixture of essential amino acids without sugar
Long-chain triglycerides oxidized only in the nucleus

sourceQuote: completely hydrolyzed starch or free glucose units). Products containing corn syrup solids
explanationCorrect: Despite the name, corn syrup solids are sugar—completely hydrolyzed starch or free glucose units—and products containing them may not be appropriate for patients with diabetes.

explanationWrong.B: They are hydrolyzed starch/glucose, not unhydrolyzed cellulose.
explanationWrong.C: They are carbohydrate, not an amino-acid mixture.
explanationWrong.D: Beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids occurs in mitochondria, and corn syrup solids are not triglycerides.

question: Which cited work is Schrödinger’s 1944 inquiry into the physical basis of living systems?

choices.text: Introduction to Nutrition and Metabolism
Textbook of Biochemistry with Clinical Correlations
What Is Life?
The Molecular Basis of Blood Diseases

sourceQuote: Schrödinger E. What Is Life? Cambridge
explanationCorrect: The biochemistry chapter bibliography lists Schrödinger’s What Is Life? (Cambridge University Press, 1944).

explanationWrong.A: That title is Bender’s nutrition and metabolism text, not Schrödinger.
explanationWrong.B: That title is Devlin’s biochemistry textbook.
explanationWrong.D: That title is Stamatoyannopoulos and colleagues’ blood-diseases text.

question: Antiviral therapy must account for the fact that viruses cannot complete their life cycle on abiotic surfaces. How are viruses defined in this key-points review?

choices.text: Eukaryotes with nuclei that grow independently in soil
Prokaryotes that always possess mitochondria and Golgi bodies
Multicellular fungi that infect only immunocompetent hosts
Fragments of nucleic acid that can replicate only in living cells

sourceQuote: Viruses are fragments of nucleic acid that can replicate only in living cells
explanationCorrect: Viruses are defined as fragments of nucleic acid that can replicate only in living cells.

explanationWrong.A: Viruses are not described as independent soil eukaryotes with nuclei.
explanationWrong.B: Prokaryotes in this passage lack a nucleus and organelles; that description is not applied to viruses as organelle-rich cells.
explanationWrong.C: Fungi typically infect immunocompromised or malnourished individuals; viruses are not defined as multicellular fungi.

question: Dosing strategies that target rapidly dividing bacteria are most relevant to which ordered four-phase bacterial growth curve?

choices.text: Lag, logarithmic, stationary, and decline
Incubation, prodromal, acme, and convalescence only, without a growth curve
Attachment, penetration, uncoating, and budding exclusively
Sporulation, germination, lysogeny, and latency as the only four phases

sourceQuote: lag, logarithmic, stationary, and decline The typical infection cycle periods
explanationCorrect: Bacteria follow a typical four-phase growth curve: lag, logarithmic, stationary, and decline. Infection-cycle periods (incubation, prodromal, acme, decline, convalescent) are listed separately.

explanationWrong.B: Those are infection-cycle periods in the host, not the bacterial growth-curve phases.
explanationWrong.C: Attachment through budding describes viral replication steps, not the four bacterial growth phases.
explanationWrong.D: Lysogeny and latency are viral concepts in later text, not the four named bacterial growth phases.

question: Colonization of the gut is not equivalent to infectious disease. How is infection defined in this introduction?

choices.text: Any contact between a human and an environmental surface
The presence of a nucleus and mitochondria in the microbe
The multiplication of microbes in human tissue
Irreversible sterilization of blood, lymph, and CSF

sourceQuote: defined as the multiplication of microbes in human tissue
explanationCorrect: Infection is defined as the multiplication of microbes in human tissue; disease potential depends on disruption of the interplay among pathogen, host, and environment.

explanationWrong.A: Mere environmental contact is not the definition given for infection.
explanationWrong.B: Possession of a nucleus and organelles defines eukaryotes, not infection.
explanationWrong.D: Sterility of internal fluids is a later host concept, not the definition of infection.

question: Empiric antibiotic selection often begins with Gram staining. What accounts for Gram-positive organisms retaining crystal violet after iodine fixation and alcohol decolorization?

choices.text: They always grow only as spiral forms called spirilla.
They retain the staining dye, a difference likely due to cell-wall content, whereas Gram-negative bacteria do not.
They lack any cell wall and therefore bind iodine irreversibly to DNA.
They are defined as eukaryotes with mitochondria.

sourceQuote: Gram-positive bacteria retain the staining dye whereas Gram-negative bacteria do not
explanationCorrect: Gram-positive bacteria retain the dye after iodine fixation and alcohol decolorization; Gram-negative bacteria do not, likely because of differences in cell-wall content.

explanationWrong.A: Bacteria exist as rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), and spirals; Gram reaction is not limited to spirals.
explanationWrong.C: The staining difference is attributed to cell-wall variation, not absence of a wall.
explanationWrong.D: Bacteria are classified among prokaryotes in this chapter, not as mitochondria-bearing eukaryotes.

question: Bacterial rods are known by which morphologic name?

choices.text: Cocci
Spirochetes only, never as single cells
Bacilli
Pili

sourceQuote: Bacteria exist in three basic shapes: rods, spheres, and spirals. Bacterial
explanationCorrect: Bacteria occur as rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), and spirals; rods are called bacilli and may be single or in chains.

explanationWrong.A: Cocci are spheres, which may form diplococci, streptococci, or staphylococcal clusters.
explanationWrong.B: Spirals include comma-shaped rods and corkscrew spirochetes; rods as a class are bacilli.
explanationWrong.D: Pili are hair-like attachment structures, not a cell-shape name.

question: Which statement about bacterial plasmids is correct?

choices.text: They are linear chromosomes that cannot transfer resistance
They are small circular DNA molecules that can replicate independent of chromosomal DNA and can convey resistance to other strains
They are flagella used exclusively for motility
They are spores produced only by mycoplasmas

sourceQuote: molecules of DNA that can replicate independent of the chromosomal DNA.
explanationCorrect: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that replicate independently of chromosomal DNA and can transfer genetic information, including resistance. Clostridium and Bacillus are noted as spore formers; mycoplasmas lack a cell wall.

explanationWrong.A: Plasmids are described as small circular, not linear chromosomal, DNA.
explanationWrong.C: Flagella are motility structures, not plasmids.
explanationWrong.D: Spores are associated with Clostridium and Bacillus; mycoplasmas are wall-less free-living microbes.

question: Beta-lactams that inhibit cell-wall synthesis are most effective when bacteria are actively dividing. During which growth phase is host susceptibility to such antibiotics described as greatest, and why do symptoms appear then?

choices.text: The lag phase only, before any chromosomal duplication
The stationary phase, when no binary fission occurs
The decline phase, when bacteria have ceased metabolism
The logarithmic phase, when bacteria double by binary fission, symptoms begin, and cell-wall–active antibiotics interfere most

sourceQuote: a host’s susceptibility to some antibiotics is greatest through the antibiotics’ interference with cell wall synthesis
explanationCorrect: In the logarithmic phase bacteria double each reproductive period; symptoms begin, and susceptibility to antibiotics that interfere with cell-wall synthesis and metabolism is greatest.

explanationWrong.A: The lag phase is adaptation to a new environment, not the phase of greatest cell-wall antibiotic susceptibility described.
explanationWrong.B: Stationary phase is not the doubling phase linked to peak beta-lactam susceptibility here.
explanationWrong.C: Decline is not identified as the phase of greatest antibiotic susceptibility.

question: During which phase of bacterial growth is host susceptibility to some cell-wall–active antibiotics described as greatest?

choices.text: The reproductive period of chromosomal duplication and binary fission, when bacteria double
The decline phase after nutrients are exhausted
The stationary phase only, when death already exceeds reproduction
A spore-only dormant phase in which no chromosomal duplication occurs

sourceQuote: reproductive period involving chromosomal duplication and binary fission.
explanationCorrect: Bacteria double during chromosomal duplication and binary fission; in that phase, susceptibility to some antibiotics (for example, those interfering with cell-wall synthesis) is greatest.

explanationWrong.B: The decline phase is described in the following passage, not as the period of greatest antibiotic susceptibility.
explanationWrong.C: Stationary phase is when reproduction and death rates equalize, not when susceptibility is described as greatest.
explanationWrong.D: The growth phase discussed involves active duplication and fission, not spore dormancy.

question: After the stationary phase of bacterial growth, which description matches the decline phase?

choices.text: Bacterial numbers continue to double with each fission cycle
An exponential decline in bacterial numbers is observed
Reproduction and death rates remain exactly equal indefinitely
Viruses, not bacteria, are quantified exclusively in this phase

sourceQuote: is the decline phase, during which an exponential decline in bacterial numbers
explanationCorrect: The last bacterial growth phase is the decline phase, during which bacterial numbers fall exponentially as host defenses, nutrient depletion, waste, and shortages of oxygen and water take effect.

explanationWrong.A: Doubling characterizes the earlier reproductive (log) phase.
explanationWrong.C: Equal reproduction and death define the stationary phase.
explanationWrong.D: The passage discusses bacterial quantification, then separately introduces viruses.

question: Herpesviruses can remain quiescent for years and then reactivate. Which virus–host relationship is described as integrating viral nucleic acid into host DNA and establishing a latent state?

choices.text: Lysogeny, which may establish latency with later reactivation
Binary fission of aerobic fungi at room temperature only
Gram decolorization of yeast hyphae
Obligate anaerobic sporulation of Pneumocystis in soil

sourceQuote: lysogeny, may establish a latent or dormant state for the virus
explanationCorrect: When viruses integrate into host-cell DNA they may become immune to normal defenses; this lysogenic relationship can establish latency with later reactivation.

explanationWrong.B: Fungi are classified as yeasts and molds with hyphae; binary fission is not the latent viral mechanism named.
explanationWrong.C: Gram staining of bacteria is not the latent viral integration process.
explanationWrong.D: Pneumocystis is discussed as yeast-like, not as the definition of lysogeny.

question: Interferon-based strategies exploit a nonspecific protein family. What dual actions are attributed to interferons?

choices.text: They raise gastric pH and digest peptidoglycan like lysozyme only.
They replace complement as the sole opsonin for bacteria.
They trigger the immune system and inhibit viral reproduction.
They are the keratin barrier of intact skin.

sourceQuote: trigger the immune system and inhibit viral reproduction
explanationCorrect: Interferons are a nonspecific group of proteins that can trigger the immune system and inhibit viral reproduction.

explanationWrong.A: Low gastric pH and lysozyme in saliva and tears are separate nonspecific defenses.
explanationWrong.B: Complement comprises more than 30 proteins that enhance phagocytosis; interferons are not said to replace them.
explanationWrong.D: Intact skin is the most important nonspecific physical barrier, not an interferon.

question: Interferons are described as which type of host defense molecules?

choices.text: Antigen-specific antibodies produced only by B-lymphocytes
Complement proteins that solely lyse SRBCs in vitro
Memory T-cell receptors that mediate delayed-type hypersensitivity
A nonspecific group of proteins that can trigger the immune system and inhibit viral reproduction

sourceQuote: nonspecific group of proteins in the human body that have the ability to trigger
explanationCorrect: Interferons are nonspecific proteins that trigger immunity and inhibit viral reproduction. Complement can enhance phagocytosis; NK cells destroy foreign cells independent of specific immunity.

explanationWrong.A: Antibodies are specific immune products, not the description given for interferons.
explanationWrong.B: Complement is discussed separately as enhancing phagocytosis.
explanationWrong.C: DTH is a Type IV mechanism in the immunology chapter, not the interferon description.

question: Fever as a nonspecific host response is defined in this passage as a body temperature above which value, and it is controlled by which structure?

choices.text: Above 37.5°C, controlled by the hypothalamus
Above 32°C, controlled by the adrenal medulla
Any temperature rise, controlled exclusively by neutrophils
Above 40°C only, with no hypothalamic role

sourceQuote: Fever, which is controlled by the hypothalamus, is defined as a body
explanationCorrect: Fever is a temperature above normal (37.5°C), controlled by the hypothalamus, and is considered by some a form of nonspecific resistance. Proinflammatory cytokines include IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α.

explanationWrong.B: The hypothalamus, not the adrenal medulla, is named; the threshold is 37.5°C.
explanationWrong.C: Neutrophils are 55–60% of leukocytes and digest engulfed material; they do not uniquely define fever.
explanationWrong.D: The stated threshold is 37.5°C, not 40°C.

question: Vaccine design differs for humoral versus cellular protection. Which lymphocyte lineages are assigned antibody-mediated immunity (AMI) and cell-mediated immunity (CMI)?

choices.text: Neutrophils mediate AMI; eosinophils mediate CMI.
B-lymphocytes are largely responsible for AMI, whereas T-lymphocytes are responsible for CMI.
Platelets mediate AMI; erythrocytes mediate CMI.
Both AMI and CMI are mediated only by circulating complement, not lymphocytes.

sourceQuote: B-lymphocytes are largely responsible for antibody-mediated immunity (AMI), whereas T-lymphocytes are responsible for cell-mediated immunity (CMI)
explanationCorrect: Lymphocytes (about 30–35% of circulating leukocytes) are foundational to specific immunity: B-lymphocytes largely mediate AMI and T-lymphocytes mediate CMI.

explanationWrong.A: Neutrophils and eosinophils are not assigned AMI and CMI in this passage.
explanationWrong.C: Platelets and erythrocytes are not the lymphocyte lineages named for AMI and CMI.
explanationWrong.D: Complement participates in immunity, but AMI and CMI are assigned to B- and T-lymphocytes.

question: Opsonization is defined as which process?

choices.text: Viral inhibition by interferons alone
Maturation of monocytes into macrophages in tissue
Enhancement of phagocytosis by antibodies or complement
Targeted cell lysis by cytotoxic T-lymphocytes

sourceQuote: The term immunoglobulin is used interchangeably with antibody. Subsequent
explanationCorrect: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (immunoglobulins) after antigen presentation by macrophages. Antibody–antigen interaction inactivates antigen or increases susceptibility to defenses such as phagocytosis; that enhancement by antibody or complement is opsonization. Some B cells become memory cells.

explanationWrong.A: Interferons are nonspecific antiviral proteins in another passage.
explanationWrong.B: Macrophage nomenclature is from the inflammation passage, not the opsonization definition.
explanationWrong.D: Cytotoxic T-cell lysis is a CMI process in the following passage.

question: Antibody-mediated immunity (AMI) versus cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is summarized how with respect to pathogens?

choices.text: AMI is irrelevant to viruses, and CMI is irrelevant to bacteria
AMI is involved in both bacterial and viral host defense, whereas CMI is essential to viral host defense
Only AMI provides memory cells; T cells never become memory cells
Vaccines cannot use specific immunity as a primary mechanism

sourceQuote: T-lymphocytes originate in the thymus and populate lymph nodes, the
explanationCorrect: T-lymphocytes originate in the thymus and populate lymphoid tissues. After macrophage antigen presentation, cytotoxic T cells migrate and lyse targets; some T cells become memory cells. AMI contributes to bacterial and viral defense; CMI is essential for viral defense. Vaccines use specific immunity.

explanationWrong.A: AMI is involved with both bacteria and viruses.
explanationWrong.C: Some T-lymphocytes also become memory cells.
explanationWrong.D: Specific immunity is a primary vaccine mechanism.

question: A positive culture from which of the following sites is stated to typically indicate infection rather than normal flora?

choices.text: Skin, which is always sterile in healthy persons
The oral cavity, which never harbors microorganisms
The vagina, which is free of all microbes in health
Blood, lymph, cerebrospinal fluid, or most internal organs, which are normally sterile
