sourceQuote: blood, lymph, cerebral spinal fluid, and most internal organs are free of microorganisms (sterile)
explanationCorrect: Infection is not synonymous with disease; skin, oral cavity, intestines, and vagina normally have flora, whereas blood, lymph, CSF, and most internal organs are sterile, so microbes there typically indicate infection.

explanationWrong.A: Skin is listed as a body area where microorganisms are found in healthy individuals.
explanationWrong.B: The oral cavity normally harbors microorganisms.
explanationWrong.C: The vagina is a normal flora site, not a sterile compartment in this review.

question: Stasis from mechanical obstruction predisposes to infection. Which sites of obstruction are listed as common examples?

choices.text: Lung, urinary tract, biliary tract, and Eustachian tubes
Only the cerebral cortex and the myocardium
Hair follicles and nail beds exclusively
The intact stratum corneum as the sole obstruction site

sourceQuote: the lung, urinary tract, biliary tract, and Eustachian tubes
explanationCorrect: Mechanical obstruction causing fluid stasis can overcome normal defenses; common sites include the lung, urinary tract, biliary tract, and Eustachian tubes. Catheters and breaches of skin are additional risk factors.

explanationWrong.B: Cortex and myocardium are not the obstruction sites listed.
explanationWrong.C: Hair follicles and nail beds are not the common obstruction examples given.
explanationWrong.D: Intact skin is a barrier; obstruction of passages, not the stratum corneum, is the mechanism named.

question: Individuals at increased infection risk because of congenital or acquired host-defense defects are referred to as which of the following?

choices.text: Healthy reservoirs only
Vectors in the epidemiologic triad
Immune-privileged hosts who cannot be infected by any microbe
Compromised hosts, in whom virtually any microorganism can become pathogenic

sourceQuote: altered phagocytosis secondary to neutropenia, malignancies, cytotoxic drug
explanationCorrect: Dysfunction of nonspecific or specific defenses (genetic defects, noninfectious disease, or immunosuppression such as neutropenia, malignancy, cytotoxic drugs, or radiation) produces compromised hosts. Disease likelihood depends on host resistance, virulence, and inoculum.

explanationWrong.A: Reservoirs are environments or hosts that support pathogen growth, discussed in the next passage.
explanationWrong.B: Vector is not used here as the name for such patients.
explanationWrong.C: Virtually any microorganism can become pathogenic in compromised hosts.

question: The most common reservoir for human pathogens is identified as which of the following?

choices.text: Other humans
Soil exclusively
Water exclusively
Inanimate fomites only, never living hosts

sourceQuote: toxins may cause disease without invasion of body tissues.
explanationCorrect: Reservoirs include water, soil, and animals, but the most common reservoir for human pathogens is other humans. A carrier has recovered yet continues to shed pathogen. Toxins can cause disease without tissue invasion; inoculum is the microbial dose.

explanationWrong.B: Soil is a possible reservoir but not the most common for human pathogens.
explanationWrong.C: Water is a possible reservoir but not the most common named here.
explanationWrong.D: Living human reservoirs are emphasized.

question: Post-exposure prophylaxis windows are planned around the interval before symptoms appear. What is that interval called, and how long can it last?

choices.text: The acme period, limited to minutes after entry
The prodromal period, defined as absence of any systemic symptoms
The incubation period, which can range from days to years
The convalescent period, which precedes microbial entry

sourceQuote: The incubation period can range from days to years
explanationCorrect: The incubation period is the time between microbial entry and the appearance of symptoms and can range from days to years. Prodrome is general symptoms; acme is specific symptoms.

explanationWrong.A: The acme period is when specific symptoms occur, not the pre-symptomatic interval.
explanationWrong.B: The prodromal period is when general symptoms such as fever and malaise manifest.
explanationWrong.D: Convalescence follows illness; it does not precede entry.

question: Untreated streptococcal pharyngitis with a rash can progress to a vascular inflammatory sequela. Which sequence is described?

choices.text: Viral croup always precedes glomerulonephritis without a bacterial phase.
Scarlet fever is strep throat with a skin rash and can lead to rheumatic fever, which may result in rheumatic heart disease and glomerulonephritis.
Influenza vaccination prevents all group A streptococcal disease.
Bordetella pertussis is the sole cause of strep throat.

sourceQuote: Scarlet fever is strep throat accompanied by a skin rash; it can lead to rheumatic fever
explanationCorrect: S. pyogenes causes strep throat; scarlet fever is strep throat with a rash and can lead to rheumatic fever, which is small-vessel inflammation that may result in rheumatic heart disease and glomerulonephritis.

explanationWrong.A: The sequela described follows streptococcal disease, not viral croup alone.
explanationWrong.C: A vaccination is said to exist only for influenza among the common-cold viruses listed, not as prevention of all streptococcal disease.
explanationWrong.D: Strep throat is attributed to S. pyogenes; pertussis is a separate bacterial URI.

question: A toddler with a distinctive cough described as a “seal’s bark” most closely matches which syndrome in this review?

choices.text: Croup, involving inflammation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, often linked to parainfluenza types 1, 2, and 3
Typical pneumococcal pneumonia with rust-colored sputum only
Pulmonary tuberculosis confined to the kidneys
Candidal vaginitis transmitted by airborne spores

sourceQuote: a distinctive cough known as a seal’s bark
explanationCorrect: Croup involves inflammation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi and is associated with a distinctive cough known as a seal’s bark; parainfluenza types 1–3 also cause acute viral laryngitis.

explanationWrong.B: Pneumonia is inflammation of bronchial tubes and lungs with abrupt systemic symptoms; the seal’s-bark cough is assigned to croup.
explanationWrong.C: TB complications include spread to kidneys, but that is not the croup syndrome.
explanationWrong.D: Candidal vaginitis is not the pediatric airway syndrome described.

question: A previously healthy adult with high fever, sharp chest pain, dyspnea, and rust-colored sputum is the classic picture of which tabulated community-acquired pneumonia pathogen?

choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast rod causing night sweats as the only CAP pattern
Bordetella pertussis, a Gram-negative rod causing malaise without pneumonia
Mycoplasma pneumoniae atypical CAP, described here as rust-colored sputum and sharp pleural pain
Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram-positive diplococcus in chains, causing CAP with rust-colored sputum

explanationCorrect: Community-acquired pneumonia due to S. pneumoniae (Gram-positive diplococcus in chains) is characterized by high fever, sharp chest pains, difficulty breathing, and rust-colored sputum.

explanationWrong.A: M. tuberculosis is an acid-fast rod associated with cough, weight loss, night sweats, and related findings, not the rust-sputum CAP row.
explanationWrong.B: Pertussis is tabulated with malaise, low-grade fever, and severe cough, not this CAP picture.
explanationWrong.C: Atypical CAP (Mycoplasma, Legionella) is listed with headache, fever, fatigue, and a dry hacking cough, not rust-colored sputum.

question: Pulmonary tuberculosis may disseminate beyond the lung. Which organs are listed as complication sites of that spread?

choices.text: Only the epidermis and nails
Only the gallbladder lumen
Kidneys, liver, bone, and meninges
Only the hair shaft, via airborne yeast cells of Cryptococcus

explanationCorrect: Spreading to other organs, including the kidneys, liver, bone, and meninges, is a complication of pulmonary tuberculosis.

explanationWrong.A: Epidermis and nails are not the extra-pulmonary TB sites named.
explanationWrong.B: The gallbladder is not listed among TB complication organs here.
explanationWrong.D: Cryptococcus neoformans is an airborne yeast affecting lungs, spinal cord, and meninges in immunocompromised hosts, not hair-shaft TB.

question: A traumatic wound contaminated with soil is at risk for gas gangrene. Which organism is identified as responsible for that disease, in contrast to tetanus?

Clostridium perfringens; Clostridium tetani instead causes tetanus
Candida albicans, which causes necrotizing fasciitis only
Streptococcus pyogenes, which is confined to athlete’s foot

explanationCorrect: Soil pathogens include C. tetani, which causes tetanus, and C. perfringens, which is responsible for gas gangrene. Staphylococci and streptococci are the most common flora of many SSTIs.

explanationWrong.C: Fungi such as those causing tinea pedis infect skin, mouth, and nails; Candida is not named as the gas-gangrene organism.
explanationWrong.D: Staphylococcal and streptococcal species are common SSTI flora, but gas gangrene is assigned to C. perfringens; tinea pedis is fungal.

question: Bacterial conjunctivitis (“pink eye”) is most often caused by which organism in this text?

choices.text: Candida albicans
Dermatophytes causing tinea pedis
Herpes simplex type 1 virus
Haemophilus aegyptius

explanationCorrect: Pink eye is most often caused by H. aegyptius. Cutaneous mycoses include tinea pedis (dermatophytes) and oral candidiasis (C. albicans). HSV-1 causes cold sores and spreads by direct contact.

explanationWrong.B: Dermatophytes cause athlete’s foot, not the named bacterial conjunctivitis.

question: Shingles (herpes zoster) occurs when varicella-zoster virus does which of the following?

Remains confined to keratinocytes with no neural involvement
Is transmitted only by blood transfusion, never by respiratory droplets
Causes measles rash, hacking cough, and photophobia as its primary syndrome

explanationCorrect: VZV causes chicken pox and shingles. Shingles follows reactivation with multiplication in nerve roots and painful blotchy red patches circling the trunk. Transmission is by respiratory droplets and direct contact, similar to measles viruses.

explanationWrong.D: Those features describe measles, not zoster, in this passage.

question: Uncomplicated cystitis is far more common in women than in men. Which anatomic reasons are given?

choices.text: A much shorter urethra and urethral proximity to the vaginal canal and anus, allowing easier bacterial migration into the bladder
Absence of any periurethral flora in women only
A longer urethra that prevents all Gram-negative colonization
Exclusive infection by Treponema pallidum as the usual cystitis pathogen

explanationCorrect: Women are affected far more commonly because of a much shorter urethra and its location relative to the vagina and anus, allowing bacteria to migrate more readily into the bladder. E. coli and Proteus mirabilis are among common bladder pathogens.

explanationWrong.B: The review explains easier migration from adjacent flora, not absence of periurethral organisms.
explanationWrong.C: Women have the shorter urethra; a longer urethra is the male anatomic comparison.
explanationWrong.D: T. pallidum causes syphilis, not typical cystitis; gonorrhea is N. gonorrhoeae with urethral discharge.

question: Primary syphilis is described as manifesting with which lesions after Treponema pallidum penetrates mucous membranes?

Purulent urethral discharge as the only stage of disease
Immediate tertiary aortitis without a primary stage
Painless ulcers known as chancres on external genitalia, perianal skin, or the mouth

explanationWrong.A: Chancroid is a different STD caused by H. ducreyi and is not the primary-syphilis lesion named here.

explanationWrong.C: Tertiary involvement of heart and CNS is a later stage.

question: Tertiary syphilis is described as most notably involving which organ systems?

Only keratinized skin with no visceral disease
Exclusive involvement of the urethra with purulent discharge
The nails alone, as a superficial mycosis

explanationCorrect: Tertiary syphilis can inflame virtually any organ; most notable are cardiovascular and CNS involvement. Chlamydia may cause purulent discharge and can be otherwise asymptomatic. Chancroid is caused by H. ducreyi; trichomoniasis is protozoal (T. vaginalis).

explanationWrong.C: Purulent urethritis is the chlamydia/gonorrhea picture, not the tertiary highlight.
explanationWrong.D: Superficial mycoses are fungal skin infections in another section.

question: AIDS-related opportunistic infection risk is explained by HIV tropism for which cell, and what immune arm fails as a result?

The helper T-lymphocyte CD4, whose failure within CMI places the host at risk for opportunistic infections

explanationCorrect: The primary target of HIV is the helper T-lymphocyte CD4; failure of this CMI cell line places the host at risk for opportunistic fungi, protozoa such as Pneumocystis, bacteria such as M. tuberculosis, and viruses such as CMV.

question: Home-canned food associated with descending paralysis, diplopia, and respiratory failure suggests which tabulated foodborne pathogen and toxin pattern?

Clostridium botulinum, a Gram-positive spore-forming rod that produces toxin and causes flaccid paralysis
Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, characterized by rust-colored sputum

question: A patient develops severe diarrhea after broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which organism and toxin-mediated colitis are identified?

Rotavirus as the sole toxin-producing bacterium of colitis
Salmonella typhi confined to the gallbladder without diarrhea

question: Helicobacter pylori is able to survive high gastric acidity, allowing peptic-ulcer infection, through which described mechanism?

Conversion of gastric acid into methane gas

stomach through the
indirect production of the neutralizing base, ammonia.
Central Nervous

question: Inflammation of brain tissue is generally referred to as which condition, and which viral illnesses are named as causes whose vaccines have markedly reduced incidence?

also cause meningitis.

explanationCorrect: Encephalitis is inflammation of brain tissue and can be caused by viruses including those of mumps and polio; vaccines have dramatically reduced their incidence.

question: Pre-travel immunization counseling for viral hepatitis should reflect which vaccine availability statement in this review?

Hepatitis B is exclusively foodborne; A is only bloodborne

question: Tissue macrophages that clear microbes arise from which circulating leukocyte after maturation in tissues?

question: Shingles is framed in this review as a condition caused by which category of microorganism?

A virus (varicella zoster is listed among candidate viral causes)
An acid-fast intestinal protozoan only
A spore-forming gastric spiral bacterium only

explanationWrong.D: A gastric spiral bacterium (H. pylori) is not the shingles pathogen class in this question.

question: When classifying microbes for antimicrobial selection, which group is identified as eukaryotic rather than prokaryotic in this answer key?

Bacteria, because they have a well-defined nucleus
Rickettsiae, described here as the only eukaryotes
Protozoa, which are eukaryotes

explanationCorrect: The answer key states that protozoa are eukaryotes, in contrast to the prokaryote options discussed in that item.

explanationWrong.A: Viruses are not described as mitochondria-bearing eukaryotes in this answer.
explanationWrong.B: Bacteria are treated among prokaryotes in this chapter, not as nucleated eukaryotes.
explanationWrong.C: Rickettsiae are grouped with prokaryotes in the item being answered, not as the only eukaryotes.

question: Infection-control planning prioritizes the most common reservoir of human pathogens. What is that reservoir according to this review?

choices.text: Other humans, although water, soil, or animals can also be reservoirs
Tap water exclusively, with no human reservoir
Pets only, never other humans
Soil only, because humans cannot harbor pathogens

sourceQuote: The most common reservoir for human pathogens, however, is other humans
explanationCorrect: Reservoirs can be water, soil, or animals, but the most common reservoir for human pathogens is other humans.

explanationWrong.B: Tap water is listed as an option, not as the most common reservoir.
explanationWrong.C: Pets are possible reservoirs but are not identified as the most common.
explanationWrong.D: Soil can be a reservoir, but humans are named as the most common.

question: Which listed additional resource is the 10th-edition microbiology textbook by Pommerville?

choices.text: Mims’ Medical Microbiology, 5th ed., Elsevier Saunders, 2013
Sherris Medical Microbiology, 6th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2014
Fundamentals of Microbiology, 10th ed., Jones and Bartlett, 2014
Review of Medical Microbiology and Immunology, 14th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2016

sourceQuote: Pommerville JC. Fundamentals of Microbiology. 10th ed. Burlington, MA: Jones and Bartlett; 2014
explanationCorrect: Pommerville JC. Fundamentals of Microbiology, 10th ed., Burlington, MA: Jones and Bartlett, 2014, is listed among the additional resources.

explanationWrong.A: Mims’ Medical Microbiology (Goering et al., 5th ed., 2013) is a different listed title.
explanationWrong.B: Ryan and Ray’s Sherris Medical Microbiology (6th ed., 2014) is a different listed title.
explanationWrong.D: Levinson’s Review of Medical Microbiology and Immunology (14th ed., 2016) is a different listed title.

question: After first antigen exposure, which antibody class do B-lymphocytes produce in the primary humoral response before later class switching?

choices.text: Only IgE, regardless of cytokine milieu
IgM, after which any of the five heavy-chain classes may be produced in subsequent responses depending on cytokines
Only kappa light chains without heavy chains
No immunoglobulin until T-independent memory is complete

sourceQuote: B-lymphocytes produce IgM (immunoglobulin M) in a primary antibody (humoral) response
explanationCorrect: B-lymphocytes produce IgM in a primary humoral response and can then produce any of the five antibody classes in subsequent responses depending on detected cytokines. An antibody has two identical heavy and two identical light chains.

explanationWrong.A: IgE is one of five classes that may appear later depending on cytokines, not the obligatory primary product.
explanationWrong.C: A complete antibody comprises two identical heavy chains (alpha, gamma, delta, epsilon, or mu) and kappa or lambda light chains.
explanationWrong.D: Immunoglobulin is produced in the primary response as IgM.

question: Hypersensitivity reactions that require prior exposure are classified into four types. Which statement matches this review?

choices.text: All four types require a presensitized host; type I is immediate (allergy) and type IV is delayed-type hypersensitivity.
Only type IV occurs in a naive host; types I–III never require sensitization.
Type II is delayed-type hypersensitivity to soluble antigen only.
Type I is cytotoxic antibody against tissue antigen, not allergy.

sourceQuote: four types of hypersensitivity, each of which requires a presensitized host
explanationCorrect: There are four hypersensitivity types, each requiring a presensitized host: I immediate/allergy, II cytotoxic antibody-dependent (tissue antigen), III antibody-dependent (soluble antigen), and IV delayed-type.

explanationWrong.B: Each of the four types requires a presensitized host.
explanationWrong.C: Type IV is delayed-type; type II is cytotoxic/antibody-dependent against tissue antigen.
explanationWrong.D: Type I is immediate hypersensitivity or allergy; type II is the cytotoxic tissue-antigen form.

question: Historical context in this introduction places a modern mechanistic understanding of immune processes in which era, relative to earlier vaccine and antisepsis advances?

choices.text: The early 16th century, before any vaccines existed
The late 18th century, simultaneous with the first vaccines and fully modern cellular immunology
The late 19th century sterilization era, which completed T-cell receptor biology
The mid-20th century, after 18th-century vaccines and 19th-century sterilization and disinfection

sourceQuote: was not initiated until the mid-20th century. This chapter gives an overview
explanationCorrect: Vaccines date to the late 18th century and sterilization/disinfection to the late 19th century, but a modern understanding of the immune system was not initiated until the mid-20th century.

explanationWrong.A: Vaccines were developed as early as the late 18th century, not the early 16th.
explanationWrong.B: Late-18th-century vaccines preceded modern cellular immunology, which began in the mid-20th century.
explanationWrong.C: Late-19th-century sterilization did not complete modern immune-process understanding as dated here.

question: Disruption of skin or gut microbiota can facilitate pathogen overgrowth. By which two modes do commensal organisms help guard those barriers?

choices.text: They abolish all hematopoietic stem-cell differentiation.
They convert all myeloid cells into lymphoid progenitors.
They secrete defense molecules that lyse or neutralize pathogens, and they colonize the site so nutrients needed by pathogens become unsustainable.
They replace the nuclear envelope of invading bacteria.

sourceQuote: secretion of defense molecules that lyse or neutralize pathogens
explanationCorrect: Commensals on skin and gut help by secreting lytic or neutralizing defense molecules and by colonizing until conditions such as available nutrients are unsustainable for pathogens.

explanationWrong.A: Immune cells arise from hematopoietic stem cells; commensals are not said to abolish that differentiation.
explanationWrong.B: Lymphoid versus myeloid categorization of immune cells is separate from commensal barrier functions.
explanationWrong.D: Replacement of a bacterial nuclear envelope is not a commensal mechanism described (and prokaryotes lack a nucleus).

question: Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes that kill virus-infected cells are identified by which co-receptor in this leukocyte table?

choices.text: CD4, which marks TH1 and TH2 cells that activate B cells
CD8, along with TCR α/β, CD3, CD28, and MHC I, on cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells
FcεR only, which defines all T-cell killing
CD19 and CD20, which mark cytotoxic T cells rather than B cells

sourceQuote: Killing of infected cells CD8, TCRα, TCRβ, CD3, CD28, MHC I
explanationCorrect: Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes kill infected cells and express CD8, TCR α/β, CD3, CD28, and MHC I. TH1/TH2 cells express CD4 and activate B cells; NK cells kill tumor and virus-infected cells with a different marker set.

explanationWrong.A: CD4 marks helper T cells (TH1/TH2) involved in B-cell activation, not the cytotoxic lineage in this table.
explanationWrong.C: FcεR is listed on eosinophils, mast cells, and basophils, not as the cytotoxic T-cell co-receptor.
explanationWrong.D: CD19 and CD20 are B-lymphocyte markers, not cytotoxic T-cell markers.

question: Autoimmune risk is reduced by central tolerance. Where do developing lymphocytes undergo selection for tolerance to self-antigens?

choices.text: Within primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus), so they react only to non-self antigens in the periphery
Only in the epidermis after they become plasma cells
Exclusively in the adrenal medulla during catecholamine secretion
Only in circulating erythrocytes that lack antigen receptors

sourceQuote: selection for tolerance to self-antigens within the primary lymphoid organs
explanationCorrect: In primary lymphoid organs—bone marrow (B cells, NK cells) and thymus (T cells)—lymphocytes obtain antigen receptors and undergo selection for self-tolerance so they recognize only non-self antigens peripherally. Secondary organs include spleen, lymph nodes, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

explanationWrong.B: Plasma-cell maturation is not the primary-organ self-tolerance selection described.
explanationWrong.C: The adrenal medulla is an endocrine tissue, not a primary lymphoid organ.
explanationWrong.D: Erythrocytes are not the cells undergoing antigen-receptor selection in marrow and thymus.

question: The thymus is identified as the primary lymphoid organ in which which cells mature from hematopoietic stem cells and undergo selection?

choices.text: Erythrocytes only
Neutrophils exclusively
Natural killer cells that never enter the bloodstream
T-lymphocytes

sourceQuote: The secondary lymphoid organs and tissues consist of the spleen, lymph
explanationCorrect: T-lymphocytes mature and are selected in the thymus, then enter the bloodstream and may migrate to secondary lymphoid tissues: spleen, lymph nodes, and MALT such as tonsils and Peyer’s patches, where naive lymphocytes meet antigen.

explanationWrong.A: Erythrocyte maturation is not the thymic function given.
explanationWrong.B: Neutrophils are not the cells named as maturing in the thymus here.
explanationWrong.C: Differentiated lymphocytes are released into the bloodstream.

question: Naive lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid tissue recognize antigen presented by an APC in the context of which cell-surface structure?

choices.text: A major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule
A ribosomal RNA codon unrelated to antigen display
A bacterial plasmid R-factor
A eutectic mixture of camphor and menthol

sourceQuote: recognizes a specific antigen presented by an APC such as a macrophage.
explanationCorrect: Antigen is presented with MHC. The complex is bound by the TCR on T cells or by membrane antibody plus accessory molecules (BCR) on B cells, triggering cytokine/chemokine production and differentiation.

explanationWrong.B: Antigen presentation is an MHC-restricted surface event, not a ribosomal process.
explanationWrong.C: R-factor plasmids are bacterial resistance elements, not lymphocyte antigen receptors.
explanationWrong.D: Eutectic mixtures are compounding chemistry, not immune recognition.

question: After a neutrophil or macrophage internalizes a bacterium, which fusion event delivers digestive enzymes onto the organism?

choices.text: Fusion of the nucleus with the Golgi stack
Fusion of mitochondria with the plasma membrane only
Immediate exocytosis of intact live organisms without a phagosome
Merger of the phagosome with a lysosome containing digestive enzymes

sourceQuote: The phagosome then merges with a specialized compartment of the phagocyte called a lysosome
explanationCorrect: Innate phagocytes envelop pathogens in a phagosome that merges with a lysosome whose enzymes digest the microorganism; peptides can then be displayed with MHC on the cell surface.

explanationWrong.A: Nuclear–Golgi fusion is not the microbicidal step described.
explanationWrong.B: Mitochondrial fusion with the plasma membrane is not the phagolysosome pathway.
explanationWrong.C: Internalization into a phagosome precedes lysosomal digestion, not immediate release of live organisms.

question: After a phagosome forms, it merges with a lysosome whose enzymes digest the microorganism. How do PMNs (neutrophils) differ from antigen-presenting phagocytes in this account?

choices.text: PMNs present digested antigen on MHC at the cell surface more efficiently than macrophages
PMNs cannot ingest extracellular pathogens at all
PMNs lack granules and cannot release lytic molecules
PMNs ingest pathogens in phagolysosomes but do not present antigen on their cell surface

sourceQuote: phagolysosomes, but they do not present antigen on their cell surface. These
explanationCorrect: The phagosome merges with a lysosome; digested bits can be combined with MHC and expressed on the phagocyte surface. PMNs ingest extracellular pathogens in phagolysosomes but do not present antigen; they can release granule contents extracellularly and are extremely short-lived.

explanationWrong.A: PMNs are explicitly said not to present antigen on their surface.
explanationWrong.B: PMNs bind and ingest extracellular pathogens in phagolysosomes.
explanationWrong.C: PMNs contain granules with antibiotic and lytic molecules that can be released outside the cell.

question: Two features that distinguish adaptive from innate immunity, as stated, are which of the following?

choices.text: Nonspecific pattern recognition and absence of lymphocytes
Specific recognition of antigens and immune memory that can provide lifelong protection against the same pathogens
Degranulation of neutrophils as the only effector mechanism
Restriction of all adaptive responses to the bloodstream rather than lymphoid tissue

sourceQuote:
unlike
innate immunity, adaptive immunity involves specific recognition of antigens.
Second, adaptive
explanationCorrect: Adaptive immunity involves specific antigen recognition and immune memory, with B- and T-lymphocytes participating. It has primary and secondary phases; the primary phase usually occurs in lymphoid tissue.

explanationWrong.A: Those features describe innate, not adaptive, responses as contrasted here.
explanationWrong.C: Neutrophil degranulation is an innate phagocyte function in the prior passage, not the distinguishing adaptive features.
explanationWrong.D: The primary adaptive phase is described as usually occurring in lymphoid tissue.

question: Therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are produced by cells analogous to terminally differentiated B-lineage effectors. What distinguishes plasma cells from memory B cells in this review?

choices.text: Plasma cells remain naive and never secrete antibody.
Memory B cells are short-lived and cannot recognize antigen again.
Plasma cells are terminally differentiated, do not proliferate, and produce and release large amounts of antibody; memory B cells are long-lived and primed for a secondary response.
Both cell types present only MHC class II on every nucleated cell in the body.

sourceQuote: plasma cells are terminally differentiated, meaning that they do not proliferate
explanationCorrect: Some activated B cells become long-lived memory cells primed for a secondary response; others mature into short-lived, terminally differentiated plasma cells that do not proliferate and secrete large amounts of antibody.

explanationWrong.A: Plasma cells are the antibody-producing effectors, not nonsecretory naive cells.
explanationWrong.B: Memory B cells are long-lived and primed to recognize antigen again.
explanationWrong.D: MHC class I is found on nearly every cell and presents intracellular antigens; that is a T-cell antigen-presentation fact, not a plasma-versus-memory distinction.

question: MHC class I molecules are found on nearly every cell and present which type of antigen?

choices.text: Only extracellular bacterial toxins ingested by APCs
Only polysaccharide capsules from extracellular pathogens
Phagocytosed antigens exclusively on B-cells via BCR internalization
Intracellular antigens from pathogens that live and reproduce inside host cells, such as viruses and obligate intracellular bacteria

sourceQuote:
MHC class I molecules are found on the cell surface
of nearly every cell
explanationCorrect: MHC class I molecules on nearly every cell present intracellular antigens (e.g., viruses and obligate intracellular bacteria). MHC class II on APCs present phagocytosed or internalized extracellular antigens.

explanationWrong.A: Extracellular antigens presented after phagocytosis are the MHC class II/APC pathway described.
explanationWrong.B: Extracellular pathogen antigens are associated with MHC class II on APCs, not MHC class I on nearly every cell.
explanationWrong.C: BCR internalization and MHC II presentation is the B-cell pathway for extracellular antigen, not the MHC I description.

question: Cytotoxic T-cells are described as expressing which coreceptor and recognizing antigen in which MHC context?

choices.text: CD4, recognizing antigen on MHC class II molecules on APCs
CD8, recognizing antigen on MHC class I molecules on infected cells
CD4, recognizing antigen on MHC class I molecules on APCs
CD8, recognizing antigen on MHC class II molecules on B-cells only

sourceQuote:
molecules on APCs. Cytotoxic T-cells express
CD8 cell surface markers in conjunction
explanationCorrect: Cytotoxic T-cells express CD8 with the TCR and recognize antigen in the context of MHC class I on infected cells; T-helper cells express CD4 and recognize MHC class II on APCs.

explanationWrong.A: That profile describes T-helper cells, not cytotoxic T-cells.
explanationWrong.C: CD4/MHC II on APCs is the helper subset; cytotoxic cells are CD8/MHC I.
explanationWrong.D: Cytotoxic T-cells recognize MHC class I on infected cells, not MHC class II on B-cells only.

question: Bivalent antibody binding depends on independent Fab arms. How many antigen-binding sites does each intact antibody molecule have, and which domains form each site?

choices.text: One site formed only by paired CH3 domains at the C-terminus
Two sites, each formed by the VL domain of one light chain and the VH domain of one heavy chain; a hinge between CH1 and CH2 allows independent movement
Four identical sites formed exclusively by carbohydrate on the Fc region
No binding sites until the antibody is cleaved into light chains only

sourceQuote: each intact antibody molecule has two antigen-binding sites
explanationCorrect: Each intact antibody has two antigen-binding sites formed by paired VL and VH domains. The hinge between CH1 and CH2 provides flexibility so the sites can operate independently.

explanationWrong.A: CH3 domains lie toward the Fc/C-terminus and are not described as forming the sole antigen-binding site.
explanationWrong.C: Two protein combining sites are formed by variable domains, not four carbohydrate-only Fc sites.
explanationWrong.D: Intact four-chain antibodies already possess two combining sites; cleavage is not required to create binding.

question: Papain cleavage of an intact immunoglobulin yields two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment. The Fc fragment consists of which structural components?

choices.text: Two intact antigen-binding sites formed solely by paired light chains
One light chain plus the VH and CH1 domains of one heavy chain
The hinge region and the CH2 and CH3 domains of the heavy chains
Only the VH domains of both heavy chains

sourceQuote: the hinge region and CH2 and CH3 domains of the heavy chains
explanationCorrect: Papain produces two antigen-binding Fab fragments and one Fc fragment. Fc comprises the hinge plus CH2 and CH3 of the heavy chains and mediates effector function.

explanationWrong.A: Antigen-binding sites reside in Fab fragments, not in Fc.
explanationWrong.B: That domain composition describes each Fab fragment (light chain plus VH and CH1).
explanationWrong.D: VH domains are part of the antigen-binding Fab region, not Fc.

question: Immunoglobulin class names (IgA, IgG, IgD, IgE, IgM) correspond to which structural feature?

choices.text: The light-chain isotype only (kappa versus lambda)
The Fc carbohydrate content exclusive of heavy-chain identity
The CDR amino-acid sequence of the antigen-binding site alone
The type of heavy chain (alpha, gamma, delta, epsilon, or mu)

sourceQuote: antibody name designations correspond to the heavy chain they possess:
explanationCorrect: Five heavy-chain types (α, γ, δ, ε, μ) differ in sequence, charge, size, and carbohydrate content; they determine function and superstructure and thus the IgA/G/D/E/M names. IgA is often a dimer in mucosal secretions.

explanationWrong.A: Class names are tied to heavy chains, not light-chain isotype.
explanationWrong.B: Carbohydrate differences exist among heavy chains but do not independently name the class apart from heavy-chain type.
explanationWrong.C: Antigen-binding specificity is not the class-naming rule given here.

question: Which antibody class is the major mediator of secondary (memory) humoral responses and crosses the placenta to provide neonatal passive immunity?

choices.text: IgG
IgM only, which cannot cross the placenta
Secretory IgA as the predominant serum antibody
IgE, the most abundant serum immunoglobulin

sourceQuote: IgG is the predominant class of antibody found in serum, with four
explanationCorrect: IgG is the predominant serum antibody (four subclasses), the major class of secondary humoral responses, and crosses the placenta. IgA is mainly secretory at mucosae; IgD is abundant on B-cell membranes; IgE is the least represented in serum.

explanationWrong.B: Placental transfer is attributed to maternal IgG.
explanationWrong.C: sIgA is the dimer in secretions; IgG predominates in serum.
explanationWrong.D: IgE is the least represented serum class and is largely membrane-bound.

question: Antibody avidity is distinguished from affinity in that avidity measures which of the following?

choices.text: The combined affinities of each paratope for all corresponding available epitopes on an antigen
Only hydrogen bonding at a single combining site
Exclusively repulsive electrostatic forces at the Fc domain
Complementarity of C1q with the antigen-binding groove

sourceQuote: the combined affinities of each paratope for all of its corresponding available epitopes
explanationCorrect: Affinity describes attractive versus repulsive forces at one epitope–paratope pair. Avidity is the sum of those affinities across all available epitopes.

explanationWrong.B: Hydrogen bonding is one force contributing to affinity at a single site, not avidity.
explanationWrong.C: Avidity is not defined by repulsive forces at Fc.
explanationWrong.D: C1q binding is an effector interaction, not a measure of avidity.

question: Which statement correctly describes pokeweed mitogen, phytohemagglutinin, and concanavalin A?

choices.text: Pokeweed mitogen is derived from red kidney beans and activates only T-cells
Pokeweed mitogen is a B-cell mitogen, whereas all three listed mitogens are T-cell mitogens
Concanavalin A is derived from pokeweed and activates only B-cells
Mitogens bind exclusively within the antigen-binding site of the receptor

sourceQuote: Pokeweed mitogen is a B-cell mitogen, whereas all three are T-cell mitogens
explanationCorrect: Mitogens cross-link antigen receptors outside the antigen-binding site. Pokeweed mitogen activates B-cells, and pokeweed mitogen, PHA, and concanavalin A all activate T-cells.

explanationWrong.A: PHA, not pokeweed mitogen, is derived from red kidney beans.
explanationWrong.C: Concanavalin A is derived from castor beans, not pokeweed.
explanationWrong.D: Mitogens bind and cross-link receptors outside the antigen-binding site.

question: Stimulation of B-lymphocytes by T-independent antigens leads to secretion of antibody almost exclusively of which class?

choices.text: IgG
IgA
IgE
IgM

sourceQuote: secrete antibody almost exclusively of the IgM class
explanationCorrect: T-independent antigens drive B-cell antibody secretion that is almost exclusively IgM, without T-cell help for class switching.

explanationWrong.A: IgG class switching typically requires T-dependent help, not T-independent stimulation.
explanationWrong.B: IgA is not the nearly exclusive product of T-independent B-cell stimulation.
explanationWrong.C: IgE is not the nearly exclusive isotype produced after T-independent activation.

question: The high-affinity receptor for IgE is present primarily on which cells?

choices.text: Circulating B-lymphocytes only
Most leukocytes as the low-affinity receptor
Mast cells and basophils
Neutrophils exclusively

sourceQuote: The high-affinity receptor is present primarily on mast cells and basophils
explanationCorrect: High-affinity FcRI is primarily on mast cells and basophils and, with the low-affinity receptor, triggers degranulation in allergic reactions.

explanationWrong.A: B-cells are not the primary site of high-affinity IgE receptors.
explanationWrong.B: The low-affinity receptor is present on most leukocytes, not the high-affinity receptor.
explanationWrong.D: Neutrophils are not the primary cells bearing high-affinity FcRI.

question: Low-affinity Fc receptors (FcRII) discussed in this immunology section are present primarily on which cells?

choices.text: Mast cells and basophils only
Most leukocytes
Mature erythrocytes exclusively
Platelets and megakaryocytes only

sourceQuote: the low-affinity receptor is present on most leukocytes
explanationCorrect: FcRII, the low-affinity receptor, is present on most leukocytes, in contrast to high-affinity FcRI on mast cells and basophils.

explanationWrong.A: Mast cells and basophils are the primary sites of the high-affinity receptor FcRI.
explanationWrong.C: Erythrocytes are not identified as the FcRII distribution here.
explanationWrong.D: Platelets/megakaryocytes are not the primary FcRII distribution given in this passage.

question: Because cytokines strongly influence nearby cells in their microenvironment, production of individual cytokines is described as which of the following?

choices.text: Constitutive and unregulated once infection begins
Transient and tightly regulated
Restricted to colony-stimulating factors only
Independent of immunoglobulin class switching in B-lymphocytes

sourceQuote:
in
their microenvironment, production of individual cytokines is transient and
tightly regulated.
explanationCorrect: Cytokine production is transient and tightly regulated because of their influence on cells in the microenvironment, including effects on nearby leukocyte differentiation and immunoglobulin class synthesized by B-lymphocytes.

explanationWrong.A: The text stresses tight regulation, not constitutive unregulated release.
explanationWrong.C: Interleukins, TNFs, IFNs, growth factors, chemokines, and CSFs are all listed as cytokine groups.
explanationWrong.D: Cytokines are described as able to influence the immunoglobulin class synthesized by nearby B-lymphocytes.

question: IFN-γ, produced by T-cells and NK cells, differs from IFN-α and IFN-β by inducing which of the following?

choices.text: Expression of both MHC class I and class II molecules
MHC class I expression only, acting solely on tissue cells
Production exclusively by macrophages
Proliferation of TH2 cells

sourceQuote: induce expression of both MHC class I and class II molecules
explanationCorrect: IFN-α/β mainly induce MHC I on tissue cells, whereas IFN-γ acts on tissue cells and leukocytes to induce both MHC I and MHC II, activate macrophages, and inhibit TH2 cells.

explanationWrong.B: MHC I–only induction on tissue cells describes IFN-α and IFN-β, not IFN-γ.
explanationWrong.C: IFN-γ is produced by T-cells and NK cells, not solely by macrophages.
explanationWrong.D: IFN-γ inhibits rather than promotes TH2 action and proliferation.

question: Which vaccines are examples of live, attenuated antigen preparations in which virulence is lost but antigens remain intact?

choices.text: Typhoid vaccine and the Salk polio vaccine
MMR and oral polio vaccines
Pneumococcal, Hib, and hepatitis B vaccines
Smallpox vaccine as it is commonly used today

sourceQuote: Live, attenuated vaccines include the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) and oral polio vaccines
explanationCorrect: Attenuation impairs virulence while leaving antigens intact. MMR and oral polio are live, attenuated vaccines.

explanationWrong.A: Typhoid and Salk polio vaccines use killed, intact organisms.
explanationWrong.C: Pneumococcal, Hib, and HBV vaccines use prepared fractionated antigen.
explanationWrong.D: Live natural organisms (smallpox) are rarely used as vaccine preparations.

question: In a complement fixation test, a tube whose antiserum contained antigen-specific antibody is recognized by which endpoint?

choices.text: Free complement remaining and lysis of sheep red blood cells
Hemolysis identical to the antibody-free control tube
Unbound complement that lyses the indicator cells
Sheep red blood cells collecting at the bottom of the tube with no cell lysis

sourceQuote: the SRBCs will collect at the bottom of the tube and there will be no cell lysis
explanationCorrect: Antigen–antibody complexes fix all complement, so added SRBCs plus anti-SRBC antibody cannot lyse; cells settle without hemolysis.

explanationWrong.A: Free complement and lysis occur when antibody is absent and complement is not fixed.
explanationWrong.B: The control (no antibody) retains free complement and does not match the positive-antibody endpoint.
explanationWrong.C: Unbound complement is the control condition, not the antigen-specific antibody condition.

question: In a complement-fixation assay, which indicator system is added to the tubes after antigen, antiserum, and complement?

choices.text: Unlabeled latex beads without antibody
Only free complement without any cells
Sheep red blood cells (SRBCs) plus a small amount of anti-SRBC antibody
Precipitin agar containing no complement

sourceQuote: an indicator cell, such as sheep red blood cells (SRBCs), and a
explanationCorrect: After the antigen–antibody–complement step, SRBCs and anti-SRBC antibody are added. Where antigen-specific antibody consumed complement, SRBCs settle without lysis; free complement in controls produces lysis.

explanationWrong.A: Latex agglutination is not the indicator described.
explanationWrong.B: Complement is already in the system; SRBCs plus anti-SRBC antibody are the indicator.
explanationWrong.D: Immunodiffusion/precipitin testing is introduced later as a different method.

question: In a hemagglutination well, what visual result indicates a sufficiently high concentration of antigen-specific antibody?

choices.text: A tight pellet of RBCs at the well bottom
A mat-like, diffuse-looking circle formed by cross-linked RBCs
Complete absence of any settled cells
Complement-mediated lysis of SRBCs as in a positive complement-fixation control

sourceQuote: the antibodies will cross-link with the RBCs and form a mat-like complex
explanationCorrect: If enough antigen-specific antibody is present, antibodies cross-link RBCs into a mat-like complex that settles as a diffuse circle; too little antibody yields a tight pellet.

explanationWrong.A: A tight pellet indicates too little or no specific antibody.
explanationWrong.C: Cells still settle; the pattern (mat versus pellet) is what differs.
explanationWrong.D: Lysis is the complement-fixation indicator, not the hemagglutination readout.

question: In an ELISA that quantifies antigen-specific antibody, fluorescence is generated after addition of which reagent to antigen-coated wells?

choices.text: Complement plus sheep red blood cells
Unlabeled Fcγ fragment scored by visual hemolysis
A fluorescent-labeled antibody specific for Fcγ, with readout in a luminometer
Pokeweed mitogen to cross-link BCRs

sourceQuote: a fluorescent-labeled antibody that is specific for Fcγ is added
explanationCorrect: After serum antibody binds plate-bound antigen, a fluorescent anti-Fcγ reagent binds those antibodies’ Fc domains and is quantified in a luminometer.

explanationWrong.A: Complement and SRBCs are used in complement fixation, not ELISA.
explanationWrong.B: ELISA uses a fluorescent anti-Fcγ antibody, not unlabeled Fcγ scored by hemolysis.
explanationWrong.D: Mitogens are lymphocyte activators, not ELISA detection reagents.

question: In an antibody-capture (sandwich) ELISA for cytokine concentration, what is coated in the wells and what is added after unbound material is washed away?

choices.text: Antigen-specific antibody is coated in the wells; after washing, a second fluorescent-labeled, antigen-specific antibody is added
Only unlabeled antigen is coated, with no detection antibody
Whole leukocytes are plated so that they secrete cytokine directly into a luminometer cuvette
Fc-specific antibody is never used in any ELISA format described

sourceQuote:
can be measured by antibody
capture or sandwich ELISA, where antigen-specific antibody
explanationCorrect: In sandwich ELISA, antigen-specific antibody coats the wells, sample is added, unbound material is washed away, then a second fluorescent-labeled antigen-specific antibody is added. Alternatively, antiserum proteins bind plastic first, then antigen-specific antibody (directly labeled or detected with fluorescent Fc-specific antibody) is added.

explanationWrong.B: A second labeled antigen-specific antibody is used after capture.
explanationWrong.C: The methods described plate antiserum or capture antibody, not whole leukocytes as the well coat.
explanationWrong.D: If the first detection antibody is unlabeled, a fluorescent-tagged Fc-specific antibody is added.

question: Type I hypersensitivity (immediate hypersensitivity/allergy) is mediated by which sequence?

choices.text: IgM-only complement fixation without mast cells
T-cell delayed responses without antibody, as the definition of atopy
Elevated IgE bound by Fc epsilon receptor on mast cells, cross-linked by antigen–allergen, leading to degranulation
Immune-complex deposition as the sole mechanism of anaphylaxis

sourceQuote:
exposed) host. Type I hypersensitivity is also known as immediate
hypersensitivity or
explanationCorrect: Type I includes atopy (allergic rhinitis, food allergy, eczema), asthma, and anaphylaxis. It requires a presensitized host and is mediated by IgE on mast-cell Fc epsilon receptors, cross-linked by allergen, causing degranulation. Hypersensitivity is classified as types I–IV.

explanationWrong.A: The Type I pathway given is IgE/mast cell, not IgM-only complement.
explanationWrong.B: Atopy is listed under Type I immediate hypersensitivity, not as antibody-independent delayed T-cell disease in this paragraph.
explanationWrong.D: Anaphylaxis is listed under Type I IgE-mediated disease, not as immune-complex (Type III) in this passage.

question: A patient at risk of anaphylaxis carries epinephrine because this agent:

choices.text: Acts as a bronchodilator
Is an H1-antihistamine equivalent to diphenhydramine
Is a corticosteroid anti-inflammatory equivalent to dexamethasone
Prevents type II hemolysis of erythrocytes

sourceQuote: Epinephrine acts as a bronchodilator, diphenhydramine is an effective antihistamine
explanationCorrect: Epinephrine bronchodilates; diphenhydramine is the antihistamine and dexamethasone the steroid anti-inflammatory in this anaphylaxis kit.

explanationWrong.B: Diphenhydramine, not epinephrine, is the effective antihistamine.
explanationWrong.C: Dexamethasone, not epinephrine, is the anti-inflammatory steroid.
explanationWrong.D: Type II hypersensitivity is cytotoxic antibody against membranes/tissues, not the role of epinephrine.

question: Myasthenia gravis is classified as which hypersensitivity pattern in this discussion?

choices.text: Type I IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation only
Type III immune-complex deposition in vessel walls only
Type II, caused by antibodies to acetylcholine receptors at nerve–muscle junctions
Type IV delayed T-cell contact dermatitis only

sourceQuote: destruction of the cell or tissue. Examples of type II hypersensitivity include transfusion-related
explanationCorrect: Type II reactions involve antibodies to surface antigens causing cell or tissue destruction. Examples include transfusion reactions, hemolytic disease of the newborn, Goodpasture syndrome, and myasthenia gravis (anti-ACh receptor antibodies).

explanationWrong.A: Type I is not the classification given for myasthenia gravis here.
explanationWrong.B: Type III (serum sickness, Arthus, SLE) is the next section.
explanationWrong.D: Type IV is delayed-type hypersensitivity such as contact dermatitis.

question: Serum sickness, the Arthus reaction, and systemic lupus erythematosus are presented as examples of which hypersensitivity type?

choices.text: Type II antibody-mediated cytolysis of surface antigens only
Type III, involving immune complexes of antibody and soluble antigen
Type IV memory T-cell delayed hypersensitivity only
Complement-fixation SRBC lysis as a diagnostic class of allergy

sourceQuote: systemic lupus erythematosus (caused by antibodies to DNA, histones, and
explanationCorrect: Type III reactions follow formation of immune complexes with soluble antigen. SLE is attributed to antibodies to DNA, histones, and nuclear antigens. Type IV (DTH) is T-cell mediated (for example, contact dermatitis).

explanationWrong.A: Type II concerns surface antigens (transfusion, HDN, Goodpasture, MG).
explanationWrong.C: Type IV is delayed-type hypersensitivity, discussed separately.
explanationWrong.D: SRBC lysis is a laboratory indicator, not a hypersensitivity class.

question: Molecular mimicry can initiate autoimmunity when which event occurs?

choices.text: MHC class I genes are deleted from all antigen-presenting cells
Antigens from a pathogen share epitopes with self-antigens
Only corticosteroid deficiency is present
Vaccines contain live natural smallpox as the usual modern preparation

sourceQuote: antigens from a pathogen share epitopes with self-antigens
explanationCorrect: Shared pathogen and self epitopes can activate B-cells that secrete self-reactive antibodies, producing immune attack on host tissues.

explanationWrong.A: Molecular mimicry is defined by shared epitopes, not deletion of MHC class I.
explanationWrong.C: Hereditary MHC II alleles and mimicry are discussed; isolated steroid deficiency is not the mechanism.
explanationWrong.D: Vaccine composition is not the definition of molecular mimicry.

question: Molecular mimicry leading to autoimmunity is described as occurring when which immunologic event takes place?

choices.text: Pathogen antigens share epitopes with self-antigens, activating B-cells that produce self-reactive antibodies
Regulatory T-cells are deleted so that all subsequent infections become autoimmune
Mast-cell Fc receptors bind IgG and trigger immediate cytotoxic killing of host valves
Complement is genetically absent, so immune complexes cannot be cleared

sourceQuote:
antigens from a pathogen
share epitopes with self-antigens; therefore, infection with this
explanationCorrect: When pathogen antigens share epitopes with self-antigens, infection can activate B-cells that secrete self-reactive antibodies and cause immune attack on host tissues, as in rheumatic fever after streptococcal infection.

explanationWrong.B: The passage attributes mimicry to shared epitopes and self-reactive antibodies, not to wholesale Treg deletion.
explanationWrong.C: Fc-receptor degranulation is not the mechanism given for molecular mimicry.
explanationWrong.D: Complement deficiency is not described as the basis of molecular mimicry.

question: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is characterized in this discussion by which primary defect?

choices.text: Complete absence of the thymus with no circulating T-cells
Isolated complement C3 deficiency with normal antibody titers
Defective T-cell signaling to B-cells, yielding defective B-cell maturation and little detectable serum antibody
Overproduction of IgE from unrestricted class switching

sourceQuote:
variable
immunodeficiency, or CVID (defective T-cell signaling to B-cells resulting in
defective
explanationCorrect: CVID is described as defective T-cell signaling to B-cells, resulting in defective B-cell maturation and little detectable serum antibody.

explanationWrong.A: Thymic aplasia is not the CVID mechanism given here.
explanationWrong.B: CVID is framed as a B-cell/antibody maturation problem, not isolated C3 deficiency.
explanationWrong.D: CVID is associated with little detectable serum antibody, not IgE overproduction from class switching.

question: Chronic granulomatous disease results from which phagocyte defect?

choices.text: HIV infection of CD4+ T-cells
Defective DNA repair causing breaks at immunoglobulin or TCR loci
Absence of all circulating complement proteins
A defect in an oxygen reduction enzyme causing faulty pathogen killing in the phagolysosome

sourceQuote: a defect in an oxygen reduction enzyme resulting in faulty pathogen killing
explanationCorrect: CGD is a phagocyte killing defect due to a faulty oxygen-reduction enzyme in the phagolysosome, distinct from AIDS, ataxia-telangiectasia, or complement deficiency.

explanationWrong.A: HIV infection of CD4+ T-cells describes AIDS, not CGD.
explanationWrong.B: DNA-repair defects at Ig/TCR loci describe ataxia-telangiectasia.
explanationWrong.C: Complement protein deficiencies are a separate immunodeficiency category.

question: MHC genes are described as codominant because:

choices.text: Only the paternal MHC haplotype is expressed
MHC class II molecules are confined to erythrocytes
All of the MHC genes are equally expressed in an individual
Matching donor and recipient MHC haplotype is unnecessary

sourceQuote: all of the MHC genes are equally expressed in an individual
explanationCorrect: Codominance means every MHC gene is equally expressed, which is why haplotype matching of donor and recipient is crucial for alloantigen reactions.

explanationWrong.A: Codominance is equal expression of all MHC genes, not paternal-only expression.
explanationWrong.B: MHC class I is on all nucleated cells; class II is on APCs, not erythrocytes.
explanationWrong.D: Matching MHC haplotype of donor and recipient is described as crucial.

question: The V domains of one heavy chain and one light chain of an antibody together comprise which functional region?

choices.text: The antigen-binding site
The Fc region
The hinge region alone
The CD8 coreceptor

sourceQuote: The V domains of one heavy chain and one light chain of an antibody comprise
explanationCorrect: Paired heavy- and light-chain variable domains form the antigen-binding site of the antibody.

explanationWrong.B: Fc is formed from constant regions of the heavy chains, not V domains.
explanationWrong.C: The hinge is not composed of the V domains of heavy and light chains.
explanationWrong.D: CD8 is a T-cell coreceptor, not an antibody domain assembly.

question: Immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by which immunoglobulin class?

choices.text: IgM
IgE
IgA
IgG2b

sourceQuote: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by A. IgM.
explanationCorrect: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated, distinguishing it from other listed isotypes in the self-assessment item.

explanationWrong.A: IgM is not the mediator of type I hypersensitivity.
explanationWrong.C: IgA is not the mediator of type I hypersensitivity.
explanationWrong.D: IgG2b is not the mediator of type I hypersensitivity.

question: Before transplantation, the most important determination in tissue typing is:

choices.text: Complement fixation titer
Antibody isotype of the recipient
Cell-adhesion molecule profile
MHC haplotype

sourceQuote: The most important determination in tissue typing is
explanationCorrect: Histocompatibility assessment centers on MHC haplotype matching between donor and recipient.

explanationWrong.A: Complement fixation is a serologic antibody test, not the primary tissue-typing determinant.
explanationWrong.B: Isotype determination is not the key tissue-typing criterion.
explanationWrong.C: Cell adhesion is not identified as the most important tissue-typing determination.

question: IgG is the predominant antibody in serum because it constitutes approximately what fraction of total immunoglobulin?
sourceQuote: it constitutes approximately 75% of total immunoglobulin in serum
explanationCorrect: IgG constitutes about 75% of total serum immunoglobulin, making it the predominant circulating class.

explanationWrong.A: 25% understates the serum IgG fraction.
explanationWrong.B: 50% understates the approximately 75% contribution of IgG.
explanationWrong.D: 95% overstates the serum IgG fraction.

question: Among autografts, isografts, xenografts, and allografts, which transplant type is the most common?

choices.text: Allograft
Xenograft
Isograft
Autograft

sourceQuote: Although xenografts, isografts, and autografts are all valid transplants, allografts are the most common
explanationCorrect: All listed graft types are valid, but allografts are the most commonly performed transplants.

explanationWrong.B: Xenografts are valid but not the most common.
explanationWrong.C: Isografts are valid but not the most common.
explanationWrong.D: Autografts are valid but not the most common.

question: In medicinal chemistry, a pharmacophore is defined as:

choices.text: An inactive analog that cannot bind any receptor
The basic set of structural and chemical features of a drug responsible for its biological activity
The pH of the compartment from which a drug is absorbed
A packaging antioxidant added to exclude oxygen

sourceQuote: A pharmacophore is the basic set of structural and chemical features of a drug
explanationCorrect: The pharmacophore is the core structural and chemical feature set that accounts for a drug’s biological activity.

explanationWrong.A: A pharmacophore is the activity-bearing feature set, not an inactive analog.
explanationWrong.C: Compartment pH relates to pH-partition theory, not the pharmacophore.
explanationWrong.D: Antioxidants are formulation stabilizers, not pharmacophores.

question: The stereochemistry of a chiral drug is assigned using which system?

choices.text: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation alone
pH-partition theory
Homologation of alkyl chains only
The R/S convention (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules)

sourceQuote: using the R/S convention (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules), and describe
explanationCorrect: Chiral configuration is assigned with the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog R/S priority rules, which also relate to how stereochemistry influences activity.

explanationWrong.A: Henderson–Hasselbalch relates ionization to pH, not R/S assignment.
explanationWrong.B: pH-partition theory addresses ionization and membrane permeation, not CIP nomenclature.
explanationWrong.C: Homologation is an SAR tactic, not a stereochemical naming convention.

question: The acid–base character of a drug in solution is determined by:

choices.text: Molecular weight alone
The intended route of administration
The functional groups in the drug molecule
Whether the tablet is scored

sourceQuote: The functional groups (Table 6-1) in a drug molecule determine the acid–base character
explanationCorrect: Most drugs behave as weak acids or weak bases, and their functional groups determine that acid–base behavior, which then influences ADME and compatibility.

explanationWrong.A: Molecular weight does not determine acid–base character.
explanationWrong.B: Route of administration may follow from acid–base properties; it does not create them.
explanationWrong.D: Tablet scoring is a formulation feature unrelated to ionization chemistry.

question: Upon ionization, an acidic drug such as aspirin undergoes which process?

choices.text: Donation of a proton to generate a conjugate base
Acceptance of a proton to generate a conjugate acid
Conversion to a nonelectrolyte
The same proton-accepting reaction as amphetamine

sourceQuote: An acidic drug (e.g., aspirin) donates a proton on ionization to generate a conjugate base
explanationCorrect: Acids donate a proton to form a conjugate base; bases such as amphetamine accept a proton to form a conjugate acid.

explanationWrong.B: Proton acceptance to form a conjugate acid describes a basic drug such as amphetamine.
explanationWrong.C: Ionization generates a charged conjugate, not a nonelectrolyte.
explanationWrong.D: Amphetamine is the example of a base that accepts a proton.

question: The nitrogen atom in pyrrole does not contribute to drug basicity because:

choices.text: Pyrrole lacks a lone pair on nitrogen
The nitrogen lone pair contributes to the aromatic sextet and is unavailable to accept a proton
Pyrrole is more basic than piperidine
The nitrogen is fully protonated at all physiologic pH values

sourceQuote: the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen contributes to the aromatic sextet
explanationCorrect: In pyrrole the nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, so it cannot accept a proton, unlike saturated heterocycles such as pyrrolidine or piperidine.

explanationWrong.A: Pyrrole has a lone pair, but it is committed to aromaticity.
explanationWrong.C: Saturated nitrogen heterocycles are basic; pyrrole is not more basic than piperidine.
explanationWrong.D: Pyrrole nitrogen is not a proton acceptor and is not persistently protonated.

question: Highly polar drugs of low lipophilicity, such as heparin, are candidates for parenteral administration because they:

choices.text: Readily cross membranes by passive diffusion
Are nonelectrolytes at all pH values
Cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
Poorly penetrate biological membranes through passive diffusion

sourceQuote: such drugs poorly penetrate biological membranes through passive diffusion
explanationCorrect: High polarity and low lipophilicity limit passive membrane penetration, so parenteral administration is used.

explanationWrong.A: Poor, not ready, passive penetration is the reason for the parenteral route.
explanationWrong.B: Heparin’s polarity, not nonelectrolyte status, is the cited limitation.
explanationWrong.C: Hydrogen-bonding groups increase aqueous solubility; they do not preclude parenteral use.

question: Highly polar, poorly lipophilic drugs such as heparin are candidates for parenteral administration because of which stated limitation, and what empiric carbon solubilizing potentials are given?

choices.text: They poorly penetrate membranes by passive diffusion; alcohols solubilize about 5 to 6 carbons and phenols about 6 to 7 carbons
They freely diffuse across all membranes and should never be injected
Alcohols solubilize 20–30 carbons, so polarity is irrelevant
Heparin is given orally because log P is extremely high

sourceQuote:
and excretion.
Highly polar drugs of low lipophilicity (e.g., heparin) are candidates
explanationCorrect: Highly polar, low-lipophilicity drugs (e.g., heparin) poorly penetrate membranes by passive diffusion and are parenteral candidates. Empirically, alcohols solubilize about 5–6 carbons and phenols 6–7 carbons relative to hydrophilic groups.

explanationWrong.B: Poor passive membrane penetration is the reason parenteral use is suggested.
explanationWrong.C: The solubilizing potentials given are 5–6 carbons (alcohols) and 6–7 (phenols), not 20–30.
explanationWrong.D: Heparin is the parenteral example for poor passive diffusion, not a high log P oral drug.

question: Log P is the log of the ratio of un-ionized drug in octanol versus water. What absorption implication is stated for high log P, and what remaining requirement is emphasized?

choices.text: High log P prevents all GI absorption because membranes are hydrophilic
Aqueous solubility is unnecessary if log P is high

High log P drugs cross lipid-bilayer membranes more easily and tend to be rapidly absorbed by passive GI diffusion, but some aqueous solubility is still required because drug in solution is needed for absorption
Log P cannot be used to estimate membrane crossing

sourceQuote:
Thus, drugs
with high log P values cross biological membranes more easily
explanationCorrect: Biological membranes have a lipophilic interior, so high log P favors passive GI absorption. Drug must still have some aqueous solubility because absorption requires dissolved drug and because fluids at the absorption site are aqueous.

explanationWrong.A: Membranes have a lipophilic interior; high log P favors crossing, not prevents absorption.
explanationWrong.B: Some aqueous solubility is still required.
explanationWrong.D: Log P is used to estimate the ability of a drug to cross biological membranes.

question: For a weakly acidic drug whose pKa is greater than gastric pH, the drug predominantly:

choices.text: Exists ionized, which limits absorption
Cannot dissolve regardless of pKa
Exists in the un-ionized state, which facilitates absorption
Is absorbed only after phase 2 conjugation

sourceQuote: the drug exists predominantly in the un-ionized state, which facilitates absorption
explanationCorrect: When a weak acid’s pKa exceeds environmental pH (e.g., gastric fluid), the un-ionized fraction predominates and absorption is facilitated.

explanationWrong.A: Ionization that limits absorption occurs when the acid’s pKa is less than environmental pH.
explanationWrong.B: pH-partition theory addresses ionization and permeation, not absolute insolubility.
explanationWrong.D: Conjugation is a metabolic process, not the gastric absorption rule given here.

question: Among drug–receptor chemical interactions, a covalent bond is characterized as:

choices.text: The strongest interaction (50–150 kcal/mol), usually irreversible, and able to destroy the receptor
A weak salt bridge of 1–2 kcal/mol
Always freely reversible without cellular consequence
Never requiring synthesis of a new receptor for recovery of function

sourceQuote: A covalent bond (50–150 kcal/mol) is the strongest of these interactions
explanationCorrect: Covalent bonding is the strongest listed interaction, is usually irreversible, can destroy the receptor, and often requires new receptor synthesis for recovery.

explanationWrong.B: Ionic bonds (salt bridges) are about 5–10 kcal/mol, not 1–2, and are weaker than covalent bonds.
explanationWrong.C: Covalent receptor interactions are usually irreversible.
explanationWrong.D: Full recovery of cellular function often requires synthesis of a new receptor.

question: Occupancy theory of drug–receptor interaction states that pharmacological response magnitude is:

choices.text: Independent of how many receptors are occupied
Directly proportional to the number of receptors bound by the agonist
Produced only by antagonist-induced nonspecific conformational change
Equal solely to collision frequency with inert plasma protein

sourceQuote: a magnitude directly proportional to the number of receptors bound by the drug
explanationCorrect: Occupancy theory holds that agonist binding causes a conformational change whose response magnitude is proportional to the number of occupied receptors.

explanationWrong.A: Occupancy theory explicitly ties response magnitude to the number of bound receptors.
explanationWrong.C: Antagonists do not induce the correct conformational change for a response in induced-fit theory; that is not occupancy theory.
explanationWrong.D: Plasma-protein collisions are not the occupancy-theory mechanism.

question: The R,R-diastereomer of labetalol binds best to which adrenergic receptor?

choices.text: Muscarinic receptor
Nicotinic receptor
α-adrenergic receptor
β-adrenergic receptor

sourceQuote: The R,R-diastereomer of labetalol binds best to the β-adrenergic receptor
explanationCorrect: Labetalol diastereomers differ in receptor preference: R,R binds best to β-receptors, whereas S,R binds best to α-receptors.

explanationWrong.A: Muscarinic receptors are not the labetalol diastereomer targets discussed.
explanationWrong.B: Nicotinic receptors are not the labetalol diastereomer targets discussed.
explanationWrong.C: The S,R-diastereomer, not R,R, binds best to the α-adrenergic receptor.

question: Ester-based procaine lasts 15 to 30 minutes because of rapid hydrolysis. Amide-based lidocaine given locally:

choices.text: Is inactivated even faster by esterases
Cannot be administered locally
Can last up to 3 hours
Is converted in vivo to aspirin

sourceQuote: The amide-based lidocaine can last up to 3 hours when given locally
explanationCorrect: Amides hydrolyze much more slowly than esters, so lidocaine’s local duration can reach 3 hours versus 15–30 minutes for procaine.

explanationWrong.A: Amides are hydrolyzed more slowly than esters, not faster.
explanationWrong.B: Lidocaine is given locally; that is the comparison setting.
explanationWrong.D: Aspirin is a separate ester-prone drug, not a lidocaine metabolite in this discussion.

question: A pharmacophore can be considered which of the following?

choices.text: The minimal set of features in a molecule required to produce a biological or pharmacological effect
Any hydrolytic degradant of an ester drug
A chelating motif used only in EDTA
An inert tablet filler

sourceQuote: the minimal set of features in a molecule required to produce a biological or pharmacological effect
explanationCorrect: The pharmacophore is the minimal three-dimensional set of features (ionizable groups, H-bond partners, lipophilic/aromatic elements) needed for the biological effect.

explanationWrong.B: Hydrolytic degradants are stability products, not pharmacophores.
explanationWrong.C: Chelating motifs are a separate chemical-motif category, not the definition of a pharmacophore.
explanationWrong.D: Fillers are formulation excipients without receptor-recognition features.

question: Captopril inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme in part through which metal-binding motif?

choices.text: A 1,3-dicarbonyl that chelates dietary calcium
A thiol group that interacts with zinc in the enzyme active site
Four EDTA carboxylates as the entire pharmacophore
A tetracycline-like 1-carbonyl, 3-hydroxyl pair

sourceQuote: These drugs possess either a thiol (captopril) or carboxyl group (lisinopril)
explanationCorrect: ACE inhibitors bind active-site zinc; captopril uses a thiol and lisinopril a carboxyl as the metal-interacting pharmacophore element.

explanationWrong.A: 1,3-Dicarbonyl chelation of calcium/magnesium is discussed for tetracycline and ciprofloxacin, not captopril.
explanationWrong.C: EDTA is a universal carboxylate chelator, not the ACE-inhibitor pharmacophore.
explanationWrong.D: That motif belongs to tetracycline/ciprofloxacin metal chelation, not captopril.

question: Tetracycline and ciprofloxacin chelate divalent metals such as calcium or magnesium. This chemistry supports which counseling point?

choices.text: Co-administer with antacids to increase absorption
Use as first-line chelators for lead poisoning
Give with metal salts to increase calcium utilization in children
They are often contraindicated in pediatric use, and co-administration with metal salts is strongly discouraged

sourceQuote: this chemical motif are often contraindicated for pediatric use
explanationCorrect: 1,3-Dicarbonyl or 1-carbonyl,3-hydroxyl motifs chelate Ca/Mg, impairing both drug absorption and metal utilization, so pediatric use and antacid coadministration are discouraged.

explanationWrong.A: Antacids supply metal salts that impair absorption; coadministration is discouraged.
explanationWrong.B: Heavy-metal chelators discussed elsewhere are dimercaprol and D-penicillamine, not these antibiotics.
explanationWrong.C: Chelation can impair the body’s use of metals, especially in growing children.

question: A bioisosteric replacement is best described as:

choices.text: Only lengthening of an alkyl chain (homologation)
Conversion of a free acid to any salt form
Replacement of a functional group with a similar group that may produce the same physiological effect
Photochemical cyclization of a benzodiazepine

sourceQuote: replacement of a functional group in a drug with a similar functional group
explanationCorrect: Bioisosterism swaps a group for a similar one that may retain the physiologic effect while improving physicochemical or pharmacokinetic properties.

explanationWrong.A: Homologation is a separate SAR operation (changing alkyl-chain length).
explanationWrong.B: Salt formation is a formulation tactic, not bioisosteric replacement.
explanationWrong.D: Light-catalyzed cyclization is a degradation pathway, not an SAR design move.

question: For sulfonamide antibacterials, disubstitution on the sulfonamide nitrogen produces which SAR outcome?

choices.text: Loss of activity
Maximal antibacterial activity exceeding monosubstitution
Obligatory conversion into a high-ceiling diuretic
Loss of acidity with improved receptor binding

sourceQuote: heteroaromatic group, but disubstitution results in loss of activity
explanationCorrect: Monosubstitution on the sulfonamide nitrogen, especially with a heteroaromatic group, enhances activity; disubstitution abolishes it. Sulfonamide acidity remains key for binding.

explanationWrong.B: Monosubstitution, not disubstitution, enhances activity.
explanationWrong.C: Diuretic sulfonamides arose from SAR but disubstitution is not said to create high-ceiling diuretics.
explanationWrong.D: Acidity of the sulfonamide is required for binding; electron-withdrawing substituents improve activity by enhancing acidity.

question: In phenylethanolamine SAR, a t-butyl substituent at R1 produces which adrenergic profile?

choices.text: Maximum α-receptor agonism
Maximum β-receptor activity (agonism)
α-receptor antagonism
Loss of all adrenergic activity

sourceQuote: A t-butyl group gives maximum β-receptor activity (agonism)
explanationCorrect: As R1 enlarges, α-agonism falls; t-butyl maximizes β-agonism, whereas groups larger than t-butyl confer α-antagonism.

explanationWrong.A: Increasing R1 size decreases α-agonism rather than maximizing it.
explanationWrong.C: α-Antagonism appears with groups larger than t-butyl (more than four carbons).
explanationWrong.D: t-Butyl maximizes β-agonism; it does not abolish adrenergic activity.

question: Fluoroquinolones, whose prototype nalidixic acid was a chloroquine-production byproduct, interfere with which bacterial process?

choices.text: Cell-wall transpeptidation
30S ribosomal decoding
Dihydropteroate synthesis
Topoisomerase maintenance of DNA supercoiling during transcription and translation

sourceQuote: interfere with the activity of topoisomerase enzymes in bacteria
explanationCorrect: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial topoisomerases that maintain correct DNA supercoiling during transcription and translation.

explanationWrong.A: Cell-wall transpeptidation is not the fluoroquinolone target described.
explanationWrong.B: Ribosomal 30S inhibition is not the mechanism given for this class.
explanationWrong.C: Folate-pathway inhibition is a sulfonamide mechanism, not a fluoroquinolone mechanism.

question: A C6 fluorine on a fluoroquinolone enhances antibacterial activity likely because of:

choices.text: Decreased lipophilicity and poorer cell entry
Obligatory agonism at GABA receptors
Increased lipophilicity and cell penetration
Phototoxicity caused by halogen at X8

sourceQuote: A fluorine substituent at the C6 position enhances activity, likely because of increased lipophilicity and cell penetration
explanationCorrect: C6 fluorine increases lipophilicity and cell penetration, which enhances activity. CNS GABA off-target effects relate to C7 piperazines, and phototoxicity is reduced by methoxy at X8.

explanationWrong.A: The C6 fluorine increases, not decreases, lipophilicity and penetration.
explanationWrong.B: GABA-related CNS effects are linked to C7 piperazine rings, not C6 fluorine.
explanationWrong.D: Methoxy rather than halogen at X8 decreases phototoxicity; that is a different position.

question: Mutations in CYP2D6 generate which phenotypic metabolizer subgroups?

choices.text: Poor, extensive, or ultrarapid metabolizers
Only slow and fast acetylators
Phase 2 conjugator subtypes exclusively
A single uniform extensive-metabolizer group

sourceQuote: three phenotypic subgroups of metabolizers (i.e., poor, extensive, or ultrarapid metabolizers)
explanationCorrect: CYP2D6 polymorphisms yield poor, extensive, or ultrarapid metabolizers, producing responses from severe toxicity to lack of efficacy for many CV and CNS drugs.

explanationWrong.B: Slow/fast acetylation refers to NAT2, not CYP2D6.
