explanationCorrect: Pharmaceutics studies the dosage form; biopharmaceutics studies factors influencing release and absorption from that dosage form.

explanationWrong.A: The drug definition is introductory context, not the definition of biopharmaceutics.
explanationWrong.B: Manufacturing hardware is not the biopharmaceutics focus stated here.
explanationWrong.C: Colorants are excipients; they do not define the field of biopharmaceutics.

question: For a gas dissolved in a liquid, increasing the temperature of the system typically does which of the following to solubility?

choices.text: Increases solubility in proportion to an endothermic solid-like lattice
Leaves solubility unchanged because gases have no vapor pressure
Decreases solubility because of the change in vapor pressure
Converts the system to a USP “very soluble” solid classification

sourceQuote: containing a gas in liquid is increased, the solubility decreases because of the change
explanationCorrect: Unlike many solids in endothermic dissolution, gas-in-liquid solubility decreases as temperature rises because of the change in vapor pressure.

explanationWrong.A: Proportional increase with temperature is described for solids with an endothermic change of state, not for gases.
explanationWrong.B: The text attributes the decrease specifically to vapor-pressure change.
explanationWrong.D: USP solubility terms apply to parts of solvent per gram of solute, not to this gas-temperature effect.

question: In the Biopharmaceutics Classification System as stated here, a drug with low solubility and high permeability is which class?

choices.text: Class 2
Class 1
Class 3
Class 4

sourceQuote: low solubility: high permeability, (3) high solubility: low permeability
explanationCorrect: BCS class 2 is low solubility with high permeability; class 1 is high/high, class 3 high/low, and class 4 low/low.

explanationWrong.B: Class 1 is high solubility and high permeability.
explanationWrong.C: Class 3 is high solubility and low permeability.
explanationWrong.D: Class 4 is low solubility and low permeability.

question: At 20°C, why must more work be expended to expand a water surface than an n-octanol surface?

choices.text: Water’s surface tension is about 27 mN and n-octanol’s is about 72 mN
Both liquids have identical surface free energy so the difference is only density
n-Octanol spontaneously assumes a cubic shape of maximum area
Water’s surface tension is about 72 mN versus about 27 mN for n-octanol

sourceQuote: Water has a surface tension at 20°C of approximately 72 mN
explanationCorrect: Surface free energy (γ) is higher for water (~72 mN) than for n-octanol (~27 mN), so more work is required to expand water’s surface.

explanationWrong.A: The values are reversed relative to the text.
explanationWrong.B: The two liquids have substantially different surface tensions.
explanationWrong.C: Liquids tend toward a spherical shape of minimum surface area, not a cube.

question: Interfacial tension at the boundary between two immiscible liquids is a measure of which of the following?

choices.text: The free energy, or work, required to expand the interfacial area, reflecting attraction and repulsion at the interface
Only the boiling points of the two bulk phases
Newtonian viscosity of the upper plate alone
The USP solubility term for the dispersed solid

sourceQuote: intermolecular forces of attraction and repulsion at the interface
explanationCorrect: Interfacial tension is the free energy (work) to expand the interfacial area and reflects intermolecular attraction and repulsion at the interface.

explanationWrong.B: Boiling point is not the definition given for interfacial tension.
explanationWrong.C: Flow between plates is introduced separately and is not interfacial tension.
explanationWrong.D: USP solubility classification is unrelated to this interface definition.

question: Concentrated colloids, suspensions, and emulsions are grouped together as exhibiting which flow behavior?

choices.text: Strictly Newtonian flow with concentration-independent viscosity
No resistance to flow at any shear stress
Non-Newtonian flow
Gas-like compressibility with a sharp melting point

sourceQuote: suspensions, emulsions) exhibit non-Newtonian flow. Analyses of non-Newtonian substances using a viscometer
explanationCorrect: Solids and heterogeneous liquids such as concentrated colloids, suspensions, and emulsions exhibit non-Newtonian flow, with shear- or time-dependent viscosity.

explanationWrong.A: Newtonian behavior is described for dilute dispersions and simple molecules.
explanationWrong.B: Viscosity is resistance to flow; these systems are not described as frictionless.
explanationWrong.D: Those are solid-state properties, not the rheology classification here.

question: Plastic (Bingham body) flow in a flocculated concentrated suspension is characterized by which statement?

choices.text: Apparent viscosity falls immediately at the smallest applied stress
The system is always dilatant (shear-thickening) at rest
Structure reforms instantly whenever stress is removed, with no yield value
Flow begins only after a limiting yield stress (yield value) is exceeded

sourceQuote: Flow begins only after a limiting yield stress (yield value) is exceeded
explanationCorrect: Bingham (plastic) bodies show no apparent response to low-level stress; flow starts only after the yield value is exceeded.

explanationWrong.A: Immediate shear-thinning without a yield value describes pseudoplastic, not Bingham, behavior.
explanationWrong.B: Dilatant flow is described for deflocculated high-solid suspensions, not as the Bingham definition.
explanationWrong.C: The text notes that dilatant/pseudoplastic structural changes do not reform immediately; Bingham flow is defined by a yield stress.

question: Polymorphs of a drug substance can differ substantially in which set of properties?

choices.text: Melting point, solubility, dissolution rate, density, and stability
Molecular formula and atomic composition only
Whether the solid is isotropic in all directions, identical to amorphous forms
Only color, never dissolution or stability

sourceQuote: melting point, solubility, dissolution rate, density, and stability can differ
explanationCorrect: Alternative crystal lattices give polymorphs different melting point, solubility, dissolution rate, density, and stability.

explanationWrong.B: Polymorphs are the same substance in different crystalline arrangements, not different molecular formulas.
explanationWrong.C: Isotropic behavior with nondistinct melting is described for amorphous solids, not as a polymorph identity.
explanationWrong.D: Dissolution rate and stability are explicitly listed as properties that can differ.

question: Transport of a drug across a biological membrane by membrane pumps that is generally energy dependent is termed:

choices.text: Passive transport dictated only by Fick’s first law
Molecular permeation that is always energy independent
Active transport
Flux proportional solely to dC/dx without transporters

sourceQuote: known as active transport and is generally energy dependent
explanationCorrect: Carrier/pump-mediated movement is active transport and is generally energy dependent, in contrast to passive diffusion down a concentration gradient.

explanationWrong.A: Passive transport is energy independent and concentration-gradient driven (Fick).
explanationWrong.B: Energy independence is the passive, not the pump-mediated, process.
explanationWrong.D: That description is Fickian passive flux, not transporter-mediated active transport.

question: Which solute is classified here as a nonelectrolyte that does not form ions on dissolution in water?

choices.text: Sodium chloride
Hydrochloric acid
Any fully dissociated strong electrolyte
Sucrose

sourceQuote: examples of this class of solutes are estradiol, glycerin, urea, and sucrose
explanationCorrect: Nonelectrolytes such as estradiol, glycerin, urea, and sucrose do not form ions in water and their solutions do not conduct electric current.

explanationWrong.A: Sodium chloride is given as an electrolyte example.
explanationWrong.B: Hydrochloric acid is listed among electrolytes.
explanationWrong.C: Strong electrolytes form ions; they are not this class.

question: A stable pharmaceutical emulsion as defined here typically has dispersed droplet diameters in which range?

choices.text: 0.1 µm to 10 µm
Greater than 0.5 mm only
Exactly 1 nm (molecular dispersion)
Larger than 1 cm after coalescence is complete

sourceQuote: The droplet diameter is usually between 0.1 µm and 10 µm
explanationCorrect: Emulsion droplets are usually 0.1–10 µm and are considered a coarse dispersion; an emulsifying agent is added to limit coalescence.

explanationWrong.B: Greater than 0.5 mm is the particle-size statement given for suspension solids, not emulsion droplets.
explanationWrong.C: A molecular dispersion is a true solution, not an emulsion.
explanationWrong.D: Complete coalescence is the unstable endpoint the emulsifier is meant to prevent, not the usual droplet size.

question: Which dispersed system is stated to follow zero-order degradation kinetics?

choices.text: Suspensions
True solutions of nonelectrolytes only
First-order exponential decay of A = A0e−kt exclusively
Gaseous molecular dispersions

explanationCorrect: The chapter states that suspensions follow zero-order kinetics, with t90 = 0.1A0/k and rate constant in concentration·time−1.

explanationWrong.B: True solutions are not the system identified as zero-order here.
explanationWrong.C: A = A0e−kt is the integrated first-order equation, not the suspension zero-order case.
explanationWrong.D: Gases are not the dosage form assigned zero-order kinetics in this section.

question: All else equal, why are drugs given in aqueous (true) solution generally absorbed faster from the gut than the same drugs in solid form?

choices.text: Solids mix more readily with the aqueous absorptive milieu than solutions
First-pass hepatic metabolism occurs only after solid dosage forms
They mix more readily with the aqueous phase at the absorptive site, whereas dissolution of solids may be rate-limiting
Oily solutions always provide faster absorption than aqueous true solutions

sourceQuote: Drugs administered in aqueous (true) solution are more rapidly absorbed than those
explanationCorrect: Aqueous true solutions mix more readily at the absorptive site; dissolution of solids can be the rate-limiting step in absorption.

explanationWrong.A: The opposite is stated: solutions mix more readily than solids.
explanationWrong.B: First-pass occurs after absorption from the GI tract for oral drugs generally, not only solids.
explanationWrong.D: Aqueous true solutions are absorbed more rapidly than oily solutions, suspensions, or solids.

question: Most drug molecules cross the GI epithelium by which mechanism?

choices.text: Pinocytosis as the dominant pathway
Paracellular flux through leaky tight junctions as the major route
Active transport against the gradient for nearly all small molecules
Passive diffusion

sourceQuote: Most drug molecules are absorbed across the GI membrane by passive diffusion
explanationCorrect: Passive diffusion is the most common GI absorption mechanism; drugs move from high concentration in gastric fluids to lower concentration in blood.

explanationWrong.A: Pinocytosis is described as playing a very small role.
explanationWrong.B: The paracellular route is relatively small because tight junctions limit absorption.
explanationWrong.C: Active (carrier-mediated, energy-requiring) transport is not the most common mechanism stated.

question: Pinocytosis is described as a minor transport path in which the cell membrane invaginates to form a vesicle. Which products are given as examples that enter cells this way, and when is carrier-mediated transport called active?

choices.text: Liposomes enter by pinocytosis; transport is active if movement is against the concentration gradient and requires energy
Liposomes diffuse passively down a gradient without carriers or vesicles
Active transport moves only with the concentration gradient and never uses energy
Pinocytosis is the main pathway for all oral drugs

contents.
Liposomes are examples of drugs that enter cells by pinocytosis.
Oral
explanationCorrect: Liposomes enter cells by pinocytosis (engulfment into a vesicle). Carrier-mediated transport uses specialized carriers; it is active if movement is against the gradient and requires energy. Movement with the gradient that uses transport proteins does not require energy.

explanationWrong.B: Liposomes are the pinocytosis example, not simple passive diffusion without vesicles.
explanationWrong.C: Active transport is against the gradient and requires energy.
explanationWrong.D: Pinocytosis plays a very small role in drug transport.

question: Oral bioavailability depends greatly on gastric pH and drug pKa. What typical pH ranges are given for stomach versus small intestine?

choices.text: Stomach pH 7–9; small intestine pH 1–3
Both sites remain pH 7.4 at all times
Stomach contents are strongly acidic, typically pH 1–3 (fasted and fed, respectively); small-intestine pH is basic, typically 7–9
Fed stomach pH is 9 and fasted intestine pH is 1

typically ranges
between 1 and 3 for fasted and fed states, respectively.
explanationCorrect: Stomach pH is typically 1–3 for fasted and fed states, respectively; small-intestine pH is typically 7–9. The pH–pKa relationship governs dissolution, ionization, and precipitation. Most products are tablets; conventional oral systems also include capsules and liquids.

explanationWrong.B: Gastric contents are strongly acidic; intestine is basic as given.
explanationWrong.D: Fed/fasted gastric values are 1 and 3 as stated, not 9; intestine is 7–9.

question: Compared with many solid oral products, a disadvantage of aqueous liquid drug products is that:

choices.text: They cannot be colored or flavored
They are always easier to store, ship, and dose accurately than tablets
They never allow fine dosage adjustments
The shelf life of many drugs is shortened in an aqueous medium

explanationCorrect: Aqueous liquids often have shortened shelf life and are more cumbersome to store, transport, and dose accurately, contributing to fewer liquid products.

explanationWrong.A: Liquids can easily be colored and flavored; masking taste is the harder problem.
explanationWrong.B: The text states liquids are more cumbersome to store/transport and harder to dose accurately.
explanationWrong.C: Liquids provide flexibility when fine dosage adjustments are needed.

question: Effervescence when an effervescent tablet is placed in water is produced by which reaction?

Polymer hydration without gas formation
Reaction in water between an acid and a base that produces carbon dioxide
Enzymatic inversion of sucrose to invert sugar only

explanationWrong.B: The defining event is carbon dioxide production, not gas-free hydration.
explanationWrong.D: Sweetener chemistry is not the source of the CO2.

question: Relative to conventional tablets, a practical storage constraint of hard gelatin capsules is that they:

choices.text: Must be stored in a humidity-controlled environment
Cannot be manufactured in more than one color
Are never designed to be swallowed whole
May not be opened even if the patient cannot swallow the shell

explanationWrong.C: Most gelatin capsules are designed to be swallowed.
explanationWrong.D: If swallowing is not possible, the capsule can be opened and contents mixed with water, juice, pudding, or applesauce.

question: A recognized disadvantage of the oral route is that some drugs are:

choices.text: Always protected from low gastric pH by first-pass metabolism
Absorbed with perfectly regular gastric emptying in the presence of food
Unable to cause emesis from GI mucosal irritation
Destroyed by digestive enzymes or low gastric pH

explanationWrong.B: Food or other drugs can cause irregularities in absorption or gastric emptying.
explanationWrong.C: Emesis from irritation of the GI mucosa is listed as a disadvantage.

question: A listed disadvantage of oral administration is slower onset (e.g., 15–90 minutes) versus nearly immediate IV effect. Which additional oral drawbacks are named?

choices.text: Oral drugs never undergo presystemic metabolism
Food never alters gastric emptying or absorption
Digestive enzymes and low gastric pH cannot destroy drugs

action.
Onset of response for these drugs is slower (e.g., 15–90 minutes)
explanationCorrect: Oral drawbacks include emesis from GI irritation, destruction by digestive enzymes or low gastric pH, food- or drug-related absorption/emptying irregularities, and presystemic metabolism by mucosa, intestinal flora, or liver, reducing drug reaching the site of action.

explanationWrong.A: Presystemic metabolism by mucosa, flora, or liver is explicitly listed.
explanationWrong.B: Irregularities in absorption or gastric emptying can occur with food or other drugs.
explanationWrong.C: Some drugs are destroyed by digestive enzymes or low gastric pH.

question: Parenteral literally means around the GI tract and in common usage is often synonymous with injectable. Why are almost all protein drugs given by injection rather than orally?

choices.text: Proteins are absorbed intact from the stomach more rapidly than small molecules

Injectable products need not be sterile

For example, almost all protein
drugs are administered by injection rather than
explanationCorrect: Almost all protein drugs are injected because they are broken down by stomach acid and digestive enzymes. Parenteral delivery is usually more rapid and predictable and is advantageous in emergencies. Injectables are sterile and may need special handling.

explanationWrong.A: Proteins are broken down, not absorbed intact more rapidly, via the oral route as described.
explanationWrong.C: Parenteral delivery is usually more rapid and more predictable, especially in emergencies.
explanationWrong.D: Injectable products are sterile products and may require special handling.

question: Intravenous administration of a true-solution drug product delivers what fraction of the dose into the systemic circulation?

choices.text: Approximately 15%, limited by capillary diffusion area
Only the unbound fraction in synovial fluid
Zero until IM depot release occurs

explanationWrong.C: IM depot release is a different parenteral route.

question: Subcutaneous injection is inappropriate for drugs that irritate tissue because of the risk of:

choices.text: Immediate 100% systemic delivery identical to an IV bolus
Precipitation embolism in the central veins only
Severe pain, necrosis, and sloughing of tissue
Mandatory use of an IV infusion pump

explanationCorrect: SC injection can be used only for drugs that are not irritating to tissue; otherwise severe pain, necrosis, and sloughing may occur.

explanationWrong.A: 100% systemic delivery is the IV true-solution statement, not SC.
explanationWrong.B: Precipitation and embolism are discussed as IV complications of poorly soluble drugs.
explanationWrong.D: IV pumps are mentioned for controlling IV drips, not as a reason to avoid SC irritants.

question: After an epidural injection, where is the drug delivered relative to cerebrospinal fluid?

choices.text: Directly into the CSF as an intrathecal bolus by definition
Exclusively into the deltoid muscle capillary bed
Only into the synovial space of a peripheral joint
To the outside of the dura and not into the cerebrospinal fluid

explanationWrong.C: Intra-articular/intrasynovial injection is a different specialized route.

question: Epidural multivesicular liposomal morphine (preservative-free in 0.9% sodium chloride), given as a single dose 30 minutes preoperatively, is described as producing which duration of postoperative analgesia?

Exactly 2 hours, because liposomes never release morphine into the intrathecal space
7 days of analgesia only when given intravenously, not epidurally
Persistent analgesia for 48 hours postoperatively; liposomes release morphine slowly through the meninges into the intrathecal space, with ADME similar to other parenteral morphine

it 
has 
produced 
persistent 
analgesia 
for 
48 
hours
postoperatively. The distribution, metabolism,
explanationCorrect: On epidural injection, multivesicular liposomes release morphine slowly into the intrathecal space through the meninges. A single dose 30 minutes preoperatively has produced persistent analgesia for 48 hours. Distribution, metabolism, and elimination resemble other parenteral morphine formulations.

explanationWrong.C: The product is injected into the epidural space, not described as a 7-day IV regimen.

question: Depot intramuscular injections (oil-based, aqueous suspensions, or microspheres) are indicated primarily for:

choices.text: Initiation of therapy rather than maintenance
Single 5 mL deltoid boluses of true aqueous solution only

Replacing all oral immediate-release products on day 1 of care

question: Depot formulations used for maintenance rather than initiation of therapy are listed in which three physical types, with which examples?

Only immediate-release IV push solutions

Rectal antiemetic suppositories as the only depot type

initiation of therapy. Depot formulations are available as oil-based injections

explanationWrong.C: Inhalers are not the depot types listed.
explanationWrong.D: Rectal antiemetics are a separate route discussion, not classified as the depot injection types.

question: A suppository base releases drug by which described mechanisms?

Only by evaporating into the systemic circulation as a gas

Only after enzymatic cleavage by pancreatic lipase in the colon

base either melts at body
temperature (cocoa butter or fat base) or

question: From an oleaginous (fatty) suppository base, which drug is released more rapidly?

question: Drug absorbed low in the rectum via the inferior and middle rectal veins reaches the systemic circulation in a way that is advantageous for high first-pass drugs because it:

Is confined to local hemorrhoidal action with zero systemic absorption
Always produces less intersubject variability than oral dosing
Avoids passing through the liver

question: Systemic absorption of a topically applied drug occurs much more readily through which skin condition?

Only through fully keratinized nails
Dry, nonhydrated stratum corneum exclusively
Abraded, burned, or denuded skin

explanationWrong.A: Intact epidermis behaves as a lipid barrier; few drugs readily penetrate intact skin.
explanationWrong.B: Nail absorption is not the pathway identified here.
explanationWrong.C: Hydrated skin is more permeable than dry skin.

question: Local ophthalmic drug effects usually require absorption through which ocular structure?

The nasal turbinates after mandatory nasolacrimal blockage
Intact skin of the eyelid as the rate-limiting lipid barrier
The cornea

sourceQuote: Local effects usually require absorption of the drug through the cornea
explanationCorrect: Local ocular effects usually require corneal absorption; infection or trauma may therefore produce more rapid absorption.

explanationWrong.A: The cornea, not sclera-only absorption, is specified for local effects.
explanationWrong.B: Nasolacrimal drainage is not the absorption path stated for local ocular effects here.
explanationWrong.C: Epidermal lipid-barrier discussion belongs to topical skin, not this ophthalmic statement.

question: For a manufactured drug product, the experimental expiration date is assigned when which statistical threshold is reached under specified storage conditions?

choices.text: The mean assay first exceeds 110% of labeled strength
USP <795> beyond-use dating for a nonsterile compound is automatically applied
Radiopharmaceutical decay reaches 50% within 1 hour
The 95% one-sided lower confidence limit crosses 90% of the labeled amount of active ingredient

sourceQuote: the 95% one-sided lower confidence limit crosses 90% of the labeled amount
explanationCorrect: FDA-aligned expiration dating uses the time when the 95% one-sided lower confidence limit crosses 90% of labeled active under specified temperature and humidity.

explanationWrong.A: The threshold described is 90% of labeled amount, not 110%.
explanationWrong.B: USP <795> guides beyond-use dates for nonsterile compounded products, a separate framework.
explanationWrong.C: Some radiopharmaceuticals decay within 1 day; that is an example of short dating, not the 90%/95% rule.

question: In tablet formulation, magnesium stearate is classified as which functional excipient?

choices.text: A diluent whose sole role is to provide bulk like lactose
A disintegrant identical to sodium starch glycolate
A lubricant that prevents adherence to punches and dies and aids ejection
A glidant whose only listed example is colloidal silica

sourceQuote: Prevent adherence of granules and powders to tablet punches and dies
explanationCorrect: Lubricants such as magnesium stearate, talc, stearic acid, PEGs, and lauryl sulfates prevent sticking to punches/dies and aid ejection from the die cavity.

explanationWrong.A: Diluents (e.g., lactose, MCC) provide bulk and dosing accuracy, not the punch-release function.
explanationWrong.B: Disintegrants promote breakup after administration; magnesium stearate is listed as a lubricant.
explanationWrong.D: Colloidal silica (Cab-O-Sil) and talc are the glidant examples for improving powder flow.

question: Which capsule excipients are listed as plasticizers that aid formation of the soft gelatin shell?

choices.text: Lactose, mannitol, and calcium carbonate
Methylparaben and potassium sorbate only
Sodium lauryl sulfate and sodium docusate only
Glycerol, sorbitol, and polypropylene glycol

sourceQuote: Aid formation of the soft gelatin capsule Glycerol, sorbitol, polypropylene glycol Preservatives
explanationCorrect: Plasticizers used to form soft gelatin capsules include glycerol, sorbitol, and polypropylene glycol.

explanationWrong.A: Those are capsule diluents for bulk and accurate dosing.
explanationWrong.B: Those are preservatives to limit microbial growth and drug degradation.
explanationWrong.C: Those surfactants wet powder after administration to aid dissolution.

question: In liquid dosage forms, sodium metabisulfite, butylated hydroxytoluene, and butylated hydroxyanisole are used as:

choices.text: Antimicrobial preservatives identical to benzalkonium chloride
Chelating agents identical to disodium EDTA
Antioxidants to prevent oxidation of the active drug
Primary suspending agents such as carbomer

sourceQuote: Prevent oxidization of active drug Sodium metabisulfite, butylated hydroxytoluene, butylated hydroxyanisole Surfactants
explanationCorrect: The liquid-excipient table lists sodium metabisulfite, BHT, and BHA as antioxidants that prevent oxidation of the active drug.

explanationWrong.A: Methylparaben, propylparaben, benzalkonium chloride, and benzyl alcohol are the antimicrobial examples.
explanationWrong.B: Disodium EDTA is the chelating agent listed for formulation stability.
explanationWrong.D: Carbomer, carrageenan, and cellulose derivatives are suspending/thickening agents.

question: This chapter’s self-assessment states that the rate of dissolution of drugs into the surrounding medium is expressed by which equation?

choices.text: The Noyes–Whitney equation
The Michaelis–Menten equation
The Stokes equation
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

sourceQuote: The rate of dissolution of drugs into the surrounding media is expressed by the
explanationCorrect: The item identifies the Noyes–Whitney equation as the expression for dissolution rate into the surrounding medium.

explanationWrong.B: Michaelis–Menten describes enzyme kinetics, not the dissolution-rate expression listed here.
explanationWrong.C: Stokes’ law addresses sedimentation of particles, not the dissolution equation in this item.
explanationWrong.D: Henderson–Hasselbalch relates pH and pKa, not dissolution rate as asked here.

question: For a 1-year-old with a bacterial infection who cannot swallow adult solids, which product type is among the antibiotic choices compared in this self-assessment?

choices.text: A transdermal opioid patch
An implantable antibiotic pellet
A dry-powder inhaler of a systemic antibiotic
A sprinkle of drug mixed with food

explanationCorrect: The pediatric item lists a sprinkle mixed with food (along with chewable tablet, dissolving strip, and liquid suspension) as an antibiotic product option for a 1-year-old.
