explanationWrong.B: An implant is not a listed option in this item.
explanationWrong.C: A DPI is not one of the compared products.

question: Conversion of a liquid to a gas requires which physicochemical change?

choices.text: A change in the compound’s molecular formula
A decrease in melting point of the crystalline solid
Overcoming the weak attractive intermolecular forces
No significant physicochemical effect because gases retain liquid-like short-range order

sourceQuote: the weak attractive forces have to be overcome
explanationCorrect: Liquids have short-range order from weak attractive forces; converting liquid to gas requires those forces to be overcome, whereas gases show no such order.

explanationWrong.A: The molecular formula does not change with a change of state.
explanationWrong.B: Melting point concerns solid–liquid transition, not vaporization as explained here.
explanationWrong.D: The answer key states gases show no order, so the change is physicochemically significant.

question: Which factor is said to have little effect on passive-diffusion transport of drug molecules?

choices.text: Surface area of the absorbing membrane
pH difference on each side of the membrane
pKa of the drug molecule
Body temperature

sourceQuote: Body temperature has little effect on transport of molecules
explanationCorrect: Passive diffusion depends strongly on absorbing surface area, transmembrane pH difference, and drug pKa; body temperature has little effect.

explanationWrong.A: Transport is extensively dependent on absorbing-membrane surface area.
explanationWrong.B: pH difference across the membrane is a major determinant.
explanationWrong.C: The drug’s pKa is a major determinant of the diffusible fraction.

question: USP Chapter <795> as cited in this chapter’s references addresses which practice area?

choices.text: Pharmaceutical compounding—nonsterile preparations
Pharmaceutical compounding—sterile preparations only
Q1A(R2) stability testing of new drug substances
Martin’s Physical Pharmacy textbook narrative

sourceQuote: United States Pharmacopeial Convention. Chapter <795>: Pharmaceutical compounding
explanationCorrect: The references cite USP Chapter <795> as pharmaceutical compounding—nonsterile preparations; sterile compounding is Chapter <797>.

explanationWrong.B: Sterile compounding is cited separately as Chapter <797>.
explanationWrong.C: Q1A(R2) is an FDA stability guidance, not USP <795>.
explanationWrong.D: Sinko’s Martin’s Physical Pharmacy is a separate textbook citation.

question: At steady state, drug concentration is determined by which parameter, and what is the effect of changing volume of distribution?

choices.text: Clearance determines Css; changes in V do not change steady-state concentration
V alone sets Css; clearance has no role
Liver function tests quantitatively set Css for all hepatically cleared drugs
Renal function cannot be used to adjust doses of renally eliminated drugs

sourceQuote: Steady-state drug concentration is determined by the clearance of the drug
explanationCorrect: Css is determined by clearance; changes in volume of distribution do not change the steady-state concentration.

explanationWrong.B: The key point states the opposite relationship between V and Css.
explanationWrong.C: LFTs measure liver damage, not function, and do not quantitatively estimate drug metabolism.
explanationWrong.D: Renal function estimated from serum creatinine is used to adjust doses of renally eliminated drugs.

question: Volume of distribution (V) is best described as which of the following?

choices.text: The measured plasma volume only, ignoring tissue distribution
The AUC ratio after oral versus intravenous dosing
A laboratory-measured anatomic compartment identical to extracellular water in all patients
The theoretical volume based on plasma concentration if the drug completely distributed throughout the body without any elimination

sourceQuote: completely distribute throughout the body without any drug elimination
explanationCorrect: V is a theoretical volume inferred from plasma concentration assuming complete distribution and no elimination, allowing estimation of amount in the body from a measured concentration.

explanationWrong.A: V is not limited to measured plasma volume; it reflects apparent distribution.
explanationWrong.B: That AUC comparison is absolute bioavailability, not V.
explanationWrong.C: V is theoretical, not a directly measured anatomic volume equal to ECW in everyone.

question: Which pair correctly matches the example drugs to the volumes of distribution cited?

choices.text: Warfarin about 66 L/kg; amiodarone about 0.14 L/kg
Both drugs have V near 1 L/kg so loading-dose weight adjustment is unnecessary
Aminophylline S = 1.0 because it is 100% theophylline
Amiodarone about 66 L/kg; warfarin about 0.14 L/kg

sourceQuote: amiodarone with an extremely large V of about 66 L/kg
explanationCorrect: Amiodarone is cited with a very large V (~66 L/kg) and warfarin with a small V (~0.14 L/kg); aminophylline is 80% theophylline (S = 0.8).

explanationWrong.A: The V values are reversed.
explanationWrong.B: The examples illustrate extremely large versus very small V, which matters for loading dose.
explanationWrong.C: S is 0.8 because aminophylline is 80% theophylline.

question: When theophylline is administered as intravenous aminophylline, which salt factor (S) is applied because of the salt’s theophylline content?

choices.text: S = 1.0, because aminophylline is 100% theophylline
S = 0.68, matching the reported volume of distribution in L/kg
S = 0.8, because aminophylline is 80% theophylline
S = 0.14, analogous to warfarin’s small volume of distribution

sourceQuote: because the drug is given as aminophylline, which is 80% theophylline.
explanationCorrect: The passage states S is 0.8 because the drug is given as aminophylline, which is 80% theophylline.

explanationWrong.A: Aminophylline is not equivalent milligram-for-milligram to theophylline.
explanationWrong.B: 0.68 L/kg is the neonate’s volume of distribution in the example, not the salt factor.
explanationWrong.D: 0.14 L/kg is warfarin’s approximate V, not a salt correction.

question: First-order elimination is defined as which kinetic pattern?

choices.text: A constant amount of drug (for example, milligrams) is removed per unit time regardless of concentration
A constant percentage of drug is eliminated per unit time, while the amount eliminated per hour changes with plasma concentration
Clearance falls to zero once distribution equilibrium is reached
Volume of distribution alone identifies the tissue into which the drug partitions

sourceQuote: The vast majority of drugs are eliminated by first-order elimination, which means a constant
explanationCorrect: Most drugs follow first-order elimination: a constant percentage is eliminated per unit time, so milligram-per-hour rates change with concentration.

explanationWrong.A: A constant amount per time describes zero-order, not first-order, elimination.
explanationWrong.C: Clearance is the parameter relating concentration to elimination rate; it is not said to fall to zero at equilibrium.
explanationWrong.D: The passage states that V alone cannot identify which tissue a drug enters.

question: During a constant intravenous infusion, steady state is reached when which condition is met?

choices.text: Volume of distribution equals the infusion rate numerically
Bioavailability F becomes zero
The amount of drug entering the body equals the amount being eliminated
Only a trough concentration has been drawn after oral dosing

sourceQuote: Steady state occurs when the amount of drug going into the body
explanationCorrect: Steady state occurs when input (XO) equals elimination; for an infusion, Css = XO/Cl, so clearance determines the concentration at which those rates match.

explanationWrong.A: V does not equal infusion rate as the steady-state definition.
explanationWrong.B: F is not set to zero to define infusion steady state.
explanationWrong.D: The infusion Css equation is distinguished from oral trough monitoring in practice.

question: Most hepatically metabolized drugs still show first-order (constant clearance) pharmacokinetics at usual doses because:

choices.text: Km is much greater than plasma concentration, so Vmax/Km behaves as a constant clearance
Km is always much smaller than C throughout the therapeutic range
Phenytoin is the template for all drugs, which are nonlinear at usual doses
A plot of ln C versus time is never linear in first-order kinetics

sourceQuote: the Km is much greater than the plasma concentration (Km>>C)
explanationCorrect: When Km >> C, Km + C ≈ Km, so Vmax/Km is a constant that is first-order clearance; phenytoin is a notable nonlinear exception.

explanationWrong.B: First-order behavior requires Km >> C, not Km << C.
explanationWrong.C: Phenytoin is highlighted as an exception, not the rule for most drugs.
explanationWrong.D: First-order kinetics yield a straight line of ln C versus time.

question: When plasma concentration approaches Km (as with phenytoin), clearance:

choices.text: Remains equal to Vmax/Km at all concentrations
Increases as concentration increases
Becomes zero at all therapeutic doses
Becomes concentration dependent and decreases as plasma concentration increases

sourceQuote:
the clearance of the drug becomes
concentration dependent
explanationCorrect: When concentration approaches Km, the Michaelis-Menten equation cannot be simplified; clearance becomes concentration dependent and decreases as plasma concentration increases.

explanationWrong.A: Vmax/Km as a constant clearance applies only while Km is much greater than C (first-order conditions).
explanationWrong.B: Clearance decreases, not increases, as concentration rises in this nonlinear setting.
explanationWrong.C: Clearance decreases with rising concentration but is not described as becoming zero.

question: Doubling the dose of a drug with nonlinear elimination is expected to:

choices.text: Produce a greater-than-proportional increase in steady-state plasma concentration
Exactly double steady-state concentration as in first-order kinetics
Reduce steady-state concentration by half
Leave steady-state concentration unchanged

sourceQuote:
will result in a greater than doubling of the steady-state plasma
concentration
explanationCorrect: Doubling the dose of a nonlinearly eliminated drug produces a greater than doubling of steady-state plasma concentration, making dosing less predictable.

explanationWrong.B: Exact doubling of Css when dose is doubled is the first-order relationship.
explanationWrong.C: Halving Css would require a dose decrease, and even then Css would fall by more than half.
explanationWrong.D: Css does change, and more than proportionally, with dose.

question: If a patient’s terminal half-life changes, the usual explanation is a change in which parameter?

choices.text: A large change in V, which is quite common, with stable clearance
Clearance (or Cl variability), because large changes in V are unusual while large changes in Cl are common
Absorption rate ka becoming slower than k in all oral drugs by definition
Elimination rate constant being independent of both V and Cl

sourceQuote: large changes in Cl are quite common because of the variability
explanationCorrect: Because t½ depends on V and Cl, half-life shifts usually reflect Cl (renal/hepatic variability), whereas large V changes are unusual.

explanationWrong.A: The text states large V changes are unusual compared with Cl changes.
explanationWrong.C: The ka >> k assumption is the usual oral case; flip-flop is the exception, not the default explanation of t½ change.
explanationWrong.D: k is related to Cl and V (terminal slope on a semilog plot).

question: When a controlled-release dosage form has an absorption rate much slower than elimination (ka << k), the terminal semilog slope is determined by:

choices.text: The elimination rate constant k, as after an immediate-release dose
Instantaneous intravenous-bolus absorption
The absorption rate rather than the elimination rate
A zero-order infusion rate equal to clearance

sourceQuote: a drug is given in a controlled-release dosage form in which ka<<k
explanationCorrect: If ka is much less than k, absorption becomes rate limiting and the semilog plot of the terminal elimination phase is determined by the absorption rate rather than the elimination rate.

explanationWrong.A: That terminal-phase relationship holds when absorption is rapid compared with elimination (ka >> k).
explanationWrong.B: An IV bolus is not the controlled-release situation described.
explanationWrong.D: Infusion equal to clearance describes a steady-state infusion, not this oral absorption case.

question: For a controlled-release drug with ka much less than k, time to reach steady state is approximately:

choices.text: One elimination half-life
Five absorption-rate half-lives
Two distribution half-lives
Independent of the absorption rate

sourceQuote:
the time to reach
steady state is five absorption rate half-lives
explanationCorrect: When ka is much less than k, time to reach steady state is five absorption-rate half-lives, and time to eliminate the drug after stopping is also five absorption half-lives.

explanationWrong.A: Elimination half-life does not determine time to steady state in this flip-flop setting.
explanationWrong.C: Distribution half-lives are not the parameter given.
explanationWrong.D: Time to steady state depends on the absorption-rate half-life when ka is rate limiting.

question: Morphine is rapidly glucuronidated hepatically, yet renal function still matters because:

choices.text: Unchanged morphine is 100% renally cleared and not metabolized
Morphine-6-glucuronide retains opiate activity and can accumulate in renal failure, risking respiratory depression
Glucuronides are inactive and cannot accumulate
Cockcroft–Gault estimates are never used for any renally adjusted drug

sourceQuote: accumulate in patients with renal failure, potentially leading to respiratory depression
explanationCorrect: Morphine-6-glucuronide is an active opioid metabolite eliminated by the kidney; it accumulates in renal failure and may cause respiratory depression, so morphine still requires renal consideration.

explanationWrong.A: Morphine is rapidly metabolized by the liver; the renal issue is the active glucuronide.
explanationWrong.C: M6G retains opiate activity.
explanationWrong.D: Cockcroft–Gault and MDRD are presented as quantitative tools to adjust renally eliminated drugs.

question: The Cockcroft–Gault equation was developed to estimate which quantity from serum creatinine?

choices.text: Hepatic intrinsic clearance in mL/minute
Volume of distribution in L/kg
Glomerular filtration rate indexed only to 1.73 m² without using age
Creatinine clearance in mL/minute from age, body weight, and serum creatinine

sourceQuote: The Cockcroft–Gault equation is the older equation, which was developed to estimate the
explanationCorrect: Cockcroft–Gault is the older equation developed to estimate creatinine clearance (mL/minute) from serum creatinine using age and body weight.

explanationWrong.A: The equation estimates renal, not hepatic, function.
explanationWrong.B: V is not the output of Cockcroft–Gault.
explanationWrong.C: Indexing GFR to 1.73 m² describes the MDRD-style result, and CG uses age and weight.

question: When creatinine clearance is estimated with Cockcroft–Gault, which sex adjustment is applied?

choices.text: Multiply the estimate by 0.85 if the patient is female
Multiply the estimate by 1.212 if the patient is female
Multiply the estimate by 0.742 if the patient is male
No sex factor is used; only African American ancestry is adjusted

sourceQuote: If the patient is female, multiply the estimate by 0.85. The MDRD
explanationCorrect: If the patient is female, the Cockcroft–Gault estimate is multiplied by 0.85. MDRD instead uses 0.742 for females and 1.212 for African American patients.

explanationWrong.B: 1.212 is the MDRD African American factor, not a female Cockcroft–Gault factor.
explanationWrong.C: 0.742 is the MDRD female factor, and it is not applied to males.
explanationWrong.D: Cockcroft–Gault does use a female multiplier of 0.85.

question: ALT, AST, GGTP, and alkaline phosphatase are of limited use for hepatic drug-dose adjustment because they:

choices.text: Quantitatively estimate metabolic capacity analogously to using SCr for renal drugs
Indicate hepatocellular damage but do not correlate quantitatively with the liver’s metabolic capacity
Directly measure liver blood flow Q for high-extraction drugs
Replace the need for any clinical judgment in cirrhosis dosing

sourceQuote: they do not correlate quantitatively with the liver
explanationCorrect: These “LFTs” reflect enzyme release from damaged cells, so they indicate injury rather than a numeric measure of drug-metabolizing function, unlike SCr-based renal nomograms.

explanationWrong.A: The chapter states there are no analogous dosing nomograms based on hepatic laboratory parameters.
explanationWrong.C: The tests do not measure Q.
explanationWrong.D: Elimination is likely decreased by an unknown amount; only general statements, not precise lab-driven doses, are available.

question: Why cannot hepatic laboratory tests be used like serum creatinine to adjust doses of hepatically cleared drugs?

choices.text: Hepatic elimination is always increased when liver enzymes are elevated
Oral drugs bypass the liver before reaching the systemic circulation
Quantitative nomograms relating ALT or AST to clearance are universally available
No dosing nomograms exist that adjust dose from hepatic laboratory parameters the way SCr is used for renally eliminated drugs

sourceQuote: no dosing nomograms for adjusting drug dose on the basis of any hepatic laboratory
explanationCorrect: Hepatic elimination is likely decreased in liver disease, but the amount is unknown and there are no SCr-like nomograms for hepatic labs.

explanationWrong.A: The text states elimination is most likely decreased, not increased, and the magnitude is unknown.
explanationWrong.B: Orally absorbed drug must pass through the liver before systemic circulation.
explanationWrong.C: The passage explicitly notes the absence of such nomograms.

question: Which three parameters determine hepatic drug disposition in the venous equilibrium model of first-pass metabolism?

choices.text: Plasma free fraction (fup), intrinsic clearance (Clint), and liver blood flow (Q)
Serum creatinine, albumin, and glomerular filtration rate
Volume of distribution, salt factor, and bioavailability fraction only
Gastric emptying time, bile salt concentration, and renal blood flow

sourceQuote: called the venous equilibrium model. Understanding this model is necessary to properly
explanationCorrect: The venous equilibrium model uses fup, Clint, and hepatic blood flow (Q) to explain hepatic and first-pass metabolism after oral dosing.

explanationWrong.B: Those are renal-function descriptors, not the three hepatic-model parameters.
explanationWrong.C: V, S, and F are not the three parameters named for this hepatic model.
explanationWrong.D: Gastric, biliary, and renal flows are not the listed hepatic disposition parameters.

question: For a hepatically eliminated high-extraction drug, the extraction ratio (ER) is described as:

choices.text: Less than or equal to 0.3, so first-pass loss is negligible
Equal to fup × Clint with Cl much less than liver blood flow
Greater than or equal to 0.7, so a large proportion is metabolized before reaching the systemic circulation after oral dosing
Undefined for oral administration

sourceQuote: ER is greater than or equal to 0.7 and a large proportion
explanationCorrect: High-extraction drugs have ER ≥ 0.7 and extensive first-pass metabolism after oral dosing, unlike low-extraction drugs with Cl << Q and F* ≈ 1.

explanationWrong.A: ER ≤ 0.3 is the low-extraction range used later in the chapter’s answers, not high extraction.
explanationWrong.B: Dependence on fup and Clint with Cl << Q describes low-extraction clearance.
explanationWrong.D: Oral first-pass (F*) is specifically discussed for high-extraction drugs.

question: When a high-extraction drug is given intravenously, hepatic clearance is equal to which physiologic parameter?

choices.text: Unbound fraction times intrinsic clearance only
Hepatic blood flow, Q
Zero, because IV dosing has no clearance
Oral F* multiplied by dose

sourceQuote: For a high-extraction drug, the Cl is equal to Q
explanationCorrect: For high-extraction drugs, Cl equals liver blood flow Q; IV administration bypasses first-pass so there is no F*.

explanationWrong.A: fup × Clint dependence is the low-extraction (and oral high-extraction simplified) pattern, not IV high-extraction Cl.
explanationWrong.C: Clearance still occurs; first-pass is what is bypassed.
explanationWrong.D: F* applies to the absorbed oral dose escaping first-pass, not IV Cl.

question: For intravenous propranolol (high extraction, ER 0.81), enzyme induction by rifampin (increased Clint) is predicted to have which effect on Css,total, Css,free, and therapeutic effect?

choices.text: Marked increase in both Css,total and Css,free
Decrease in Css,free only, with doubled therapeutic effect
Complete loss of β-blockade because Q falls to zero
No change in Css,total, Css,free, or therapeutic effect

sourceQuote: and Css,free. Propranolol is a high-extraction drug (ER is 0.81) being given
explanationCorrect: IV high-extraction propranolol has Cl = Q, so increasing Clint from rifampin induction does not change Css,total, Css,free, or therapeutic effect per the table discussed.

explanationWrong.A: The table prediction is no change, not an increase in concentrations.
explanationWrong.B: Neither free concentration nor effect is predicted to change in this IV high-extraction case.
explanationWrong.C: Liver blood flow Q is not described as falling to zero; clearance equals Q for this IV high-extraction example.

question: If the same high-extraction drug (propranolol) is given orally and Clint increases (e.g., induction), what happens to steady-state concentrations and why does the IV dose differ from oral?

choices.text: Css,total and Css,free both rise because first-pass extraction falls
Css,total and Css,free both decrease, likely decreasing therapeutic effect; first-pass metabolism explains why a usual IV propranolol dose is much smaller than oral
Only Css,total falls; Css,free and effect are unchanged, as with IV dosing
Oral induction has no effect because Clint does not appear in oral Css equations

sourceQuote: the increase in the Clint alters both the Css,total and the Css,free,
explanationCorrect: For oral high-extraction propranolol, Clint is in the Css,total and Css,free equations and is inversely related to concentrations, so induction lowers both and likely reduces effect. First-pass metabolism also explains why a normal therapeutic IV dose is about one-tenth the oral dose (text cuts off at “one-t”).

explanationWrong.A: Induction increases Clint and decreases, rather than raises, oral Css.
explanationWrong.C: Unlike IV dosing, oral high-extraction Css,total and Css,free both decrease.
explanationWrong.D: Clint is in both oral Css equations for high-extraction drugs.

question: The FDA definition of bioavailability quoted here is the rate and extent to which the active ingredient or moiety is:

choices.text: Compressed into a tablet regardless of absorption
Eliminated unchanged in urine only
Absorbed from a drug product and becomes available at the site of action
Bound to plasma protein as Css,total

sourceQuote: the rate and extent to which the active ingredient or active moiety is absorbed
explanationCorrect: FDA bioavailability is the rate and extent the active ingredient/moiety is absorbed from a product and becomes available at the site of action; in practice this is often framed as appearance in systemic circulation.

explanationWrong.A: Formulation without absorption is not bioavailability.
explanationWrong.B: Urinary excretion of unchanged drug is not the definition given.
explanationWrong.D: Protein binding is a disposition factor, not the FDA bioavailability definition.

question: Absolute bioavailability of an oral product is calculated from AUC and dose versus which reference, and what is F after intravenous dosing?

choices.text: Another oral tablet only; IV F is undefined
An intravenous dose; IV F is always considered to be 1
Intramuscular depot AUC only; IV F is 0
Protein-binding ratio; IV F equals fup

sourceQuote: When a drug is given intravenously, the F is always considered to be 1
explanationCorrect: Absolute F compares extravascular AUC (dose-normalized) with IV AUC; intravenous F is taken as 1. Relative bioavailability compares two non-IV forms.

explanationWrong.A: Comparing two oral forms is relative, not absolute, bioavailability.
explanationWrong.C: The IV reference defines absolute F; IV F is not 0.
explanationWrong.D: F is not set equal to fup in this definition.

question: If relative bioavailability F is near 1 for two oral formulations of the same drug, what does the text say that comparison does and does not establish?

choices.text: The dosage forms have the same bioavailability, which is not the same as bioequivalence, because bioequivalence also assesses rate and extent of absorption
The products are automatically therapeutically inequivalent
Absolute bioavailability versus IV administration has been proven
Only the absorption rate was compared, never the extent

sourceQuote: is not the same as bioequivalence, which includes assessing the rate and
explanationCorrect: Relative F near 1 means the two non-IV dosage forms have the same bioavailability. That is not bioequivalence, which includes assessing both rate and extent of absorption. Relative F is not a comparison to intravenous administration.

explanationWrong.B: Same bioavailability is not described as proving inequivalence.
explanationWrong.C: Relative bioavailability explicitly is not comparison to intravenous drug.
explanationWrong.D: Bioequivalence includes both rate and extent; F near 1 speaks to extent of relative bioavailability as defined here.

question: Pharmaceutical equivalents are defined as products that contain which of the following?

choices.text: The same therapeutic moiety but any salt, ester, amount, or dosage form
Different active moieties that share a pharmacologic class
Identical amounts of the identical active drug ingredient (same salt or ester of the same therapeutic moiety) in identical dosage forms
Any two products for which FDA has waived all in vivo study requirements

sourceQuote:
that contain identical amounts of the identical active drug
ingredient (i.e., the
explanationCorrect: Pharmaceutical equivalents contain identical amounts of the identical active ingredient (same salt or ester) in identical dosage forms. Pharmaceutical alternatives contain the identical therapeutic moiety or precursor but not necessarily the same amount, dosage form, or salt/ester. BCS may justify waiving some in vivo BA/BE requirements.

explanationWrong.A: That description matches pharmaceutical alternatives, not equivalents.
explanationWrong.B: Equivalents require the identical active ingredient, not merely the same class.
explanationWrong.D: FDA generally requires in vivo BA/BE; BCS can justify a waiver, which is not the definition of pharmaceutical equivalents.

question: Ketoconazole coadministered with lovastatin increases rhabdomyolysis risk primarily by which mechanism?

choices.text: Induction of CYP3A4, lowering lovastatin exposure
A purely pharmacodynamic overlap with no change in lovastatin levels
Potent CYP3A4 inhibition that decreases lovastatin metabolism
Inhibition of renal creatinine secretion only

sourceQuote: decreases the metabolism of lovastatin, potentially increasing the risk of rhabdomyolysis
explanationCorrect: Ketoconazole is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor that decreases lovastatin metabolism, raising exposure and the risk of rhabdomyolysis—a pharmacokinetic drug–drug interaction.

explanationWrong.A: The interaction is inhibition, not induction.
explanationWrong.B: The example is pharmacokinetic (altered metabolism), not merely PD overlap.
explanationWrong.D: Renal creatinine handling is not the mechanism given for this pair.

question: Amiodarone increases digoxin bioavailability because amiodarone:

choices.text: Induces intestinal CYP2D6
Is a potent P-glycoprotein inhibitor, reducing efflux of the P-gp substrate digoxin into the gut lumen
Cheates digoxin in the intestinal lumen
Synergizes as a CNS depressant identical to alprazolam plus alcohol

sourceQuote: Digoxin is a P- glycoprotein substrate drug whose bioavailability is increased by amiodarone
explanationCorrect: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein, which otherwise pumps substrates from enterocytes back to the lumen; digoxin F therefore increases.

explanationWrong.A: The transporter mechanism named is P-gp, not CYP2D6 induction.
explanationWrong.C: Luminal chelation is not the mechanism described.
explanationWrong.D: Alprazolam plus alcohol is the separate pharmacodynamic CNS-depressant example.

question: Concurrent milk reduces tetracycline effectiveness primarily because:

choices.text: Grapefruit juice induces intestinal CYP3A4
Gentamicin blocks biliary excretion of tetracycline
Phenytoin induces renal clearance of tetracycline
Calcium forms an insoluble salt, reducing bioavailability

sourceQuote:
Milk contains calcium, which combines with
tetracycline to form an insoluble salt
explanationCorrect: Milk contains calcium, which combines with tetracycline to form an insoluble salt and reduces the antibiotic's bioavailability and effectiveness.

explanationWrong.A: Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and can increase bioavailability of substrates such as lovastatin; it is a separate interaction.
explanationWrong.B: Gentamicin is discussed for renal elimination, not tetracycline-milk binding.
explanationWrong.C: Phenytoin is discussed as a hepatically eliminated drug, not as inducing tetracycline clearance.

question: A CYP2D6 poor metabolizer given codeine is expected to:

choices.text: Fail to convert codeine to morphine and lack significant analgesia
Form excess morphine and always have greater analgesia
Bypass CYP2D6 via the VKORC1 pathway
Convert codeine to morphine faster than an ultrarapid metabolizer

sourceQuote:
will not convert codeine to morphine and will
not have a significant analgesic response
explanationCorrect: Codeine is a prodrug requiring CYP2D6 conversion to morphine; poor metabolizers will not convert codeine to morphine and will not have a significant analgesic response.

explanationWrong.B: Excess morphine formation is not the poor-metabolizer phenotype described.
explanationWrong.C: VKORC1 affects warfarin sensitivity, a pharmacodynamic interaction, not codeine activation.
explanationWrong.D: Poor metabolizers convert less, not faster, than ultrarapid metabolizers.

question: Compared with competitive enzyme inhibition, the onset and offset of enzyme-induction interactions are generally longer because:

choices.text: Induction increases Km immediately at the first dose, like competitive inhibition
Maximum induction requires 2 to 4 weeks after the inducer reaches steady state, and enzyme levels take 2 to 4 weeks to return to baseline after stopping
Induction never changes Vmax
Inhibition requires new enzyme synthesis whereas induction does not

sourceQuote: maximum effect will not occur until 2 to 4 weeks after the interacting drug reaches steady state
explanationCorrect: Induction increases Vmax via new enzyme synthesis, so full effect is delayed 2–4 weeks after inducer steady state and offset is similarly slow; competitive inhibition changes Km and tracks the inhibitor’s half-life.

explanationWrong.A: Competitive inhibition increases Km; induction does not change Km.
explanationWrong.C: Induction increases Vmax.
explanationWrong.D: The opposite is stated: induction requires production of more enzyme.

question: Regarding tissue unbound fraction (fut) and loading dose, which clinical statement is made?

choices.text: fut is routinely measured in plasma like fup and always dictates a new loading dose
There are no known drug interactions that alter unbound volume of distribution and require a change in loading dose
VT in patients is highly variable from hour to hour, so loading doses cannot be calculated
Any change in fup requires an automatic matching change in fut

sourceQuote: no known drug interactions that alter the unbound volume of distribution
explanationCorrect: fut cannot be measured as fup can, and clinically there are no documented interactions that change unbound V enough to require altering the loading dose.

explanationWrong.A: The text stresses that fut cannot be measured the way fup can.
explanationWrong.C: VT is generally treated as a constant in a given patient.
explanationWrong.D: No such automatic fut linkage is described; the clinical point is loading dose is not adjusted for known unbound-V interactions.

question: A pediatric patient on cyclosporine oral solution with 43% bioavailability must switch to a generic with 28% bioavailability. To keep the same systemic exposure, the new dose should be:

choices.text: Lowered because 28% is a stronger product
Unchanged, because salt factor S always equals 1
Increased in proportion to 43/28 so that F × dose remains constant
Converted using phenytoin’s V of 0.7 L/kg instead of F

sourceQuote: The bioavailability of the dosage form he previously used is 43%
explanationCorrect: Systemic exposure is F × dose; going from F = 0.43 to F = 0.28 requires a higher milligram dose (about 43/28 times the old dose) to maintain the same amount absorbed.

explanationWrong.A: Lower F means less, not more, drug reaches the systemic circulation per milligram.
explanationWrong.B: S is not the issue in this product-switch item; F differs.
explanationWrong.D: The cyclosporine item is a bioavailability adjustment, not a phenytoin loading-dose V problem.

question: In the phase III dosing vignette, an oral regimen is needed to maintain an average steady-state concentration of 50 ng/mL. What single-dose results are provided as the basis for that design?

choices.text: IV AUC of 50 ng/mL × h after 10.3 mg
Oral half-life of 50 hours after a 962 mg dose
Steady-state concentration of 80 ng/mL after 12 hours only
An oral dose of 80 mg resulted in an AUC of 962 ng/mL × h and an elimination half-life of 10.3 hours

sourceQuote: an oral dose of 80 mg resulted in an AUC of 962
explanationCorrect: The stem states that 80 mg orally gave an AUC of 962 ng/mL × h and a half-life of 10.3 hours, to support designing a regimen that maintains average Css of 50 ng/mL.

explanationWrong.A: Those numbers are not the single-dose results given.
explanationWrong.B: Half-life is 10.3 hours after 80 mg, not 50 hours after 962 mg.
explanationWrong.C: The target average Css is 50 ng/mL; the test dose is 80 mg.

question: For the mexiletine regimen design problem, which population PK values, dosage forms, and fluctuation target are specified?

choices.text: Cl = 6 L/h/kg, V = 0.5 L/kg, only 500 mg tablets, fluctuation up to 400%
Cl = 0.5 L/h/kg, V = 6 L/kg; 150, 200, and 250 mg capsules; target average about 1 mg/L with peak-to-trough fluctuation ≤100% (0.75–1.5 mg/L)
No bioavailability is stated, and any peak-trough ratio is acceptable
Therapeutic range is 10–20 mg/L with once-weekly dosing only

sourceQuote:
distribution are Cl = 0.5 L/h/kg and V
= 6 L/kg, respectively.
explanationCorrect: Population Cl is 0.5 L/h/kg and V is 6 L/kg. Capsules are 150, 200, and 250 mg with oral bioavailability of 0.9%. Target average concentration is about 1 mg/L with ≤100% peak-to-trough fluctuation (0.75–1.5 mg/L); the described therapeutic range is 0.5–2 mg/L.

explanationWrong.A: Clearance and volume values are reversed in that choice.
explanationWrong.C: Bioavailability of 0.9% is stated, and large peak-to-trough fluctuations should be avoided.
explanationWrong.D: The therapeutic range given is 0.5–2 mg/L, not 10–20 mg/L.

question: According to the dabigatran atrial-fibrillation dosing table in this item, the labeled oral dose for CrCl 15–30 mL/min is:

choices.text: 150 mg twice daily
75 mg twice daily
No recommendation provided, identical to CrCl < 15 mL/min
325 mg once daily

sourceQuote: CrCl 15–30 mL/minute 75 mg po twice daily
explanationCorrect: The table lists 150 mg twice daily for CrCl > 30 mL/min, 75 mg twice daily for CrCl 15–30 mL/min, and no recommendation below 15 mL/min.

explanationWrong.A: 150 mg twice daily is the regimen for CrCl > 30 mL/min.
explanationWrong.C: “No recommendation provided” applies to CrCl < 15 mL/min, not the 15–30 range.
explanationWrong.D: 325 mg daily is not a listed dabigatran AF dose here.

question: A new drug completely metabolized by CYP2D6 to an inactive urinary metabolite has oral bioavailability of 12% in a CYP2D6-normal subject. After a 10 mg intravenous dose, AUC is 1,260 ng/mL·h. Which statement is a fact supplied by this information?

choices.text: Oral bioavailability must be 100% because the metabolite is inactive
The intravenous dose used to compute AUC was 150 mg twice daily
Volume of distribution is reported as 12% of body weight
Oral bioavailability is 12% and the intravenous AUC after 10 mg is 1,260 ng/mL·h

sourceQuote: given a 10 mg intravenous dose, the calculated AUC is 1,260
explanationCorrect: The passage states oral F is 12% and that a 10 mg IV dose yields AUC 1,260 ng/mL·h in a subject with a normal CYP2D6 genotype.

explanationWrong.A: Bioavailability is given as 12%, not 100%.
explanationWrong.B: 150 mg twice daily is an unrelated dosing option earlier in the item set, not the IV AUC dose.
explanationWrong.C: 12% is bioavailability, not a V expressed as percent of body weight.

question: An oral drug with very low bioavailability that is completely metabolized by CYP2D6 to an inactive metabolite is classified in the answer key as which of the following?

choices.text: A high-extraction drug that undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism
A low-extraction drug whose poor F is explained only by incomplete gut absorption
A drug for which no kinetic conclusion is possible without knowing V
A mandatory P-glycoprotein substrate solely because F is low

sourceQuote: undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism. C. This new drug
explanationCorrect: The keyed interpretation is that such a drug is a high-extraction compound undergoing extensive first-pass metabolism; V is not required for that conclusion.

explanationWrong.B: Low extraction with poor absorption is the distractor labeled C in the source item.
explanationWrong.C: The source states that conclusion is possible without knowing V.
explanationWrong.D: Being a P-glycoprotein substrate is not required by the given information.

question: A patient whose blood pressure is controlled on oral metoprolol starts paroxetine. Paroxetine is identified as which type of CYP2D6 interacting drug?

choices.text: A CYP2D6 inducer that would lower metoprolol levels
A CYP2D6 substrate with no inhibitory effect
A CYP2D6 inhibitor
An enzyme that metabolizes metoprolol by glucuronidation only

sourceQuote: he was started on paroxetine (a CYP2D6 inhibitor) 20 mg per day
explanationCorrect: The item states paroxetine is a CYP2D6 inhibitor and metoprolol is a CYP2D6 substrate, so an interaction affecting metoprolol exposure is expected.

explanationWrong.A: Paroxetine is labeled here as an inhibitor, not an inducer.
explanationWrong.B: It is specifically called a CYP2D6 inhibitor.
explanationWrong.D: Metoprolol is identified as a CYP2D6 substrate, not as solely a UGT substrate in this item.

question: During medication reconciliation, a pharmacist notes concomitant warfarin and carbamazepine. Because of carbamazepine’s effect on warfarin, which pharmacokinetic interaction is stated?

choices.text: Carbamazepine inhibits warfarin clearance and always raises INR within hours
The combination has no effect on warfarin elimination
Carbamazepine induces the elimination of warfarin
Warfarin induces carbamazepine metabolism exclusively, with no effect on anticoagulation

sourceQuote: carbamazepine induces the elimination of warfarin, the pharmacist
explanationCorrect: The passage states that carbamazepine induces the elimination of warfarin, so the anticoagulant effect may decrease; management still depends on duration of combined use and recent INRs (next item).

explanationWrong.A: Induction increases elimination rather than inhibiting clearance.
explanationWrong.B: An induction interaction is explicitly identified.
explanationWrong.D: The stated direction is carbamazepine inducing warfarin elimination.

question: If a patient has already been taking warfarin together with an enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant, what is the most appropriate initial pharmacist action described?

choices.text: Warn the prescriber that anticoagulation will inevitably decrease starting today, without checking history
Determine how long the combination has been used and obtain recent INR values
Instruct the patient to take an extra warfarin dose immediately
Switch the anticonvulsant before reviewing INR trends

sourceQuote: learn how long the patient has been taking this drug combination and obtain recent
explanationCorrect: The keyed approach is to learn the duration of combined therapy and review recent INRs, because a stable long-term combination may already have been dose-adjusted.

explanationWrong.A: A future decrease is not assumed if the pair has been long-standing and INRs are known.
explanationWrong.C: Unsupervised extra doses are not the recommended first step.
explanationWrong.D: Suggesting a non-inducing anticonvulsant is an option in the source item, not the preferred first action.

question: When computing the time interval between two vancomycin concentrations drawn at 13:20 and 04:30 the next calendar day, the answer key uses which time convention?

choices.text: 12-hour clock without converting afternoon hours
24-hour clock time, which is used in all hospitals
Julian day count ignoring clock time
Only the date, assuming each sample is 24 hours apart by default

sourceQuote: Time in this case is 24-hour clock time, which is used in all hospitals
explanationCorrect: Hospital clock times are 24-hour; the interval is calculated from 13:20 to 24:00 plus 04:30, then used to estimate k and half-life.

explanationWrong.A: The key explicitly uses 24-hour clock time.
explanationWrong.C: Clock times on both dates are required, not a Julian-day shortcut.
explanationWrong.D: The samples are not a default 24 hours apart; the interval must be calculated from the recorded times.

question: In the answer key, pharmacokinetic “flip-flop” refers to which relationship between absorption and elimination rate constants?

choices.text: ka much less than k, so the terminal decline is governed by absorption rather than elimination
ka much greater than k, the usual oral assumption
Clearance equal to volume of distribution
Zero-order infusion without first-order constants

sourceQuote: This is the pharmacokinetic “flip-flop” with the ka<<k
explanationCorrect: Flip-flop occurs when ka << k, so the terminal slope (and the time for concentration to fall) is governed by the slow absorption rate, not k.

explanationWrong.B: ka >> k is the usual assumption that absorption is complete before the terminal phase, not flip-flop.
explanationWrong.C: That equality is not the flip-flop definition.
explanationWrong.D: The item uses first-order ka and k, not a zero-order infusion.

question: After calculating absorbed cyclosporine from the old product (F = 43%), the new milligram dose is obtained by dividing that absorbed amount by which bioavailability?

choices.text: 100%, assuming IV administration
43%, repeating the old F
The generic product’s 28% bioavailability
S = 0.92 as if the drug were phenytoin acid

sourceQuote: dose needed based on bioavailability of the new dosage form (28%)
explanationCorrect: Match absorbed amount (old dose × 0.43) to new dose × 0.28, so the new dose uses the generic’s 28% F.

explanationWrong.A: This is an oral-to-oral F adjustment, not an IV conversion.
explanationWrong.B: Using 43% again would not account for the less available generic.
explanationWrong.D: S = 0.92 belongs to the phenytoin loading-dose item, not this cyclosporine switch.

question: Why is it inappropriate to lock in a dabigatran dose from a single eGFR/CrCl when it is unknown whether kidney function is stable?

choices.text: Serum creatinine has a long half-life as renal function declines and may continue to rise for days in acute kidney injury
MDRD values in mL/min/1.73 m² can never be converted to mL/min
Cockcroft–Gault always overestimates GFR by a fixed 50% in every adult
Dabigatran labeling ignores CrCl entirely

sourceQuote: The serum creatinine has a long half-life as renal function declines
explanationCorrect: SCr lags declining GFR, so a single value may not reflect ongoing AKI; dosing from an unverified “stable” CrCl/eGFR is therefore inappropriate.

explanationWrong.B: The key explains conversion by calculating BSA and dividing by 1.73.
explanationWrong.C: No such fixed 50% rule is given; the issue is unknown stability.
explanationWrong.D: The table is CrCl-based (150 mg vs 75 mg vs no recommendation).

question: A digoxin concentration of 1.7 ng/mL drawn 5 hours after the dose, with heart rate 81 bpm, is best interpreted how?

choices.text: It is a valid trough proving the dose must be halved today
It may be falsely elevated because of the distribution phase; the therapeutic range is based on troughs, so redraw later in the interval
Distribution is complete by 1 hour, so 5 hours is always a trough
Heart rate 81 bpm independently proves toxicity regardless of sampling time

sourceQuote: If a level is drawn less than 8 hours after administration of the dose
explanationCorrect: Digoxin has a two-compartment distribution phase; levels drawn <8 hours postdose can be falsely high versus a true trough, and HR 81 bpm does not suggest overdose.

explanationWrong.A: A 5-hour level is not a trough; immediately halving the dose on that number is the error the key warns against.
explanationWrong.C: The key uses an 8-hour threshold, not 1 hour.
explanationWrong.D: HR 81 bpm is cited as not suggesting the dose is too high.

question: Lidocaine (high-extraction, given by IV infusion) faces increased α1-acid glycoprotein after myocardial infarction, lowering fup. The expected change in active free concentration is:

choices.text: Css,free increases in parallel with total concentration
Css,free is unchanged because IV high-extraction drugs ignore protein binding
The decrease in fup decreases the active free drug concentration
Clearance falls to zero because Q stops

sourceQuote: decrease the active free drug concentration, resulting in a decrease in the
explanationCorrect: For IV high-extraction lidocaine, lower fup (more AAG binding) is expected to decrease Css,free and thus the pharmacologic effect, per the venous-equilibrium discussion in the key.

explanationWrong.A: The key predicts a decrease in active free concentration, not an increase.
explanationWrong.B: Table 10-1/the key specifically apply a fup change to IV high-extraction disposition.
explanationWrong.D: Hepatic blood flow is not described as stopping; the change modeled is fup.

question: The FDA draft guidance cited for bioavailability and bioequivalence studies submitted in NDAs or INDs is dated:

choices.text: March 2014
1992, coinciding with Gibaldi’s second edition only
2018, matching Goodman & Gilman’s 13th edition year alone
No date is provided in the references

sourceQuote: Draft Guidance. March 2014. Available at: https://www.fda.gov/downloads/drugs/guidancecomplianceregulatoryinformation/guidances/ucm389370.pdf. Editor’s Note: This chapter is
explanationCorrect: The references list the FDA draft guidance on BA/BE studies in NDAs or INDs as March 2014.

explanationWrong.B: Gibaldi 1982 is a separate pharmacokinetics textbook citation.
explanationWrong.C: Goodman & Gilman 13th edition (2018) is a separate citation; the BA/BE guidance date given is March 2014.
explanationWrong.D: The date March 2014 is explicitly listed.

question: In DNA base pairing as stated in the key points, which pairs form?

choices.text: Adenine with cytosine, and guanine with thymine
Adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine
Adenine with guanine, and cytosine with thymine
Uracil with thymine on both DNA strands

sourceQuote: adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine
explanationCorrect: DNA strands are held by hydrogen bonds between base pairs: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

explanationWrong.A: A does not pair with C in the pairing rule given.
explanationWrong.C: Purine–purine and pyrimidine–pyrimidine pairing is not the rule stated.
explanationWrong.D: Thymine, not uracil, is the DNA base paired with adenine in this description.

question: The pharmacogenetics study checklist includes genetic polymorphisms of which three medication-related protein classes?

choices.text: Only structural collagens with no PK/PD effect
Metabolic enzymes, drug transporters, and drug targets
Dietary fiber receptors exclusively
Radiocontrast osmolarity proteins only

sourceQuote: Genetic polymorphisms of metabolic enzymes, drug transporters, and drug targets
explanationCorrect: Learners are directed to polymorphisms of metabolic enzymes, transporters, and targets and their PK/PD effects, plus disease-associated variants and clinical PGx resources.

explanationWrong.A: The checklist is about drug-related proteins, not inert collagens.
explanationWrong.C: Fiber receptors are not the listed polymorphism classes.
explanationWrong.D: Contrast agents are not the focus of this checklist item.

question: In the historical table, succinylcholine was observed in 1954 to produce which adverse response after normal doses?

choices.text: Primaquine-type hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Isoniazid neurotoxicity
Prolonged neuromuscular blockade
Warfarin-related skin necrosis

sourceQuote: Succinylcholine was observed to produce prolonged neuromuscular blockade
explanationCorrect: The 1954 observation was prolonged neuromuscular blockade after usual succinylcholine doses; isoniazid neurotoxicity (1954) and primaquine–G6PD hemolysis (1956) are separate milestones.

explanationWrong.A: Primaquine hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is listed as 1956.
explanationWrong.B: Isoniazid neurotoxicity is a separate 1954 observation.
explanationWrong.D: Warfarin necrosis is not the succinylcholine table entry.

question: In the chapter’s terminology, a haplotype is defined as:

choices.text: The presence of identical alleles at a locus on homologous chromosomes
A combination of alleles at multiple loci that travel together during recombination
An insertion or deletion mutation only
Any protein that catalyzes a chemical reaction

sourceQuote: A combination of alleles at multiple loci that travel together during recombination
explanationCorrect: A haplotype is a combination of alleles at multiple loci that travel together during recombination; homozygous refers to identical alleles at a locus, and an indel is an insertion/deletion.

explanationWrong.A: That definition is homozygous, not haplotype.
explanationWrong.C: That definition is indel.
explanationWrong.D: That definition is enzyme.

question: A single nucleotide polymorphism is described as a base-pair substitution occurring with what average frequency?

choices.text: Once per chromosome arm only
In every three hundred bases, on average
Only in RNA, never DNA
Once per 3 billion bases, i.e., a unique genome-wide event

sourceQuote: base pair substitution occurring in every three hundred bases, on average
explanationCorrect: An SNP is defined as a base-pair substitution occurring on average every 300 bases.

explanationWrong.A: The stated average is every 300 bases, not per chromosome arm.
explanationWrong.C: The definition is for DNA sequence variation.
explanationWrong.D: 3 billion is the approximate human genome size mentioned later, not the SNP spacing given here.

question: Complementary DNA strands can separate and serve as templates because base pairs are held by which interactions?

choices.text: Covalent bonds of the same strength as the sugar–phosphate backbone
Ionic lattice bonds identical to NaCl crystals
Relatively weak noncovalent hydrogen bonds
Disulfide bridges between thymine dimers only

sourceQuote: held together by the relatively weak attraction of noncovalent hydrogen bonds
explanationCorrect: Unlike covalent bonds in the rest of the molecule, complementary base pairs use relatively weak hydrogen bonds, so strands can come apart as templates for information transfer.

explanationWrong.A: The text contrasts these interactions with covalent bonds elsewhere in the molecule.
explanationWrong.B: Ionic crystal bonding is not the description given.
explanationWrong.D: Thymine dimers are not the pairing interaction described.

question: Among individuals, about what percentage of genetic variation is attributed to single nucleotide polymorphisms?

choices.text: 100%, with no other variation types

sourceQuote: account for about 90% of genetic variations among individuals
explanationCorrect: SNPs are the most common variation type and account for about 90% of genetic differences among individuals; indels and copy-number variants also occur.

explanationWrong.A: 90%, not 10%, is the figure given.
explanationWrong.B: The stated proportion is about 90%.
explanationWrong.D: Indels and copy-number variations are also listed.

question: In addition to primers and a buffered cationic solution, PCR requires which pair of reagents?

choices.text: Ribosomes and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases
DNA nucleotides (dNTPs) and thermostable DNA polymerase
Restriction endonucleases as the sole enzyme
ddNTPs without any dNTPs

sourceQuote: DNA nucleotides (deoxynucleotide triphosphates, or dNTPs) and thermostable DNA polymerase
explanationCorrect: PCR uses dNTPs and a thermostable DNA polymerase with primers that direct bidirectional synthesis across the region of interest.

explanationWrong.A: Those are translation components, not PCR reagents listed here.
explanationWrong.C: Restriction enzymes are not the PCR enzyme named.
explanationWrong.D: ddNTPs are introduced later for sequencing, not as the PCR nucleotide mix.

question: Sanger-type sequencing as described uses limited amounts of which chain-terminating nucleotides?

choices.text: Standard dNTPs only, with no modified bases
Specially modified dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs)
Thermostable RNA primers in both directions like PCR
Unlabeled rNTPs for bidirectional synthesis

sourceQuote: limited quantities of specially modified dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs), the DNA to be sequenced
explanationCorrect: Sequencing mixes polymerase, dNTPs, limited ddNTPs, template, and a single primer; synthesis is unidirectional and each chain is fluorescently tagged at its 3′ end.

explanationWrong.A: Limited ddNTPs in addition to standard nucleotides are required for termination.
explanationWrong.C: Unlike PCR, sequencing uses one primer and is unidirectional.
explanationWrong.D: The description is DNA sequencing with ddNTPs, not rNTP transcription.

question: DNA microarrays can be used to determine which genomic information in an individual?

choices.text: Only the mass of ribosomal RNA in milligrams
Crystal structures of membrane transporters
Genotype or gene sequence at thousands of positions in the genome
Serum creatinine as a numeric GFR

sourceQuote: determine the genotype or gene sequence at thousands of positions in the genome
explanationCorrect: Hybridization to an oligonucleotide array can genotype or sequence thousands of genomic positions; arrays can also profile mRNA expression patterns.

explanationWrong.A: rRNA mass is not the microarray application stated.
explanationWrong.B: Protein crystallography is not this nucleic-acid hybridization method.
explanationWrong.D: GFR estimation is unrelated to microarray scanning.

question: The stated goal of pharmacogenetics is to use an individual’s genetic profile to optimize therapy by:

choices.text: Maximizing toxicity to ensure target engagement
Ignoring dose while selecting only brand-name products
Minimizing the likelihood of toxicity while maximizing efficacy via the most effective drug or dose
Replacing all clinical monitoring with a single ancestry questionnaire

sourceQuote: minimizing the likelihood of toxicity while maximizing efficacy by choosing the most effective
explanationCorrect: Pharmacogenetics aims to minimize toxicity and maximize efficacy by choosing the most effective drug or dose, using variants in metabolizing enzymes, transporters, targets, and disease-associated genes.

explanationWrong.A: The goal is to minimize, not maximize, toxicity.
explanationWrong.B: Dose selection is explicitly part of optimization.
explanationWrong.D: A genetic profile of relevant genes, not a generic ancestry form, is the tool described.

question: CYP2C19 intermediate or poor metabolizers treated with clopidogrel have which predicted platelet and cardiovascular outcome?

choices.text: Increased active-metabolite formation and fewer ischemic events
Reduced platelet inhibition and increased risk for adverse cardiovascular events
No change in bioactivation because clopidogrel is not a prodrug
Guaranteed therapeutic voriconazole levels at standard doses

sourceQuote: Reduced platelet inhibition and increased risk for adverse cardiovascular events in IMs and PMs
explanationCorrect: Clopidogrel bioactivation is CYP2C19-dependent; IMs and PMs have reduced platelet inhibition and higher risk of adverse cardiovascular events.

explanationWrong.A: Reduced, not increased, activation/inhibition is predicted in IMs/PMs.
explanationWrong.C: The implication table treats clopidogrel as requiring CYP2C19-dependent effect.
explanationWrong.D: Voriconazole UMs have decreased likelihood of therapeutic concentrations—a different row of the same table.

question: Reduced or absent dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPYD) activity with capecitabine, fluorouracil, or tegafur can result in:

choices.text: Loss of all fluoropyrimidine toxicity because the drugs cannot be activated
Severe toxicity such as neutropenia, severe diarrhea, mucositis, and hand–foot syndrome
Isolated bilirubin-related discontinuation identical to atazanavir PMs only
G6PD-related hemolysis as a sex-linked dominant trait

sourceQuote: Reduced or absent DPYD activity can result in severe toxicity
explanationCorrect: DPYD deficiency impairs fluoropyrimidine inactivation and can cause severe toxicity including neutropenia, GI injury, mucositis, and hand–foot syndrome.

explanationWrong.A: The table lists severe toxicity, not absence of toxicity.
explanationWrong.C: Bilirubin-related discontinuation is the UGT1A1–atazanavir implication.
explanationWrong.D: G6PD deficiency is a separate sex-linked recessive cause of hemolysis with oxidative drugs.

question: CYP2D6 is distinctive among CYPs in this chapter because it:

choices.text: Has fewer alleles than any other CYP and metabolizes <1% of drugs
Metabolizes as much as 25% of medications and has more than 100 known alleles
Exists only as ultrarapid metabolizer genotypes
Does not form active metabolites from any prodrug

sourceQuote: as much as 25% of all medications are metabolized by CYP2D6
explanationCorrect: CYP2D6 has the largest number of CYP variants (>100 alleles) and metabolizes as much as 25% of medications; PMs have two or more nonfunctional alleles.

explanationWrong.A: The opposite scale is stated (>100 alleles; ~25% of drugs).
explanationWrong.C: PM, IM, NM, RM, and UM phenotypes are all described in the accompanying table.
explanationWrong.D: The phenotype table includes generation of active metabolites, which UMs increase and PMs decrease.

question: Slow N-acetyltransferase (NAT) acetylators are at increased risk of which adverse syndromes?

choices.text: Hydralazine- and procainamide-induced lupus-like syndrome and sulfonamide hypersensitivity
CYP2C9-related warfarin resistance from ultrarapid clearance
UGT1A1-related irinotecan inactivity without toxicity
Complete protection from arylamine carcinogen acetylation effects

sourceQuote: hydralazine- and procainamide-induced lupus- like syndrome and sulfonamide hypersensitivity
explanationCorrect: NAT acetylates arylamines; slow acetylators can experience hydralazine- or procainamide-induced lupus-like syndrome and sulfonamide hypersensitivity.

explanationCorrect: Chains and buying groups can choose which generics to stock and negotiate lower prices on large volumes, whereas health plans do not choose which generics pharmacies dispense, so manufacturers have little incentive to negotiate generic prices with plans.

explanationWrong.A: Health plans do not choose which generic is dispensed; pharmacies do.
explanationWrong.B: Manufacturers have no incentive to negotiate generic price terms with a health plan even if the plan buys large volume.
explanationWrong.D: The passage lists AMP among retail price measures but does not assign generic leverage solely to wholesaler–CMS AMP negotiation.

question: Average manufacturer price (AMP) reflects which manufacturer rebates?

choices.text: Rebates to wholesalers and retail pharmacies, but not rebates to PBMs, Medicaid, or other third-party payers
Only Medicaid best-price rebates paid to states
Only PBM rebate contracts
All copays paid by patients at the counter

sourceQuote: It reflects all rebates paid by manufacturers to wholesalers and retail pharmacies.
explanationCorrect: AMP includes manufacturer rebates to wholesalers and retail pharmacies and excludes rebates to PBMs, Medicaid, and other third-party payers; manufacturers report AMP to CMS for Medicaid rebate calculations.

explanationWrong.B: Medicaid rebates are excluded from AMP as defined here, though AMP is used to calculate them.
explanationWrong.C: PBM rebates are specifically excluded from AMP.
explanationWrong.D: Patient copays are not manufacturer rebates included in AMP.

question: Average wholesale price (AWP) is best described as:

choices.text: The actual transaction cost paid by all retail pharmacies
Equivalent to wholesale acquisition cost for every generic drug
A published list price, often used as a discounted payment basis rather than the price actually paid
The FDA-imposed ceiling price during shortages

sourceQuote: the AWP is not the price paid by retail pharmacies and nonretail providers
explanationCorrect: AWP is a published list price; in practice it is not the price paid by pharmacies and is often used as a discounted basis for payment by Medicaid, PBMs, and health plans.

explanationWrong.A: The passage states AWP is not the price paid by retail pharmacies and nonretail providers.
explanationWrong.B: WAC is discussed separately and is meaningful mainly for single-source (patent-protected) drugs.
explanationWrong.D: An FDA shortage ceiling price is not the definition of AWP.

question: About half of REMS programs include elements to assure safe use, which require:

choices.text: Automatic over-the-counter switch of the drug
Clinicians or health care settings to become certified before prescribing
Removal of all boxed warnings from labeling
Manufacturer exemption from FAERS reporting

sourceQuote:
requiring clinicians or health care settings to become certified
before prescribing
explanationCorrect: ETASU require clinicians or health care settings to become certified before prescribing and to participate in additional REMS activities such as training, counseling, and monitoring.

explanationWrong.A: REMS certification is not an OTC switch.
explanationWrong.C: Boxed warnings are a separate labeling tool discussed in this section, not removed by ETASU.
explanationWrong.D: REMS does not exempt manufacturers from safety reporting.

question: Which statement about branded OTC product lines is illustrated by the Dulcolax examples?

choices.text: Every product under one brand name must contain the same active ingredient.
Brand names are legally required to match a single monograph ingredient.
Some products share a sales-leading brand name but contain different active ingredients.
All Dulcolax products contain polyethylene glycol 3350.

sourceQuote: Some drug products are branded with a sales-leading product’s name, but contain different active ingredients.
explanationCorrect: Dulcolax tablets/suppositories contain bisacodyl, while other Dulcolax-branded items contain docusate, magnesium hydroxide, or PEG 3350.

explanationWrong.A: The examples show different actives under one brand family.
explanationWrong.B: No such legal requirement is stated; the point is brand-name sharing with different actives.
explanationWrong.D: PEG 3350 is only Dulcolax Balance in the examples; tablets contain bisacodyl.

question: In the United States, reporting of adverse events and medication errors by health care providers and consumers is:

choices.text: Mandatory for every over-the-counter purchase
Required before a prescription may be dispensed
Limited to manufacturers, never clinicians or consumers
Voluntary

sourceQuote:
Reporting of adverse events and medication errors by health care providers and consumers is
voluntary
explanationCorrect: Reporting of adverse events and medication errors by health care providers and consumers is voluntary in the United States.

explanationWrong.A: OTC purchases do not trigger mandatory MedWatch reporting.
explanationWrong.B: Dispensing is not conditioned on an adverse-event report.
explanationWrong.C: Providers and consumers may report directly; manufacturers also receive and must forward reports.

question: If a manufacturer receives an adverse event report, the manufacturer:

choices.text: Is required to send the report to the FDA
May destroy the report after internal review
Must wait until FAERS requests the file
May report only if the patient consents in writing

sourceQuote:
a manufacturer receives an adverse event report, it is required to send the
report to the FDA
explanationCorrect: If a manufacturer receives an adverse event report, it is required to send the report to the FDA; reports then enter FAERS after clinical review.

explanationWrong.B: Destruction after internal review would violate the forwarding requirement.
explanationWrong.C: The manufacturer must send the report; it does not wait for a FAERS request.
explanationWrong.D: A written patient-consent requirement for manufacturer reporting is not stated.

question: If a take-back, mail-back, or drop-box program is unavailable, unused tablets should be discarded by:

choices.text: Crushing them and flushing the powder down the toilet
Mixing intact tablets with an unpalatable substance such as dirt, cat litter, or used coffee grounds, then sealing and trashing the mixture
Placing the labeled vial intact in household trash
Mailing remaining doses to the FDA

sourceQuote: mix the medications (do not crush tablets or capsules) with an unpalatable substance
explanationCorrect: Most unused medicines may go in household trash after mixing (without crushing) with an unpalatable substance and placing the mixture in a sealed container; scratch personal information from empty packaging.

explanationWrong.A: Tablets and capsules should not be crushed, and flushing is not the household method described.
explanationWrong.C: Personal information on the label should be made unreadable; leftover drug should be mixed first.
explanationWrong.D: FDA mailing is not the household disposal method given.

question: If a DEA-authorized collector or take-back program is unavailable, the FDA recommends flushing which medications?

choices.text: All unused oral antibiotics
All over-the-counter analgesics
A few select medications, especially certain controlled substances
Any labeled vial placed in household trash without further precautions

sourceQuote:
the FDA recommends that these
medications be disposed of by flushing them down the toilet
explanationCorrect: For safety, the FDA recommends flushing only a few select medications (notably certain controlled substances) when a take-back option is unavailable.

explanationWrong.A: Flushing is not recommended for all unused antibiotics.
explanationWrong.B: OTC analgesics are not the select group described for wastewater disposal.
explanationWrong.D: Controlled substances should not be discarded in the trash because of accidental-access risk; labels on empty packaging should be made unreadable.

question: In some studies, approximately what fraction of initial drug prescriptions were not filled within 9 months?

choices.text: One-tenth
Almost one-third
Three of four
Nearly all prescriptions

sourceQuote:
almost one-third of all initial drug prescriptions were not filled within 9
months
explanationCorrect: Almost one-third of initial prescriptions were not filled within 9 months, with nonadherence highest for expensive drugs and chronic preventive therapies.

explanationWrong.A: One-tenth is lower than the almost one-third figure given.
explanationWrong.C: Three of four consumers admit they do not always take medications as directed; that is a different statistic.
explanationWrong.D: Nearly all unfilled is not the fraction stated.

question: Which set of factors is identified as affecting patient medication nonadherence?

choices.text: Only tablet color
Only pharmacy hours of operation
Only the prescriber’s DEA number
Illness seriousness, treatment cost, and treatment side effects

sourceQuote: The seriousness of the illness, the cost of treatment, and treatment side effects can all affect adherence.
explanationCorrect: Nonadherence has many facets, including illness seriousness, cost, side effects, age, mental status, regimen complexity, duration, and health literacy.

explanationWrong.A: Appearance alone is not the cluster of factors listed.
explanationWrong.B: Hours of operation are not among the adherence factors named.
explanationWrong.C: DEA numbering is unrelated to the adherence determinants described.

question: A pharmacist recovery network (PRN) is described as:

choices.text: A public disciplinary docket of all impaired pharmacists
An FDA manufacturing-inspection program
A DEA take-back contractor
A confidential program assisting recognition and treatment of substance abuse

sourceQuote:
A
PRN is a confidential program providing assistance in the recognition and treatment of substance abuse
explanationCorrect: A PRN is a confidential program providing assistance in the recognition and treatment of substance abuse of affected pharmacists.

explanationWrong.A: Confidentiality is emphasized; it is not described as a public docket.
explanationWrong.B: FDA inspections are unrelated to the PRN definition given.
explanationWrong.C: DEA take-back programs are a disposal topic, not the PRN.

question: After a pharmacist demonstrates commitment to recovery, state-board reinstatement generally requires the pharmacist to:

choices.text: Complete rehabilitation, maintain counselor contact, submit to random drug testing, and attend support groups
Pay a fine with no further monitoring
Transfer permanently to a non-patient-care career
Avoid all support-group contact to protect confidentiality

sourceQuote:
submit to random drug testing, and participate in support group
meetings on a regular basis
explanationCorrect: Generally the board requires completion of a rehabilitation program, regular counselor contact, random drug testing, and regular support-group participation.

explanationWrong.B: A fine alone without monitoring is not the reinstatement process described.
explanationWrong.C: Reinstatement to pharmacy practice can begin after demonstrated recovery, not a mandatory career change.
explanationWrong.D: Participation in support-group meetings on a regular basis is required, not avoided.

question: Management is defined as the art of maximizing productivity by:

choices.text: Using and developing people’s talents while providing self-enrichment and opportunities for growth
Minimizing all staff training to reduce payroll
Replacing communication with written warnings only
Eliminating planning so that work remains flexible

sourceQuote: Management is the art of maximizing productivity by using and developing people’s talents,
explanationCorrect: Classical management maximizes productivity by developing talent and offering growth, using functions such as planning, organizing, commanding, coordinating, and controlling.

explanationWrong.B: Developing people’s talents is central to the definition, not minimizing training.
explanationWrong.C: Leadership, decision making, and communication are listed management skills.
explanationWrong.D: Planning is a classical management element, not something to eliminate.

question: Which sequence is listed for the controlling function of management?

choices.text: Pay, hire, terminate, then replace staff
Market, promote, price, then place the service
Plan, lead, and organize without measuring results
Establish standards, measure actual performance, compare with standards, and take corrective or preventive measures

sourceQuote: 1. Establish performance standards based on organizational objectives
explanationCorrect: Controlling verifies that functions go according to plan by establishing performance standards, measuring and reporting actual performance, comparing results with standards, and taking corrective or preventive measures.

explanationWrong.A: Those personnel actions are not the four controlling steps listed.
explanationWrong.B: Those are marketing mix actions, not the controlling steps.
explanationWrong.C: Controlling specifically includes measuring performance against standards.

question: According to principles of pharmacy practice management, which activities specifically constitute managing human resources?

choices.text: Establishing goals and performance standards and providing feedback
Restricting communication to written policies so that verbal coaching is unnecessary
Delegating vision-setting exclusively to front-line staff without managerial standards
Evaluating only technical compounding skills and omitting outcome measures

sourceQuote: establishing goals and performance standards and providing feedback. Employees look
explanationCorrect: Managing human resources is described as establishing goals and performance standards and providing feedback so employees have clear expectations.

explanationWrong.B: Communication is identified as a critical management skill, not something to replace with policies alone.
explanationWrong.C: Managers, not solely front-line staff, establish expectations and outcome measures.
explanationWrong.D: Performance standards and outcome measures go beyond a single technical skill domain.

question: Which action is listed as a strategy for the managing-up process?

choices.text: Withhold complete information to test the supervisor
Publicly embarrass the supervisor when disagreeing
Assist a supervisor in better managing his or her time
Ignore role expectations to appear independent

sourceQuote: Assist a supervisor in better managing his or her time.
explanationCorrect: Managing-up strategies include clarifying roles, recognizing the supervisor’s styles, providing complete information, being dependable, assisting with time management, showing appreciation, and disagreeing with tact.

explanationWrong.A: The text advises providing a supervisor with complete information.
explanationWrong.B: Disagreement should be with tact and respect, not public embarrassment.
explanationWrong.D: Clarifying roles and expectations is recommended, not ignoring them.

question: Tools for appropriate medication use—such as an error-prone abbreviations list, high-alert medications, and a “Do Not Crush” list—are attributed in this review to which organization?

The Institute for Safe Medication Practices
The Drug Enforcement Administration only
State Medicaid agencies exclusively

explanationWrong.C: DEA is not the source of the ISMP tools listed.

question: The FAERS self-assessment item names clinical reviewers in which FDA centers as evaluating reports, and how is FAERS characterized in that item?

explanationWrong.B: State boards are not the named FAERS reviewers.

question: If a take-back program is not available, which disposal method for noncontrolled medications is listed in the self-assessment item?

Mix them with an unpalatable substance and place them in the trash

be mixed with an unpalatable
substance and placed in the trash.
9.

It also presents claims about DEA-authorized collectors and adherence (once- or twice-daily dosing vs four-times-daily; prescribers overestimating adherence).

question: Which of the following is not an element of the Pharmacists’ Patient Care Process?

question: Which statement about medication take-back programs is supported by this answer key?

choices.text: Controlled substances are never acceptable for take-back programs
Controlled substances are acceptable for take-back programs, and law enforcement sites can serve as take-back sites in addition to approved pharmacists

question: The FDA Purple Book lists:

Approved small-molecule drugs with therapeutic-equivalence codes only

Controlled-substance schedules by DEA code

question: For 2016, which source accounted for the largest listed share of U.S. national health-care expenditures?

explanationWrong.C: Compounding regulation is not the system-level focus described.

question: Medicare and Medicaid were created by which legislation signed on July 30, 1965?

choices.text: The Social Security Amendments of 1965
The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003
The Affordable Care Act of 2010
The Drug Quality and Security Act of 2013

explanationCorrect: President Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965, creating Medicare and Medicaid, which later covered more than 43 million Americans.

explanationWrong.C: The ACA is a 2010 coverage-expansion statute, not the 1965 creating law.

question: Enrollment in Medicare Part D is described as:

Optional for beneficiaries enrolled in Part A or B
Prohibited if the beneficiary has any chronic disease

explanationWrong.D: Chronic disease is an MTMS criterion, not a bar to Part D enrollment.

question: The wellness model for preventing disease and promoting health receives approximately what share of health-care spending?

explanationWrong.A: 34% is the private-insurance share of expenditures from the prior chapter, not wellness spending.

explanationWrong.D: 18% is not the wellness-model share stated here.

question: Which organization form is described as the newest cost-control model that ties payment to performance (quality of care)?

choices.text: Independent cash-pay solo practice
Traditional indemnity insurance without networks
Mail-order pharmacy cooperatives
The accountable care organization (ACO)

explanationCorrect: HMOs and PPOs are the two main managed-care configurations; the ACO is the newest form and ties payment to quality/performance.
