explanationWrong.C: Mail-order cooperatives are not the ACO model named here.

question: After universal (single-payer) coverage was abandoned as unlikely to pass Congress, what mechanism was chosen as the foundation for increasing insurance coverage?

choices.text: An individual mandate requiring U.S. citizens to purchase health insurance, under financial penalty
Elimination of all private insurers
A statutory ban on Medicaid expansion
Exclusive VA coverage for all civilians

explanationCorrect: Reform used an individual mandate plus subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and insurance exchanges after single-payer coverage was judged unlikely to pass.

question: Horizontal integration in health-care delivery occurs when:

Patients self-refer across unaffiliated states

question: Vertically integrated health systems in this chapter are described as financed under which managed-care model?

choices.text: Unmanaged indemnity only
The HMO managed care model
Workers’ compensation exclusively
TRICARE for civilians

question: Semi-integrated delivery models in this chapter are characterized by which arrangement?

Independent entities contract with an HMO plan to deliver care

Payers are prohibited from coordinating among independent providers

question: In a semi-integrated model, how do physicians who join independent physician associations typically differ from physicians in a vertically integrated system?

They cannot join IPAs
PPOs were developed to increase restrictions on patient choice beyond HMOs

question: The Veterans Health Administration is a component of which federal department?

The Department of Defense exclusively
The Department of Commerce
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs

question: In the three-level PBM service model, which activities are classified as advanced services?

Hospital medical-staff credentialing
DEA registration of pharmacies

question: Which program is funded by federal and state governments and is the main coverage for people uninsured by the commercial market?

question: Medicare Part C, also known as Medicare Advantage, is described as including:

question: Which statute created Medicare Part D?

choices.text: The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003
The Social Security Amendments of 1965
The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration Act of 1970

sourceQuote: The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 created Part D.
explanationCorrect: The MMA of 2003 created Part D; the 1965 amendments created Medicare/Medicaid, not Part D.

explanationWrong.B: The 1965 amendments created Medicare and Medicaid, not Part D.
explanationWrong.C: The FDCA is drug-safety law, not the Part D authorizing statute.
explanationWrong.D: OSHA addresses workplace safety, not Medicare drug benefits.

question: Incidence, as defined in this chapter, measures:

choices.text: All existing cases, new or old, during a time period
Only deaths in a population
The occurrence of new cases of disease in a population at risk during a time period
Health-related quality-of-life utilities

sourceQuote: Incidence is the occurrence of new cases of disease in a population at risk during a time period.
explanationCorrect: Incidence counts new cases among those at risk; prevalence includes new or old cases; mortality rate is incidence of death and may be age-adjusted.

explanationWrong.A: That definition is prevalence, not incidence.
explanationWrong.B: Deaths are measured by mortality rate, a special incidence of death.
explanationWrong.D: Utilities belong to pharmacoeconomics, not this epidemiologic definition.

question: How does a case-control study evaluate risk for a specific condition?

choices.text: It randomizes patients to exposure versus placebo and follows them prospectively only
It compares an exposed cohort with an unexposed cohort without using disease status to sample
It retrospectively compares a group with the disease to a group without the disease
It is identical to passive surveillance reporting of single unusual cases

sourceQuote: A case-control study is a retrospective study evaluating the risks for a specific condition
explanationCorrect: A case-control study is retrospective and compares patients who have the disease with patients who do not. A cohort compares occurrence in exposed versus unexposed groups.

explanationWrong.A: Randomized assignment is not the case-control design described.
explanationWrong.B: That sampling approach describes a cohort, not a case-control study.
explanationWrong.D: Single or multiple unusual-condition reports are distinguished from case-control design.

question: Passive pharmacovigilance is incomplete for which listed reasons?

choices.text: It always captures every adverse effect from all institutions in real time
Reporting takes time, reporters may fear malpractice, and they may believe someone else already reported the case
It is identical to planned systematic collection of adherence and adverse-effect data
It never uses a central database

sourceQuote: the belief that someone else has already reported the information. Active
explanationCorrect: Passive surveillance is voluntary reporting to a central database and may be incomplete because of reporting delay, fear of malpractice, and the belief that someone else already reported. Active surveillance is planned and more accurate but may cover few institutions.

explanationWrong.A: Incompleteness is the point of the passage.
explanationWrong.C: Planned systematic collection defines active, not passive, surveillance.
explanationWrong.D: Reports go to a central database.

question: Compared with randomized controlled trials, pharmacoepidemiologic studies after approval are particularly useful because they:

choices.text: Always establish causality more strongly than RCTs
Can evaluate medication use in a larger and broader population and identify rare adverse effects
Replace the need for any premarketing trials
Eliminate confounding by indication automatically

sourceQuote: pharmacoepidemiological studies can evaluate the use of medications in a larger and broader population,
explanationCorrect: Pharmacoepidemiology supports postmarketing safety surveillance in broader populations, detecting rare ADEs and efficacy shifts that RCTs may miss because of small size, short duration, and strict eligibility.

explanationWrong.A: RCTs remain best for establishing causal relationships.
explanationWrong.C: FDA approval still rests on RCTs; pharmacoepidemiology complements them after approval.
explanationWrong.D: Observational designs do not automatically remove confounding.

question: Continual post-approval monitoring is needed in part because randomized trials are limited by:

choices.text: Excessively large enrolled populations
Unlimited study duration in routine practice
Complete absence of inclusion and exclusion criteria
Relatively small enrollment, short duration, and strict inclusion and exclusion criteria

sourceQuote:
the relatively small
number of patients enrolled in RCTs, the short study duration of RCTs
explanationCorrect: RCTs may not show the true treatment effect because of relatively small enrollment, short duration, and strict inclusion and exclusion criteria.

explanationWrong.A: RCT samples are described as relatively small, not excessively large.
explanationWrong.B: Short, not unlimited, study duration is cited as a limitation.
explanationWrong.C: Strict inclusion and exclusion criteria are cited, not their absence.

question: Merck voluntarily withdrew rofecoxib (Vioxx) because of concerns about which risk with long-term, high-dosage use?

choices.text: Heart attack and stroke
Agranulocytosis
Achilles tendon rupture
Isolated QTc prolongation without vascular events

sourceQuote:
increased risk of
heart attack and stroke associated with long-term, high-dosage use
explanationCorrect: Vioxx was withdrawn because of concerns about increased risk of heart attack and stroke associated with long-term, high-dosage use based on clinical-trial data.

explanationWrong.B: Agranulocytosis is not the risk cited for the Vioxx withdrawal.
explanationWrong.C: Tendon rupture is not the risk cited in this passage.
explanationWrong.D: The stated concerns are myocardial infarction and stroke, not isolated QTc prolongation.

question: If 10,000 disease-free persons generate 200 new cases over 2 years, the incidence proportion is:

choices.text: 10 cases per 1,000 person-years as the only valid expression
2 cases per person
20 cases per 1,000 persons

sourceQuote: the incidence proportion is 20 cases per 1,000 persons.
explanationCorrect: Incidence proportion is 200/10,000 = 20 per 1,000 persons; the corresponding incidence rate if the population is constant for 2 years is 10 per 1,000 person-years.

explanationWrong.A: 10 per 1,000 person-years is the incidence rate, not the incidence proportion.
explanationWrong.B: 200 cases in 10,000 people is 2%, not 200%.
explanationWrong.C: Two cases per person is not the calculated proportion.

question: Person-time incidence rate is more appropriate than a simple incidence proportion when:

choices.text: Every subject is followed for identical calendar time
Only existing (prevalent) cases can be counted
Time at risk differs among individuals in the population
Disease risk is known to be constant at every point in time

sourceQuote:
incidence rate is
more appropriate when the time during which each individual is at risk differs
explanationCorrect: Incidence rate is more appropriate when the time during which each individual is at risk differs among the population.

explanationWrong.A: Equal follow-up time is the setting in which a simple incidence proportion is more straightforward.
explanationWrong.B: Counting only existing cases describes prevalence, not incidence rate.
explanationWrong.D: The passage notes that incidence rate still does not capture risk that differs at specific points in time.

question: If a community of 100,000 people has 20 new and 580 existing prostate cancer cases in 2008, the prevalence rate is:

choices.text: 0.2 per 1,000 people
6 per 1,000 people
20 per 1,000 people
580 per 1,000 people

sourceQuote:
the prevalence rate is 6 per 1,000 people
in 2008
explanationCorrect: Prevalence includes new plus existing cases (600/100,000), which equals 6 per 1,000 people in 2008; incidence is 0.2 per 1,000.

explanationWrong.A: 0.2 per 1,000 is the incidence estimate from the 20 new cases, not prevalence.
explanationWrong.C: Twenty per 1,000 would imply 2,000 cases, not 600.
explanationWrong.D: 580 per 1,000 would describe a much larger case burden than 580 existing cases in 100,000 people.

question: A case report or small case series is best characterized as:

choices.text: Purely descriptive and not suitable for inferences about the general population with that disease
A randomized allocation of exposure
The gold standard for proving causality
Equivalent to a meta-analysis of RCTs

sourceQuote: This type of study is purely descriptive and cannot be used to make inferences about the general population
explanationCorrect: Case reports/series are descriptive, may generate hypotheses, and can lead to analytic case-control or cohort studies; they do not support population inference.

explanationWrong.B: There is no randomized exposure assignment in a case series.
explanationWrong.C: Descriptive reports cannot establish causality.
explanationWrong.D: They are not systematic reviews or meta-analyses.

question: Case-control studies compare which quantities between cases and controls?

choices.text: Incidence density in person-years only
Randomized treatment assignment
Rates of exposure to risk factors for a specific condition
Future disease-free survival after exposure is assigned

sourceQuote: Case control studies compare rates of exposure to risk factors
explanationCorrect: Case-control studies compare rates of exposure to risk factors for a specific condition between subjects who have the condition (cases) and those who do not (controls).

explanationWrong.A: Person-time incidence is a cohort/surveillance measure, not the case-control comparison described.
explanationWrong.B: Randomization is an RCT feature, not case-control design.
explanationWrong.D: Prospective follow-up after exposure assignment describes a cohort study.

question: In the case-control 2-by-2 table, the odds of exposure in the cases is:

choices.text: b/d
a/c
a/(a+b)
c/(c+d)

sourceQuote: The ratio of a/c is the odds of exposure in the cases
explanationCorrect: The ratio a/c is the odds of exposure in the cases, b/d is the odds of exposure in the controls, and the odds ratio is the ratio of those two odds.

explanationWrong.A: b/d is the odds of exposure in the controls, not the cases.
explanationWrong.C: a/(a+b) is the risk of disease in the exposed group in a cohort table, not case-control exposure odds.
explanationWrong.D: c/(c+d) is the risk of disease in the unexposed group in a cohort table.

question: Case-control studies are particularly useful when:

choices.text: The outcome is nearly universal in the population
Only a 30-year prospective follow-up design is acceptable
The disease under study is rare, because they guarantee a sufficient number of cases
Randomization of a known harmful exposure is ethical

sourceQuote: particularly useful for the study of a rare disease because they guarantee a sufficient number of cases
explanationCorrect: Case-control studies are faster and less costly than cohorts and are especially useful for rare diseases, but they are prone to bias and depend on selecting an appropriate control group.

explanationWrong.A: Rarity of disease, not a nearly universal outcome, is the stated advantage.
explanationWrong.B: Case-control studies are usually faster than long prospective cohorts.
explanationWrong.D: These studies are observational; they do not randomize harmful exposures.

question: In a cohort study, selection of exposed and unexposed groups should be:

choices.text: Based on already having the disease of interest at baseline
Restricted to prevalent cases from a disease registry
Performed only after the outcome has occurred
Independent of the occurrence of the condition of interest

sourceQuote:
the selection of a cohort is independent of the occurrence of the
condition of interest
explanationCorrect: Cohort members should be at risk but free of the disease at the start, so selection is independent of whether the condition of interest occurs.

explanationWrong.A: Subjects should be free of the disease at the beginning of the cohort study.
explanationWrong.B: Registry-based listing of people who already have a disease describes a disease registry, not cohort selection.
explanationWrong.C: Selecting on the outcome is the case-control approach, not cohort selection.

question: In a cohort 2-by-2 table, a relative risk greater than 1 is interpreted as:

choices.text: Those with exposure are more likely to develop the disease than those without exposure
The exposure is protective against the disease
There is no association between exposure and disease
Absolute risk reduction equals Punexposed plus Pexposed

sourceQuote:
An RR
greater than 1 shows association between exposure and disease outcome
explanationCorrect: An RR greater than 1 shows association and means exposed persons are more likely to develop the disease than unexposed persons.

explanationWrong.B: An RR less than 1 means the exposure is protective.
explanationWrong.C: RR of 1, not greater than 1, would indicate no increased or decreased risk.
explanationWrong.D: ARR is Punexposed minus Pexposed, not the sum of those risks.

question: Relative risk obtained from a cohort study is described as:

choices.text: Less informative than an odds ratio for measuring association
A more powerful association measure than the odds ratio of case-control studies
Unusable whenever disease is incident
Numerically identical to NNH in all examples

sourceQuote: The RR is a more powerful association measure than the OR of case control studies;
explanationCorrect: Cohorts can estimate disease risk and RR, and can be prospective or retrospective; they are costlier and more prone to loss to follow-up than case-control studies.

explanationWrong.A: The text states RR is more powerful than OR, not less.
explanationWrong.C: Cohorts are designed around incident disease in initially disease-free subjects.
explanationWrong.D: ARI and NNH are separate measures; they are not identical to RR.

question: Passive surveillance of medication safety is characterized by:

choices.text: Organized complete capture of all ADE outcomes
Mandatory investigation at designated sentinel sites only
Prospective enrollment of every drug user in a cohort
Reliance on voluntary reports of adverse drug effects

sourceQuote:
Passive surveillance
relies on voluntary reports of adverse drug effects (ADEs)
explanationCorrect: Passive surveillance relies on voluntary ADE reports and does not involve organized efforts to collect complete ADE and outcome data.

explanationWrong.A: Complete organized data collection is the opposite of the passive approach described.
explanationWrong.B: Sentinel sites are a feature of active surveillance, not the definition of passive surveillance.
explanationWrong.C: Prospective cohort enrollment is not how passive surveillance is defined here.

question: Systematic evaluation of spontaneous postmarketing reports can identify which finding?

choices.text: Rare adverse effects that were not identified at the time of approval
Guaranteed complete capture of every adverse event
Causal proof equivalent to a randomized trial
Exact incidence in every demographic subgroup

sourceQuote:
rare adverse effects that were not identified at the time of the medication’s
approval
explanationCorrect: Systematic evaluation of voluntary reports can identify rare adverse effects not found at approval and can identify risk factors for those effects.

explanationWrong.B: Spontaneous reports are described as often incomplete.
explanationWrong.C: Voluntary reports generate safety signals; they are not described as RCT-level causal proof.
explanationWrong.D: Incomplete reporting precludes exact subgroup incidence from these reports alone.

question: The National Poison Data System (formerly TESS) is cited as an example of:

choices.text: A randomized controlled trial network
A hospital P&T committee
A cost-utility model
A sentinel surveillance system

sourceQuote: An example of a sentinel surveillance system can be found in the National Poison Data System (NPDS),
explanationCorrect: NPDS, maintained by AAPCC, uploads U.S. poison-center calls in near real time and can flag emerging public-health hazards for CDC follow-up.

explanationWrong.A: NPDS is surveillance of poison-center calls, not an RCT network.
explanationWrong.B: Formulary committees are not the example given.
explanationWrong.C: Pharmacoeconomic models are not this surveillance system.

question: When the National Poison Data System detects emerging public-health poison concerns, which agency notifies state health departments?

choices.text: The Joint Commission
The Drug Enforcement Administration
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sourceQuote:
notifies state health departments about the potential need for
intervention
explanationCorrect: When NPDS detects public-health concerns, the CDC notifies state health departments about the potential need for intervention.

explanationWrong.A: The Joint Commission is not the agency named for NPDS-triggered notifications.
explanationWrong.B: DEA is not named as the NPDS notification agency.
explanationWrong.C: SAMHSA is not named for this poison-surveillance notification role.

question: The Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program of the National Cancer Institute began collecting cancer-case data in which year?
sourceQuote: The SEER Program began collecting data on cancer cases in 1973
explanationCorrect: SEER began collecting data on cancer cases in 1973 and supports estimates of incidence, survival, and prevalence.

explanationWrong.B: 1999 is not the year given for the start of SEER data collection.
explanationWrong.C: 2008 is used elsewhere as a prevalence-example year, not SEER's start date.
explanationWrong.D: 2018 is not the year given for the start of SEER.

question: Randomized clinical trials may fail to characterize adverse-drug-effect risk at approval because of:

choices.text: Small numbers of patients, short study duration, and strict inclusion criteria
Randomization itself, which conceals all safety events
Follow-up of millions of unselected patients for decades
Complete absence of any eligibility criteria

sourceQuote: Randomized clinical trials cannot adequately address the risk of adverse drug effects
explanationCorrect: The listed reasons RCTs cannot adequately address ADE risk at approval are small samples, short duration, and strict inclusion criteria—not randomization.

explanationWrong.B: Randomization is not presented as the reason ADEs are missed.
explanationWrong.C: RCTs are limited by short duration and small size, not million-patient decades-long follow-up.
explanationWrong.D: Strict inclusion criteria, not their absence, limit generalizability.

question: Which statement is identified as an incorrect description of epidemiology?

choices.text: Epidemiologic tools have established major causes of diseases such as cholera and lung cancer
Epidemiologic findings can be refuted by randomized controlled trials
Epidemiology uses randomization to compare two groups
Epidemiology uses data generated through real-world practice environments

sourceQuote: Epidemiology uses randomization to compare two groups. 4.
explanationCorrect: The review item marks “Epidemiology uses randomization to compare two groups” as the incorrect description; epidemiology typically observes real-world populations rather than randomizing groups.

explanationWrong.A: That statement is presented as a correct description.
explanationWrong.B: That statement is presented as correct: RCTs can refute epidemiologic findings.
explanationWrong.D: Use of real-world practice data is listed as a correct feature.

question: Which element is identified as not part of the epidemiologic triad?

choices.text: Host
Environment
Agent
Vector

sourceQuote: is not part of the epidemiologic triad? A. Host B.
explanationCorrect: The epidemiologic triad consists of host, environment, and agent; vector is the option identified as not part of that triad.

explanationWrong.A: Host is a triad component.
explanationWrong.B: Environment is a triad component.
explanationWrong.C: Agent is a triad component.

question: Which characteristic is listed for a passive surveillance system?

choices.text: Sentinel sites as the defining feature
Requirement by the federal government for every medication
Voluntary reporting
Disease or exposure registries as the sole structure

sourceQuote: Which of the following is a characteristic of a passive surveillance system?
explanationCorrect: Passive surveillance is characterized by voluntary reporting, in contrast to planned active systems such as sentinel sites or registries.

explanationWrong.A: Sentinel sites are listed as an active/sentinel approach, not the passive characteristic.
explanationWrong.B: A federal requirement for all medications is not the passive-system trait given.
explanationWrong.D: Registries are listed separately from passive voluntary reporting.

question: Why does randomization not explain why RCTs cannot adequately detect adverse drug effects?

choices.text: Randomization is the principal reason RCTs miss safety events
Randomization does not influence the ability of an RCT to detect adverse drug effects
Randomization automatically expands sample size to millions
Randomization removes the need for inclusion and exclusion criteria

sourceQuote: Randomization does not influence the ability of an RCT to detect adverse drug effects.
explanationCorrect: ADE detection is limited by small samples, short duration, and strict eligibility; randomization improves baseline comparability but does not drive ADE detection capacity.

explanationWrong.A: The answer key states randomization does not influence ADE detection.
explanationWrong.C: Randomization does not enlarge sample size.
explanationWrong.D: RCTs still use strict inclusion and exclusion criteria.

question: Compared with epidemiologic studies, randomized controlled trials make groups comparable at baseline primarily because they:

choices.text: Enroll only real-world practice patients without protocol constraints
Avoid all ethical constraints on exposing patients to harm
Use randomization
Are always less expensive for detecting rare events

sourceQuote:
they use randomization, which makes different groups
comparable at baseline
explanationCorrect: RCTs use randomization, which makes different groups comparable at baseline; they are also considered the highest level of evidence.

explanationWrong.A: Epidemiologic data come from real-world practice; RCTs use protocol-defined groups.
explanationWrong.B: Giving a known-harmful medication solely to measure adverse effects is described as unethical.
explanationWrong.D: RCTs are described as expensive and inferior to epidemiologic designs for detecting rare adverse effects.

question: The epidemiologic triad consists of which three components?

choices.text: Incidence, prevalence, and mortality
The host, the agent, and the environment
Cases, controls, and confounders
Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value

sourceQuote: The epidemiologic triad consists of the host, the agent, and the environment
explanationCorrect: The epidemiologic triad consists of the host, the agent, and the environment.

explanationWrong.A: Incidence, prevalence, and mortality are epidemiologic measures, not the triad.
explanationWrong.C: Cases and controls are study-design elements, not the triad components.
explanationWrong.D: Those terms describe diagnostic-test performance, not the epidemiologic triad.

question: Relative to passive systems, active surveillance databases are described as:

choices.text: Inexpensive and free of selection bias
Incomplete because all reporting is purely voluntary
Having a low amount of selection bias and low implementation cost
More complete in their information, yet costly to maintain and subject to selection bias

sourceQuote: the information contained in active surveillance systems is complete as compared to that in passive systems.
explanationCorrect: Planned, required data elements make active systems more complete, but fewer reporters and nonvoluntary participation introduce selection bias, and the systems are costly.

explanationWrong.A: Active systems are described as costly and affected by selection bias.
explanationWrong.B: Completeness is an advantage of active versus passive systems.
explanationWrong.C: The text cites significant selection bias and high cost, not low bias and low cost.

question: In the radium watch-dial painter example, why is the design classified as a cohort study?

choices.text: Subjects were randomly assigned to radium versus placebo
Patients were sampled only after bone cancer developed, without an exposure group
Congenital anomalies were treated as the exposure of interest
Subjects were identified by radium exposure and followed for bone cancer compared with unexposed persons

sourceQuote: Cohort studies compare the risk of developing a disease between those who are exposed
explanationCorrect: Cohort studies compare disease risk in exposed versus unexposed persons. Painters were identified by radium exposure and followed for bone cancer; they were not randomized. Congenital anomalies are disease outcomes, not risk factors.

explanationWrong.A: The explanation states subjects were not assigned to treatment.
explanationWrong.B: Sampling by disease status would be case-control, not this example.
explanationWrong.C: Congenital anomalies are identified as outcomes, not risk factors.

question: Which 2017 FDA educational resource is listed among additional epidemiology/pharmacovigilance materials?

choices.text: An FDA Basics Webinar giving a brief overview of risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS)
A USP Chapter <797> sterile compounding risk-level table
The Oath of a Pharmacist as a federal regulation
A Cockcroft–Gault dosing nomogram for hepatic drugs

sourceQuote: a brief overview of risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS). 2017. U.S.
explanationCorrect: The additional resources include a 2017 FDA Basics Webinar on REMS, CDC epidemiology principles (3rd ed., 2012), and the NCI SEER program.

explanationWrong.B: USP <797> is not listed in this resource block.
explanationWrong.C: The Oath appears in the ethics chapter, not this FDA/CDC bibliography.
explanationWrong.D: No hepatic Cockcroft–Gault nomogram is cited here.

question: In typical outpatient prescription payment, the patient pays:

choices.text: Only a portion of medication cost through a copay or coinsurance
The full AMP plus WAC at the counter
Only the manufacturer rebate amount
Nothing whenever a brand-name drug is dispensed

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: The typical patient pays only a portion of the cost of prescription medications, either
explanationCorrect: Patients typically share cost via copay or coinsurance; hospitals pay discounted rates and may receive volume-based manufacturer/supplier rebates.

explanationWrong.B: Patients do not pay AMP plus WAC as described here.
explanationWrong.C: Rebates accrue to purchasers/payers, not as the patient’s usual out-of-pocket charge.
explanationWrong.D: Brand dispensing does not imply zero patient cost-sharing in this description.

question: A quality-adjusted life year, as framed in this study guide, is based on:

choices.text: AMP divided by AWP
Hospital census alone
Utility tied to a specific health outcome
Ingredient acquisition cost alone

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: calculate a quality-adjusted life year based on utility tied to a specific health outcome.
explanationCorrect: The checklist requires understanding QALY calculation from utility linked to a health outcome, along with types of cost-effectiveness analyses.

explanationWrong.A: AMP/AWP are price measures, not QALY inputs.
explanationWrong.B: Census is a forecasting input, not a QALY element.
explanationWrong.D: Acquisition cost is a cost input, not the utility basis of a QALY.

question: In the grouping of Mankiw’s 10 Principles of Economics given here, the first four principles relate to:

choices.text: International trade law only
How people make decisions
Central-bank open-market operations exclusively
Hospital accreditation standards

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: The first four principles relate to how people make decisions, the next three relate
explanationCorrect: Mankiw’s first four principles concern individual decisions; the next three concern the economy as a whole; the last three concern how people interact.

explanationWrong.A: Trade appears later among interaction principles, not as the first-four grouping.
explanationWrong.C: Monetary operations are not the first-four category named.
explanationWrong.D: Accreditation is not part of Mankiw’s grouping.

question: According to the Mankiw principle quoted in the text, a rational decision maker takes action:

choices.text: Regardless of cost
Only when average cost equals total revenue
Only when ordered by a central planner
If and only if the marginal benefit of the action exceeds the marginal cost

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: takes action if and only if the marginal benefit of the action exceeds the marginal cost.
explanationCorrect: “Rational people think at the margin”: act only when marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.

explanationWrong.A: Cost is explicitly compared with benefit at the margin.
explanationWrong.B: The rule is marginal benefit versus marginal cost, not average cost versus total revenue.
explanationWrong.C: Central planning is contrasted later with market organization, not this rationality rule.

question: In market economies, the “invisible hand” metaphor describes which idea?

choices.text: A central planner must set every price for efficiency to occur
Households and firms cannot interact without government assigning all trades
Households and firms acting in markets are guided toward efficient resource allocation
Monopoly and pollution never justify public policy

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: that leads the market to allocate resources efficiently. The opposite
explanationCorrect: Households and firms interact as if guided by an invisible hand that allocates resources efficiently, in contrast to organization by a central planner. Principle 7 notes governments can sometimes improve outcomes (for example, monopoly and pollution).

explanationWrong.A: Central planning is presented as the opposite of the invisible-hand market.
explanationWrong.B: The passage describes market interaction of households and firms, not mandatory assignment of every trade.
explanationWrong.D: Governments can sometimes improve market outcomes via policies against monopolies and pollution.

question: According to the listed principle of economics, what happens when a government creates large quantities of the nation’s money?

choices.text: The value of money rises and prices fall
The value of money falls and prices increase
Unemployment permanently falls with no inflation trade-off
Supply and demand cease to influence prices

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: “Prices rise when the government prints too much money.” When
explanationCorrect: Creating large quantities of money lowers money’s value, so more money is required to buy goods and prices rise. A separate principle notes a short-run inflation–unemployment trade-off.

explanationWrong.A: The text states the value of money falls and prices increase.
explanationWrong.C: Reducing inflation often causes a temporary rise in unemployment.
explanationWrong.D: Supply and demand remain the basic model of price change.

question: In 2015, U.S. health spending was described as more than $3 trillion per year, or roughly what share of GDP?
chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: it accounted for more than $3 trillion of spending per year, or roughly 18%
explanationCorrect: GDP measures goods and services produced in a country over time; in 2015 health spending was >$3 trillion, about 18% of GDP.

explanationWrong.B: 3% is not the GDP share stated for 2015 health spending.
explanationWrong.C: 34% is a payer-mix figure from another chapter, not this GDP share.
explanationWrong.D: Half of GDP is far above the 18% figure given.

question: Government intervention in health-care markets may “crowd out”:

choices.text: All FDA regulation
Patient copays exclusively
Private business investment in health care
Measurement of GDP

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: Government intervention to health care markets may “crowd out” private business investment in health care,
explanationCorrect: Because government programs often obtain the lowest prices, greater public intervention can reduce private firms’ incentive to invest and may lower GDP growth related to health services.

explanationWrong.A: Crowd-out refers to private investment, not elimination of FDA regulation.
explanationWrong.B: Copays are patient cost-sharing, not the crowded-out activity named.
explanationWrong.D: GDP is an economic measure, not what is crowded out.

question: At a societal level, CDC guidance that directs state and local health departments includes:

choices.text: Setting average wholesale price for vaccines
Licensing compounding pharmacies
Approving REMS elements to assure safe use
Regular guidance on vaccination schedules for infants, children, and adults

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote:
the CDC provides regular guidance on vaccination schedules for infants, children,
and adults
explanationCorrect: The CDC provides regular guidance on vaccination schedules for infants, children, and adults, directing state and local health departments as well as health systems and providers.

explanationWrong.A: The CDC is not described as setting AWP.
explanationWrong.B: Compounding licensure is a board-of-pharmacy/FDA topic, not this CDC role.
explanationWrong.C: REMS approval is an FDA function, not the CDC vaccination-schedule role described.

question: Widespread vaccination that reduces disease spread even among unvaccinated persons is an example of:

choices.text: A positive externality
A negative externality such as air pollution
A private good with no spillover effects
An adverse-selection death spiral

chapter: Economic and Humanistic Outcomes of Health Care Delivery
sourceQuote: creating what economists refer to as a positive externality
explanationCorrect: By limiting infectious-disease spread, CDC vaccination guidance creates a positive externality: others benefit even if they are not vaccinated.

explanationCorrect: Finding and hiring people whose values align with the organization's mission is described as key for success, and recognition supports retention.

explanationWrong.C: Recognition and awards are listed as retention strategies, not practices to avoid.
explanationWrong.D: Progressive discipline is used for employees who are not performing; termination is not the first step described.

question: Pharmacy managers should recruit talented individuals:

choices.text: Only when a vacancy has been open 90 days
Only among recent retirees
Even if there are currently no open positions
Only after a national advertising campaign

sourceQuote: Pharmacy managers should continually recruit talented individuals, even if there are currently no open positions.
explanationCorrect: Continual recruiting builds a future applicant pool and informs managers about labor supply; open jobs should first be shared with current staff, and pay should be equitable.

explanationWrong.A: Recruiting is not limited to long-open vacancies.
explanationWrong.B: Recent retirees are not the specified talent pool.
explanationWrong.D: Advertising is typically used when a specific position is open, not as the sole method.

question: Adequate pharmacy facilities for receiving, storing, and preparing medications are required in order to:

choices.text: Maximize retail front-end planograms
Replace primary engineering controls with anterooms alone
Maintain product integrity and personnel safety
Eliminate the need for hazardous-waste procedures

sourceQuote:
allocated to receive, store, and prepare medications in order to
maintain product integrity and personnel safety
explanationCorrect: Adequate facilities must be allocated to receive, store, and prepare medications in order to maintain product integrity and personnel safety.

explanationWrong.A: Front-end merchandising is not the purpose given for medication storage and preparation space.
explanationWrong.B: The passage addresses facility allocation for integrity and safety, not replacing PECs.
explanationWrong.D: Infection prevention and hazardous-waste management remain listed safety responsibilities.

question: Planning is described as a key managerial function that supports which other three functions?

choices.text: Budgeting, compounding, and dispensing
Leading, controlling, and organizing
Marketing, merchandising, and advertising
Hiring, firing, and payroll processing only

sourceQuote:
Planning is a key
managerial function that actually supports the other three functions
explanationCorrect: Planning is a key managerial function that supports leading, controlling, and organizing.

explanationWrong.A: Those operational tasks are not the three functions named.
explanationWrong.C: Marketing is a later section, not the triad that planning supports.
explanationWrong.D: Human-resources tasks are not the three functions listed.

question: Business planning, as contrasted with strategic planning in Table 17-1, is characterized as:

choices.text: Organization-wide in scope and 5–20 years in horizon
Short term (1–5 years) and used for decisions to start, expand, or terminate a business
Limited to competitor SWOT only
A replacement for all operational budgets

sourceQuote: Possible use for decisions to start, expand, or terminate a business; short term (1 –5 years)
explanationCorrect: Business planning is short-term (1–5 years) to judge program feasibility and guide investment; strategic planning is organization-wide, external, and long-term (5–20 years).

explanationWrong.A: That description is strategic planning, not business planning.
explanationWrong.C: SWOT supports strategy; it is not the defining business-plan horizon.
explanationWrong.D: Business plans inform investment; they do not replace operating budgets.

question: In strategic planning, vision is defined as:

choices.text: The organization's present-centered purpose in one or two sentences
A SWOT inventory of competitors' products
Daily operational staffing ratios
What the organization wants to be at some future point

sourceQuote: Vision is what the organization wants to be at some future point
explanationCorrect: Vision is what the organization wants to be at some future point and is used at both the beginning and the end of strategic planning.

explanationWrong.A: Present-centered purpose describes the mission, not the vision.
explanationWrong.B: SWOT analysis is not the definition of vision given here.
explanationWrong.C: Staffing ratios are operational details, not the vision statement.

question: An organization's mission statement should be which of the following?

choices.text: Short (one to two sentences) and able to differentiate the organization from similar providers
A complex future-state description used only after planning is finished
A list of national awards and charitable-giving policies
Identical to every competitor's purpose statement

sourceQuote:
This mission
statement should also be short, such as one to two sentences
explanationCorrect: The mission is the organization's purpose and should be short (one to two sentences) while differentiating the organization from others that provide similar products and services.

explanationWrong.B: Vision, not mission, is the future-state description; mission is present-centered.
explanationWrong.C: Awards and charitable giving are not the mission's required content.
explanationWrong.D: The mission should differentiate the organization from similar providers.

question: Failure to implement a strategic plan is due most often to:

choices.text: Excessive measurement of progress
Overstaffing of project managers
Too much available time
Lack of time, unavailability of resources, or failure to measure progress

sourceQuote: due most often to lack of time, unavailability of resources, or failure to measure progress.
explanationCorrect: Implementation also requires assigned responsibility, timeline, and budget, plus communication and continuous adjustment to environmental change.

explanationWrong.A: Failure to measure progress is a listed cause of failed implementation, not excessive measurement.
explanationWrong.B: Resource unavailability, not overstaffing, is named.
explanationWrong.C: Lack of time, not excess time, is named.

question: A listed method for marketing clinical pharmacy services in the community is:

choices.text: Cold-calling inpatients without consent
Replacing all counseling with social media only
Printed materials (fliers) placed inside prescription bags
Unsolicited texting of controlled-substance refill reminders

sourceQuote:
fliers (i.e., printed
materials) placed inside prescription bags
explanationCorrect: Marketing techniques include fliers (printed materials) placed inside prescription bags, plus radio and television advertisements, billboards, and promotion at local health fairs.

explanationWrong.A: Unconsented inpatient cold-calling is not a listed method.
explanationWrong.B: The passage lists multiple traditional techniques, not social-media replacement of counseling.
explanationWrong.D: Unsolicited controlled-substance texting is not listed.

question: Relationship marketing is described as using and going beyond which traditional marketing mix?

choices.text: SWOT analysis only
The four "Ps" (product, price, promotion, and place)
The five rights of medication administration
Plan-do-check-act cycles exclusively

sourceQuote:
the traditional four “Ps” of
marketing (product, price, promotion, and place)
explanationCorrect: Relationship marketing uses and goes beyond the traditional four Ps of marketing: product, price, promotion, and place.

explanationWrong.A: SWOT is a planning tool, not the marketing mix named here.
explanationWrong.C: The five rights are a safety framework, not the four Ps.
explanationWrong.D: PDCA is a quality-improvement cycle, not the marketing mix described.

question: Medication therapy management service should be provided:

choices.text: In a semiprivate or private area by a pharmacist whose time can be devoted to the patient
Only at a crowded checkout counter
Exclusively by technicians without pharmacist involvement
Only via public social media

sourceQuote: The MTM service should be provided in a semiprivate or private area by a pharmacist
explanationCorrect: HIPAA requires confidentiality; MTM belongs in a semi-/private space with dedicated pharmacist time. Payers may limit payment, but pharmacies may still offer fee-for-service MTM.

explanationWrong.B: A public checkout lacks the privacy required.
explanationWrong.C: The service is to be provided by a pharmacist.
explanationWrong.D: Public social media would violate confidentiality.

question: Reverse distribution in the pharmaceutical supply chain refers to:

choices.text: Shipping only on a first-in, first-out basis
Direct-to-patient courier from the manufacturer
Borrowing inventory from another hospital
Collection of damaged, outdated, or unsold goods for return to the supplier or manufacturer

sourceQuote: the collection of damaged, outdated, or unsold goods and delivery back to the supplier
explanationCorrect: Reverse distribution is the collection of damaged, outdated, or unsold goods and delivery back to the supplier or manufacturer.

explanationWrong.A: FIFO inventory control is not the definition of reverse distribution.
explanationWrong.B: Manufacturer courier to patients is not reverse distribution.
explanationWrong.C: Interhospital borrowing is not the process named.

question: The four main factors described as driving drug expense are:

choices.text: Utilization, price, mix, and innovation
Malpractice risk, advertising, rent, and utilities
Nursing wages, dietary cost, laundry, and linen
Copayment, deductible, premium, and coinsurance only

sourceQuote:
Four main factors drive drug expense: utilization, price, mix,
and innovation
explanationCorrect: Four main factors drive drug expense: utilization, price, mix, and innovation.

explanationWrong.B: Those overhead items are not the four factors named.
explanationWrong.C: Nursing and dietary expenses are not listed as the four drug-expense drivers.
explanationWrong.D: Patient cost-sharing terms are not the four organizational drug-expense factors given.

question: When forecasting production needs, hospital pharmacies review:

choices.text: Only community AWP trends
Only mail-order website visit counts
Patient acuity levels and census information
Only capsule-size fill-weight tables

sourceQuote: Hospital pharmacies review patient acuity levels and census information when considering future production needs.
explanationCorrect: Forecasting often starts from revenue/sales projections: hospitals use acuity and census, retail pharmacies use past dispensing, and mail-order sites project visits and capture rate.

explanationWrong.A: AWP trends are not the hospital forecasting inputs named.
explanationWrong.B: Website visits are described for online/mail-order pharmacies.
explanationWrong.D: Capsule tables are compounding references, not hospital volume forecasts.

question: When projecting demand, merchandising and manufacturing pharmacies are described as relying on which input?

choices.text: Patient acuity levels and hospital census
Projected sales of their goods
Website visits and capture rate of purchases
Only last year’s industry-wide prescription volume

sourceQuote: Merchandising and manufacturing pharmacies project sales of their goods
explanationCorrect: The passage states merchandising and manufacturing pharmacies project sales of their goods when forecasting.

explanationWrong.A: Acuity and census are what hospital pharmacies review.
explanationWrong.C: Website visits and capture rate are described for online and mail-order pharmacies.
explanationWrong.D: The text lists several forecasting factors, not a single prior-year industry volume.

question: A pharmacy benefits manager (PBM) is best described as:

choices.text: A hospital group-purchasing organization for inpatient drugs
A third-party administrator that manages prescription drug programs for plan beneficiaries
A state board of pharmacy inspector
An FDA coordinator of drug-shortage allocations

sourceQuote:
A PBM is a third-party
administrator contracted by employers, health care plans, unions, and government entities
explanationCorrect: A PBM is a third-party administrator contracted by employers, health plans, unions, and government entities to manage prescription drug programs for beneficiaries.

explanationWrong.A: A GPO is not the PBM definition given.
explanationWrong.C: State board inspectors are regulators, not PBMs.
explanationWrong.D: FDA shortage coordination is not the PBM role described.

question: Annual drug-expense budgeting is typically based on the cost of approximately how many high-priority drugs?

choices.text: 5 to 6
Every NDC in the wholesaler catalog equally

sourceQuote: is typically based on the cost of 50 to 60 drugs.
explanationCorrect: Drug budgets focus on the top 50–60 agents, build in new drugs, account for nonformulary items, and include cost-containment for patent changes and interchanges; a capital budget covers equipment and buildings.

explanationWrong.A: Five to six drugs understates the stated top-spend group.
explanationWrong.C: Hundreds of equal-priority NDCs is not the method described.
explanationWrong.D: The process prioritizes high-spend drugs rather than weighting every NDC equally.

question: Besides setting expectations, budgets are sometimes used to:

choices.text: Replace all clinical practice guidelines
Eliminate capital planning for equipment and buildings
Serve as an incentive for individuals to perform well and be paid for that performance
Hide performance results from departments

sourceQuote:
budgets are used as an incentive for individuals to perform well and be paid for
that performance
explanationCorrect: Sometimes budgets are used as an incentive for individuals to perform well and be paid for that performance.

explanationWrong.A: Budgets do not replace clinical guidelines.
explanationWrong.B: Capital budgets for equipment and buildings are part of the budgeting discussion, not eliminated.
explanationWrong.D: Performance targets should be shared so team members focus on the same goals.

question: High-risk medications are defined as those that:

choices.text: Produce only nonpreventable allergic reactions
Carry a greater risk for fatality in the event of an error
Cannot be involved in sentinel events
Are exempt from monitoring after dispensing

sourceQuote:
High-risk medications
are those that carry a greater risk for fatality
explanationCorrect: High-risk medications carry a greater risk for fatality if an error occurs, and some are used in high-risk situations.

explanationWrong.A: Nonpreventable effects such as intolerances and anaphylaxis are a separate category from high-risk medications.
explanationWrong.C: Sentinel events cause significant harm and may involve high-risk medications.
explanationWrong.D: The passage discusses errors in prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering, or monitoring, not monitoring exemptions.

question: Transitions of care refer to:

choices.text: Only changes in a drug’s NDC
Only PBM formulary tier changes
Only USP CSP risk-level changes
Patient movement between providers, locations, or different levels of care as the patient’s condition changes

sourceQuote: Transitions of care refer to patient movement between health care providers, locations, or different levels of care
explanationCorrect: Transitions are a subset of care coordination; pharmacists can reduce medication errors, readmissions, and length of stay. Medication reconciliation builds the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking.

explanationWrong.A: NDC changes are product identifiers, not care transitions.
explanationWrong.B: Formulary tiers are benefit design, not patient movement.
explanationWrong.C: CSP risk levels classify sterile compounding, not patient transfers.

question: Medication reconciliation is the process of creating the most accurate list of a patient's medications and comparing that list against:

choices.text: Wholesale acquisition-cost files
The pharmacy's inventory-turn report
The physician's orders, with the goal of providing correct medications at care transitions
PBM formulary exclusion lists only

sourceQuote: creating the most accurate list possible of all medications a patient is taking
explanationCorrect: Medication reconciliation compares the most accurate medication list against the physician's orders so patients receive the correct medications at all health-care transition points.

explanationWrong.A: WAC files are pricing data, not the comparison source for reconciliation.
explanationWrong.B: Inventory metrics are not the comparison target in the definition given.
explanationWrong.D: Formulary exclusions are not the stated comparison in medication reconciliation.

question: Quality data of the type used in pharmacy risk management is often publicly reported for which purpose?

choices.text: To replace inspections by state boards of pharmacy
To better inform consumer decisions
To set DEA controlled-substance production quotas
To calculate average-wholesale-price discounts

sourceQuote: quality data is often publicly reported to better inform consumer decisions
explanationCorrect: This type of quality data is often publicly reported to better inform consumer decisions, in addition to internal improvement and payer incentives.

explanationWrong.A: Public reporting is not described as replacing board of pharmacy inspections.
explanationWrong.C: DEA quota setting is not the stated purpose of public quality reporting.
explanationWrong.D: AWP discounting is a payment-practice issue, not the purpose given here.

question: Screening prospective candidates for a pharmacy position should begin by:

choices.text: Comparing the candidates’ experience to the job description
Comparing the candidates to recent retirees
Comparing the candidates’ current salary to the hiring manager’s salary
Comparing the candidates’ national origins

sourceQuote: Screening prospective candidates for a pharmacy position should begin by
explanationCorrect: Screening starts by matching experience to the job description; retiree comparisons, the manager’s salary, and national origin are not appropriate starting screens.

explanationWrong.B: Recent retirees are not a relevant screening comparator.
explanationWrong.C: The hiring manager’s salary is not the screening standard.
explanationWrong.D: National origin is not an appropriate screening criterion.

question: Pharmaceutical expenses are typically reduced when:

choices.text: Generics are converted to brands
Shortages of raw materials occur
Group purchasing arrangements are used
The FDA approves new indications

sourceQuote: When are pharmaceutical expenses typically reduced? A. Generics are converted to brands.
explanationCorrect: Group purchasing arrangements typically reduce pharmaceutical expenses; brand conversion, shortages, and new indications do not.

explanationWrong.A: Converting generics to brands would increase, not reduce, expense.
explanationWrong.B: Raw-material shortages typically raise prices.
explanationWrong.D: New indications often expand use and spending.

question: Which type of question is usually best to ask a candidate during a job interview?

choices.text: True or false
Open-ended
Multiple choice
Yes or no

sourceQuote: Open-ended questions are ideal because they allow the interviewer to hear more from the candidate.
explanationCorrect: Open-ended questions elicit fuller responses; true/false, multiple-choice, and yes/no items typically yield short answers that reveal little.

explanationWrong.A: True/false items produce short responses with little information.
explanationWrong.C: Multiple-choice items likewise limit what is learned about the candidate.
explanationWrong.D: Yes/no questions typically produce short responses.

question: In hiring interviews, open-ended questions are preferred because they:

choices.text: Force yes-or-no answers that speed screening
Conceal the candidate's communication style
Allow the interviewer to hear more from the candidate
Replace the need for a written job description

sourceQuote: Open-ended questions are ideal because they allow the interviewer to hear more from the candidate
explanationCorrect: Open-ended questions are ideal because they allow the interviewer to hear more from the candidate; other question types typically produce short responses.

explanationWrong.A: Short yes-or-no answers are the limitation of non-open-ended questions.
explanationWrong.B: Hearing more from the candidate reveals, rather than conceals, communication style.
explanationWrong.D: Interview-question type does not replace a job description.

question: Preventable adverse drug effects that can be serious are exemplified by:

choices.text: Expected opioid constipation disclosed in counseling
Sentinel events
A known penicillin rash that was anticipated
Transient nausea from a labeled side effect

sourceQuote: Preventable adverse drug effects are errors that can be serious, such as sentinel events
explanationCorrect: Preventable adverse drug effects are errors that can be serious, such as sentinel events, whereas side effects, hives, and nausea are examples of nonpreventable effects.

explanationWrong.A: Typical side effects are listed as nonpreventable adverse drug effects.
explanationWrong.C: Hives are given as an example of a nonpreventable adverse effect.
explanationWrong.D: Nausea and vomiting are listed as nonpreventable adverse drug effects.

question: Which statement about drug spending versus reimbursement is given?

choices.text: Reimbursement is increasing faster than drug spending in all cases
Drug spending is falling because of AMP reporting
Formulary management has eliminated all drug-cost growth
Drug spending is increasing at a rate faster than the rate of reimbursement, which is in many cases decreasing

sourceQuote: Drug spending is increasing at a rate faster than the rate of reimbursement, which is, in many cases,
explanationCorrect: Health-system drug spending is rising faster than reimbursement, and reimbursement is often decreasing, intensifying pressure on pharmacy budgets.

explanationWrong.A: The relationship stated is the opposite: spending outpaces reimbursement.
explanationWrong.B: AMP reporting is not described as causing falling drug spend.
explanationWrong.C: Formulary tools control cost but are not said to eliminate growth.

question: A cited Academy of Managed Care Pharmacy resource emphasizes the importance of pharmacists in which process?

choices.text: Nuclear pharmacy compounding only
Community merchandising planograms
Transitions of care
Patent-term restoration

sourceQuote: Amin R, Badgett C. Importance of pharmacists in transitions of care
explanationCorrect: Amin and Badgett's cited AMCP resource is titled on the importance of pharmacists in transitions of care.

explanationWrong.A: Nuclear compounding is not the cited topic.
explanationWrong.B: Merchandising is not the cited AMCP topic.
explanationWrong.D: Patent-term restoration is not the cited topic.

question: The cited Medication Therapy Management service-model core elements document (Version 2.0) was issued in:

choices.text: September 2004
March 2008
February 2018
May 1999

sourceQuote: Core Elements of an MTM Service Model, Version 2.0. March 2008
explanationCorrect: Medication Therapy Management in Pharmacy Practice: Core Elements of an MTM Service Model, Version 2.0, is dated March 2008 (APhA and NACDS Foundation).

explanationWrong.A: September 2004 is the Vioxx withdrawal month/year, not the MTM core-elements date.
explanationWrong.C: February 2018 appears on other citations, not this MTM document.
explanationWrong.D: May 1999 is not the date given for Version 2.0.

question: Which listing correctly ranks the five principal types of statutory law of general interest to pharmacy practice from highest to lowest authority?

choices.text: Statute, treaty or international agreement, Constitution, regulation, ordinance
Constitution, treaty or international agreement, statute, regulation, and ordinance
Treaty or international agreement, Constitution, statute, ordinance, regulation
Constitution, statute, treaty or international agreement, ordinance, regulation

sourceQuote: in descending order of authority: Constitution, treaty or international agreement
explanationCorrect: The five principal types of statutory law, in descending order of authority, are Constitution, treaty or international agreement, statute, regulation, and ordinance.

explanationWrong.A: A statute ranks below both a constitution and a treaty.
explanationWrong.C: A constitution outranks a treaty; an ordinance is the lowest of the five types listed.
explanationWrong.D: A treaty outranks a statute, and a regulation outranks an ordinance.

question: Why does the legal glossary in this chapter caution pharmacists about ordinary conversational usage of legal words?

choices.text: Legal terms are interchangeable with medical terminology
Everyday meanings of legal words are preferred in court
Legal terms are defined only at the federal level
Several legal words have a distinctly different and very specific meaning other than everyday conversation

sourceQuote: distinctly different and very specific meaning other than how they are used
explanationCorrect: Some words used in legal matters have a distinctly different and very specific meaning other than how they are used in everyday conversation.

explanationWrong.A: The passage compares legal language to medical terminology; it does not treat them as interchangeable.
explanationWrong.B: The glossary exists because everyday meanings often do not match the legal meanings.
explanationWrong.C: The passage does not limit legal definitions to federal law.

question: In this legal glossary, what is a bill?

choices.text: A draft version of a potential law presented to a legislature for consideration of amendments and enactment
A collection or compendium of laws adopted by a state or nation
A request asking another court to decide whether a trial was conducted properly
Evidence that may be heard by a jury and considered by a judge

sourceQuote: A draft version of a potential law presented to a legislature
explanationCorrect: A bill is a draft version of a potential law presented to a legislature for consideration of amendments and enactment.

explanationWrong.B: That definition describes a code (code of law), not a bill.
explanationWrong.C: That definition describes an appeal.
explanationWrong.D: That definition describes admissible evidence.

question: Which states use "commonwealth" as part of their official name?

choices.text: California, Texas, Florida, and New York
All 50 states equally
Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia
Only territories of the United States

sourceQuote:
states of Kentucky, Massachusetts,
Pennsylvania, and Virginia as part of their official name
explanationCorrect: Commonwealth is used by Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Virginia as part of their official name.

explanationWrong.A: Those states are not the four named commonwealths.
explanationWrong.B: Only four states are listed as using commonwealth in their official name.
explanationWrong.D: The term is illustrated with four states, not only territories.

question: A felony is defined as a crime that:

choices.text: Is punishable only by a monetary fine
Carries a penalty of more than 1 year in prison
Never requires an indictment
Is limited to civil damages paid to a plaintiff

sourceQuote: A crime that carries a penalty of more than 1 year in prison
explanationCorrect: A felony is a crime that carries a penalty of more than 1 year in prison; an indictment is an official written statement charging a person with a crime, primarily for a felony.

explanationWrong.A: A fine-only offense is not the felony definition given.
explanationWrong.C: Indictments are described primarily for felonies.
explanationWrong.D: Damages are money paid in a civil case, not the definition of a felony.

question: Which statement correctly characterizes a tort?

choices.text: It is a crime tried in a criminal court
It is limited to breach of contract
It is a wrongful act causing injury, other than a breach of contract, for which damages may be obtained in a civil court
It is a law passed by a legislature

sourceQuote: it is not a crime and is tried in a civil court
explanationCorrect: A tort is a wrongful act causing injury to person, property, or reputation (other than a breach of contract) for which relief may be obtained as damages; it is not a crime and is tried in a civil court.

explanationWrong.A: The passage states a tort is not a crime and is tried in a civil court.
explanationWrong.B: A tort is defined as other than a breach of contract.
explanationWrong.D: A statute is a law passed by a legislature.

question: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 is published in Public Law as which citation?

choices.text: Title 21 of the U.S. Code
21 CFR Part 1306

sourceQuote: published in Public Law at P.L. No. 104-191
explanationCorrect: HIPAA is published in Public Law at P.L. No. 104-191 and regulates the privacy and security of an individual’s health information.

explanationWrong.A: 15 USC 1471–74 is the Code citation given for the Poison Prevention Packaging Act of 1970.
explanationWrong.C: The passage does not cite HIPAA as Title 21 of the U.S. Code.
explanationWrong.D: The passage does not give 21 CFR Part 1306 as HIPAA’s citation.

question: Which statement about regulation of the professions is supported by this comparison of federal and state powers?

choices.text: Federal laws do not regulate professions; such regulation is based in state authority
Only Congress may issue licenses for pharmacy practice
Professional licensure is a shared federal–state power listed with printing money
The Constitution forbids states from issuing professional licenses

sourceQuote: Federal laws do not regulate professions; such regulation is based
explanationCorrect: Federal laws do not regulate professions; such regulation is based in state authority, and states issue licenses for marriage, driving, and professions.

explanationWrong.B: Issuing licenses for professions is listed as a state government power.
explanationWrong.C: Printing money is a federal power; professional licensure is not grouped with it as shared.
explanationWrong.D: States are listed as issuing licenses for professions.

question: Relative to state board of pharmacy rules and regulations, how is a typical pharmacy practice act described?

choices.text: It is longer and more detailed than the board rules
It exclusively sets license fees, which the board may not address
It replaces the need for board rules and regulations
It is relatively brief compared to the depth and scope of board rules and regulations

sourceQuote: the pharmacy practice act is relatively brief compared to the depth
explanationCorrect: Typically the pharmacy practice act is relatively brief compared with the depth and scope of state board of pharmacy rules and regulations, which supply details such as license procedures, fees, and operational standards.

explanationWrong.A: The act is described as relatively brief; the rules provide the details.
explanationWrong.B: Board rules generally establish the procedures, requirements, and fees for licenses.
explanationWrong.C: The rules address details of matters mentioned in the practice act; they are not unnecessary.

question: Beyond original English principles, what else does the common law include?

choices.text: Only treaties and international agreements
Only statutes passed by Congress
That body of law created by the courts through judicial opinions
Only ordinances adopted by municipalities

sourceQuote: body of law created by the courts through judicial opinions
explanationCorrect: The common law involves more than original English principles; it also includes that body of law created by the courts through judicial opinions, and it continues to evolve as cases are decided.

explanationWrong.A: Treaties are a separate type of statutory law, not the definition of common law given here.
explanationWrong.B: Statutes are legislative enactments; common law is judicially created.
explanationWrong.D: Ordinances are local legislative acts, not judicial common law.

question: When does a statute become effective as law after passage by the legislature?

choices.text: Immediately upon a majority vote of either chamber
Only after approval by the President for a federal statute or by the state governor for a state statute
When a court first interprets it
When an administrative agency promulgates it as a regulation

sourceQuote: It must be approved by the President of the United States
explanationCorrect: A statute does not become effective upon being passed by the legislature; it must be approved by the President of the United States for a federal statute or by the state governor for a state statute.

explanationWrong.A: Passage by the legislature is not enough; executive approval is required.
explanationWrong.C: Judicial interpretation is not the event that makes a statute effective.
explanationWrong.D: Regulations are a lower type of law and are not how a statute becomes effective.

question: If the President or a governor vetoes a bill, what may the legislature do according to this chapter?

choices.text: Nothing; a veto is final in all cases
Vote to override the veto
Convert the bill into a regulation automatically
Require a treaty to enact the bill

sourceQuote: If a veto occurs, the legislature may vote to override the veto
explanationCorrect: After a presidential or gubernatorial veto, the legislature may vote to override it.

explanationWrong.A: The passage explicitly allows a legislative override.
explanationWrong.C: Regulations are promulgated by agencies, not created by converting a vetoed bill.
explanationWrong.D: Treaties are a different, superior legal category; they are not required to enact a statute after veto.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes ordinances from federal administrative regulations affecting pharmacy?

choices.text: Ordinances are enacted by the FDA, CMS, and DEA
Ordinances are enacted by local bodies such as a city council or county commission, whereas CMS, FDA, and DEA issue federal regulations
Ordinances always supersede the U.S. Constitution
Case law is enacted by city councils as ordinances

sourceQuote: Ordinances are laws enacted by local lawmaking bodies such as
explanationCorrect: Federal agencies named are CMS, FDA, and DEA. Ordinances come from local lawmaking bodies (city council or county commission). Cities had limited ephedrine/pseudoephedrine sales before later state and federal statutes. Case law is created by judges.

explanationWrong.A: Those agencies issue federal regulations, not local ordinances.
explanationWrong.C: Statutes and ordinances must be consistent with constitutions.
explanationWrong.D: Case law is created by judges, not by councils as ordinances.

question: Under the concept of criminal law presented here, against whom is a crime committed?

choices.text: Society as a whole, not just one individual within the society
Only the named plaintiff in a civil complaint
Only the federal government, never a state
Only the contracting parties to an agreement

explanationCorrect: The six types are statutory, case, civil, criminal, substantive, and procedural law. Anecdotal law is not a type of law.

explanationWrong.A: Statutory law is one of the six listed types.
explanationWrong.C: Substantive law is one of the six listed types.
explanationWrong.D: Procedural law is one of the six listed types.

question: Which reference is cited among the chapter’s additional resources for definitions of legal terms?

choices.text: Goodman and Gilman’s The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 12th ed.
Remington: The Science and Practice of Pharmacy, 22nd ed.
Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 19th ed.
Garner BA, ed. Black’s Law Dictionary. 10th ed.

sourceQuote: Garner BA, ed. Black’s Law Dictionary. 10th ed.
explanationCorrect: The additional resources include Garner BA, ed., Black’s Law Dictionary, 10th edition (Thomson Reuters, 2014).

explanationWrong.A: Goodman and Gilman is not listed in this resource section.
explanationWrong.B: Remington is not listed in this resource section.
explanationWrong.C: Harrison’s is not listed in this resource section.

question: In statistics as defined in this chapter, what is a population?

choices.text: Any convenience subset chosen by the investigator
Only the patients who complete a trial protocol
All entities that one is interested in at a given time
The four measures of a frequency distribution

sourceQuote: a population includes all entities that one is interested in
explanationCorrect: In statistics, a population includes all entities that one is interested in at a given time. A sample is a collection of entities that are part of a population.

explanationWrong.A: A convenience subset is a sample, not the population as defined here.
explanationWrong.B: Completers are a subset (sample), not the full population of interest.
explanationWrong.D: Frequency, cumulative frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative relative frequency are measures in a frequency distribution, not the definition of a population.

question: Which pair of frequencies is listed on the study-guide checklist specifically under chi-square tests?

choices.text: Bayesian prior and posterior frequencies
Observed and expected frequencies
Incidence and prevalence frequencies
Sensitivity and specificity frequencies

sourceQuote: evaluation of the regression equation, correlation model Chi-square tests: observed and expected frequencies
explanationCorrect: The study-guide checklist lists chi-square tests as covering observed and expected frequencies.

explanationWrong.A: Bayesian priors and posteriors are not listed under chi-square tests.
explanationWrong.C: Incidence and prevalence are not the chi-square frequencies named here.
explanationWrong.D: Sensitivity and specificity appear under evaluation of screening tests, not chi-square tests.

question: How can data used in statistical analysis arise, according to this chapter?

choices.text: Only from randomized controlled trials
Only from qualitative interviews, never numbers
Only when the entire population is measured
As numbers resulting from measuring or counting

sourceQuote: These numbers can be the result of measuring (e.g., height, weight, blood pressure) or counting
explanationCorrect: In statistics, data can be defined as numbers. These numbers can be the result of measuring (e.g., height, weight, blood pressure) or counting (e.g., the number of patients discharged from a hospital on a given day).

explanationWrong.A: Data are not restricted to randomized trials; they are numbers from measuring or counting.
explanationWrong.B: Data are defined as numbers, not as non-numeric interviews.
explanationWrong.C: The chapter notes that conclusions are drawn from limited amounts of data, not only complete populations.

question: Which feature characterizes a discrete random variable?

choices.text: It can assume any value within an interval between two of its values
It is characterized by interruptions or gaps in its values
Its attributes, not amounts, are measured, as with sex
Its future values can be exactly predicted in advance

sourceQuote: A discrete random variable is characterized by interruptions or gaps
explanationCorrect: A discrete random variable is characterized by interruptions or gaps in its values; values are absent between particular values. An example is the number of admissions to a hospital.

explanationWrong.A: Assuming any value within an interval describes a continuous variable, not a discrete random variable.
explanationWrong.C: Measuring attributes such as sex describes a qualitative variable.
explanationWrong.D: A random variable’s values cannot be exactly predicted in advance.

question: What defines a simple random sample?

choices.text: A sample in which every possible sample of the same size has the same chance of being drawn
Any consecutive series of clinic arrivals
The entire population of interest
A grouping of observations into 6 to 15 overlapping class intervals

sourceQuote: every possible sample of the same size has the same chance
explanationCorrect: A simple random sample is selected from a population such that every possible sample of the same size has the same chance of being drawn.

explanationWrong.B: Consecutive clinic arrivals are not the definition of simple random sampling.
explanationWrong.C: The entire population is not a sample.
explanationWrong.D: Class intervals should be contiguous and nonoverlapping; overlapping intervals are incorrect, and that rule is about grouping data, not simple random sampling.

question: When a data set contains an even number of ordered values, how is the median determined?

choices.text: It is the most frequent observation only
It cannot be calculated if any two values differ
It is the average of the two middle values in the ordered array
It is always equal to the arithmetic mean

sourceQuote: When an even number of values exists, the median is the average
explanationCorrect: When an even number of values exists, the median is the average of the two middle values in the ordered array. When the number of values is odd, the median is the middle value.

explanationWrong.A: The most frequent observation is the mode, not the even-n median rule.
explanationWrong.B: The median is still the average of the two middle ordered values.
explanationWrong.D: Mean and median are different measures and are not described as always equal.

question: Why can the coefficient of variation be used to compare dispersion of variables measured in different units?

choices.text: It equals the square of the variance and retains those units
It is independent of the unit of measurement because the mean and standard deviation units cancel
